I was torn over which frame to select – there are some lovely ones of him sprinting across the turf, flanked by Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon – but this one of him being embraced by Bellingham serves as a perfect reminder of their twin heroics at the tournament. It’s clean, nicely balanced and full of bromance.

21

Gómez goes berserk

View image in fullscreen Gustavo Gómez of Paraguay looks delighted after José Canale scored the winning penalty in a shootout against Germany in Boston. Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty Images

The guaranteed agony and ecstasy of penalty shootouts always makes for brilliant images. This year, Gustavo Gómez of Paraguay takes the crown for the wildest reaction. After beating Germany during sudden death, Gómez, who scored his own spot-kick, surged across the pitch like a heron taking flight, almost vaulting his teammates José Canale and Orlando Gill as he went to embrace them. He then careered through the photographers behind the goal in pursuit of a mobile phone so that he could document the moment himself.

22

Living statue

View image in fullscreen Michel Nkuka Mboladinga, also known as Lumumba Vea, holds firm in the stands during their match against Colombia. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters

Michel Nkuka Mboladinga, also known as Lumumba Vea, is dubbed a “living statue” because he doesn’t move during games. Instead, the DRC fan poses on a plinth for the entire match, raising his right arm to mimic the statue of Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the First Congolese Republic, which stands in Kinshasa. Why anyone would go to a football match and not respond to the on-pitch action is beyond me, but Mboladinga insists it’s his patriotic duty.

23

Senegal swan dive

View image in fullscreen Youri Tielemans heads in Belgium’s second goal against Senegal at Seattle Stadium. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/Fifa/Getty Images

Youri Tielemans scored twice in Belgium’s stunning comeback against Senegal in the last 32. This 89th-minute header might have been a little trickier to control had the defender Moussa Niakhaté competed for the ball instead of diving theatrically to the ground at the first sign of contact. The virtue of modern cameras, many of which shoot 30 frames per second, is that the full sequence of this goal was captured, and we could choose the exact frame when Tielemans’s head connects with the ball.

24

Comeback king

View image in fullscreen Sasa Kalajdzic after scoring Austria’s third goal during a thrilling game against Algeria at Kansas City Stadium. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty Images

Sasa Kalajdzic overcame three anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the years and months prior to the 2026 World Cup, but the Austrian enjoyed a moment to savour when he netted a 96th-minute equaliser against Algeria to keep his side in the tournament. The game ignited accusations of fixing, because a 3-3 draw ensured both sides went through, but a finale like that – and celebrations like this – cannot be scripted.

25

View image in fullscreen Connor Metcalfe of Australia shows the referee his bloodied forehead against Paraguay at San Francisco Bay Area Stadium. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

Australia’s Connor Metcalfe needed three stitches in his eyebrow after being clipped by a stray boot from Andrés Cubas during the Socceroos’ group match with Paraguay. Maybe it’s the slumped shoulders or the shirt pulled up around his neckline, but he looks like a forlorn child who needs a parent to clean him up.

26

Big Dan Burn

View image in fullscreen England’s Dan Burn blocks a bicycle kick from Raúl Jiménez during the last-16 match in Mexico City. Photograph: Jam Media/Getty Images

You could say this is just another “two men and a ball” photograph (an expression the Guardian’s photographer, Tom Jenkins, uses to describe generic images of sporting action). But I particularly like this one because of the contrast of sporting prowess – the acrobat versus the brick wall – and for the misshapen ball which appears ready to pop. Dan Burn has become a cult figure for England, in the mould of Peter Crouch. Many supporters call the 6ft 7in defender Big Dan Burn, but Bellingham apparently calls him Burninho. There’s no way Raúl Jiménez, the Mexico striker, was ever getting the ball past him.

27

Emotional Messi

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Lionel Messi after their 3-2 victory over Egypt at Atlanta Stadium. Photograph: Patrick Smith/Fifa/Getty Images

Let’s be honest, Lionel Messi is not very good at penalties. He’s missed four of eight in World Cup matches and 34 of 151 in his career, including shootouts. A botched effort against Egypt, in a match which the African side went on to lead 2-0, could have been a pitiful ending to his gilded international career. Instead, Messi scored the equaliser and drove his team to a remarkable 3-2 win in normal time. This picture, taken after the match, speaks to the weight he carries on his shoulders. Is it relief or guilt? Either way, he looks tortured by expectation.

28

Crowd scene

View image in fullscreen Canada fans take in their game against Bosnia and Herzegovina at Toronto Stadium. Photograph: Joosep Martinson/Fifa/Getty Images

The composition of this photograph is simple but beautiful. The intersecting diagonals, the contrast between light and shade, and the depth within the scene … it makes for rich viewing.

29

Koné’s injury pain

View image in fullscreen Canada’s Ismaël Koné on the ground after sustaining a broken leg against Qatar. Photograph: Lee Smith/Reuters

Ismaël Koné’s eyes say it all. The Canada midfielder had just broken the tibia and fibula bones in his lower left leg after a challenge by Qatar’s midfielder Assim Madibo, who would receive a red card and a five-match ban. As a photo editor, when incidents like this occur you have to weigh up decency and news value before publishing (I still feel traumatised by the uncensored images I saw of Eduardo’s broken leg in 2008). I think this image conveys the severity of the incident without being unduly graphic. Koné left the pitch on a stretcher but waved to fans as he exited.

30

Cubarsi’s cartwheel

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Enzo Fernández fouls Spain’s Pau Cubarsi and is later shown a second yellow card leading to a red. Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Fifa/Getty Images

I’d typically include a celebration photograph from the World Cup final among my favourites from a tournament, but this ‘tackle’ by Enzo Fernández was so bad – and the image of Pau Cubarsi flying through the air so striking – that I couldn’t look beyond it when reviewing the match. Cubarsi looks like he’s falling from space. An absolutely dreadful final sparked into life at this defining moment. Cubarsi rose from the turf to claim the title of ‘best young player’ of the tournament and, more importantly, a World Cup winner’s medal.

Sports.title: Kane says Tuchel will ‘learn a lot’ from England pressures after exit to Argentina
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has backed Thomas Tuchel to learn from England’s World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina and believes they must use the forthcoming Nations League campaign to gain experience of playing against the top teams.

Kane was an unused substitute as England sealed third place with an entertaining 6-4 victory against France on Saturday – their best finish at a World Cup on foreign soil. Tuchel, who signed a contract extension before the tournament, has been criticised heavily for his tactics against Argentina when he opted to switch to a back five to try to defend a 1-0 lead.

Kane admitted England had fallen short against Lionel Scaloni’s side but described the environment Tuchel has created since succeeding Gareth Southgate in 2025 as “the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness”.

The captain said: “I know there are a lot of questions after the other night. We have to process it as players. I’m sure the manager will. It’s his first major tournament. He’ll learn a lot from the players, the situations, the pressures, the travel.

“There are also a lot of things as players we can learn from the other night. For now it’s just trying to process everything. We had a lot of good things, a lot of tough situations we overcame. The group is incredible, the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness. The boss was a big part of creating that as well.

“Fans are going to be angry and we understand it. It’s a major tournament and that’s why you dream so big. When it doesn’t go your way you have to take the criticism. We’re all willing to do that, to dare to reach the biggest goal of all. We know over the next two years until we’re facing that situation again there is always going to be a question mark. It’s something we have to take and use as motivation.”

England missed out on facing regular top-class opposition in the buildup to the World Cup after being relegated from the top Nations League group in 2022 under Southgate. They were promoted in 2024 and will face Spain, Croatia and Czechia, starting with a rematch of the Euro 2024 final against Luis de la Fuente’s side on 26 September at Wembley. After beating France – albeit in a largely meaningless game – Kane thinks England must take the competition seriously if they are to thrive in tournaments.

View image in fullscreen Defeat to an established opponent was a familiar feeling for England. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

“The last 30 minutes of Argentina is not the team we want to be,” he said. “We spent a lot of time over the last two years talking about that situation, to attack those moments. The bottom line is we lost anyway. It’s easy to go away and talk about it. We need to get better at actually being in those situations. We can train, play the qualifiers … I think the Nations League will be big for us, against Spain and Croatia, big teams.

“Getting used to those big environments and finding our best form against those teams, like we did against France, albeit not in the most competitive match. We have to learn, improve. The coach will have improved from these learnings. I can talk as much as I want but ultimately it’s about showing it next time we’re in that situation.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Kane has been on the losing side in two World Cup semi-finals and two European Championship finals and he believes Tuchel is the man to help England to make the final step.

“The enthusiasm he has, the emotion he brings, the tactical experience he has … it doesn’t mean you’re going to get it right every time. We want to get it right on the biggest occasions and he expects that from himself as well. He’s a fantastic coach. He not only gave the players belief but he gave the country belief that it was our year. That is why it hurts even more than other years because everyone believed we were going all the way.

“Everyone has to process it. He has to process it himself. We’re still in that grieving stage, the emotional stage, and we’ll be in that for the next few weeks. It won’t be until the next camp where you think about what the future holds and what the next target is. We’ll have conversations as captain and manager and with other teammates and staff, to see where we can be better.”

Sports.title: England 2026 World Cup squad: player-by-player ratings
Sports.content:
Goalkeepers

Jordan Pickford Could he have done better with Enzo Fernández’s equaliser for Argentina? Jude Bellingham certainly thought so. But the man who has made more World Cup finals appearances than any other Englishman made some crucial saves, including a brilliant stop from Nicolas González in the semi-final. 7

Dean Henderson Had to wait until the third-place playoff for some action and ended up conceding four goals despite a strong performance. Will hope to challenge Pickford over next two years. 7

Defenders

Djed Spence Emerged as an unlikely cult hero thanks to some wholehearted performances. He will always be remembered for snubbing Thomas Partey’s handshake and his tackle on Giuliano Simeone against Argentina. 8

Marc Guéhi Somehow wasn’t Thomas Tuchel’s first-choice initially, although that was rectified after the Croatia game. England’s most consistent and reliable defender – the way he handled Erling Haaland was a masterclass. 8

John Stones Arrived painfully short of match fitness and it showed in the opening game against Croatia. Much improved when called upon in the quarter- and semi-finals. A huge asset when he plays. 7

Ezri Konsa A few shaky moments during the group stage but recovered well and filled in capably at right-back when needed. At 28, young enough to be there again in four years. 7

View image in fullscreen Dan Burn’s headed block from this Raúl Jiménez bicycle kick cleared the halfway line. Photograph: Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images

Dan Burn Showed his limitations against Argentina. But he will always have those two epic appearances off the bench against Mexico and Norway. No one will forget the clearing headers so powerful they ended up in the opposition’s half. 7

Nico O’Reilly Had his strongest game against Norway in the quarter-final when he was at his marauding best. Will be disappointed not to have scored and to have been on the pitch as a substitute when Argentina instigated their semi-final comeback. 6

Reece James Such a good player when fit, which is sadly far too rare. Missed most of the tournament owing to a hamstring injury and England suffered when he went off against Argentina. 6

Trevoh Chalobah The Chelsea player was a surprise choice to replace Tino Livramento, who pulled out injured at the last minute. Managed only six minutes against France in the end. 6

Jarell Quansah Brought in to solve the right-back conundrum against Panama, he was doing well until the rush of blood against Mexico and subsequent red card. Recalled for the France game and had to be replaced. 5

Midfielders

Jude Bellingham Showed his supreme quality when it mattered and could not be more committed to his country’s cause, even if his rocky relationship with Tuchel had to be carefully managed. 9

Elliot Anderson Didn’t allow himself to be distracted by his £116m move to Manchester City and grew as the tournament progressed. Ran his heart out against Norway and Argentina. 8

View image in fullscreen Morgan Rogers (left) crossed for Anthony Gordon to put England ahead against Argentina. Photograph: Julian Finney/FIFA/Getty Images

Morgan Rogers Made the most of his limited minutes in unfamiliar roles. Showed what a good player he is by playing as one of the two central midfielders against Norway before setting up Anthony Gordon from the right wing against Argentina. 8

Declan Rice Clearly affected by the hamstring and back problems that marred the second half of his season with Arsenal, even if his effort – as ever – could not be faulted. Needs a long rest to recharge his batteries but may not get one. 6

Eberechi Eze Could not have the impact he would have wished for in four substitute appearances before starting against France. Did a decent job in central midfield against Panama but was largely on the periphery when given a chance on the left in the quarter-final. 6

Jordan Henderson Spent 12 minutes on the pitch, in a historic appearance against Panama when he became the first England men’s player to appear at seven major international tournaments. But managed to get booked against Mexico as a substitute and break an arm celebrating the win. 5

Forwards

Bukayo Saka Three goals and three assists despite playing through the pain of an achilles injury was a courageous effort from Arsenal’s talisman. It was a huge surprise not to see him come off the bench against Argentina and he showed what England were missing against France. 8

Anthony Gordon A quiet start having been preferred to Rashford before responding magnificently to being dropped. Three assists and a goal against Argentina showed why Barcelona were so keen to sign him. 8

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s two goals against the Democratic Republic of the Congo saved England from an early exit. Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA

Harry Kane Sadly his tournament will be remembered for a largely anonymous display against Argentina rather than rescuing England against the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Will he ever have a better chance to win the World Cup? 8

Marcus Rashford Made a good start to his third World Cup by coming off the bench to score against Croatia, and started against Panama. But wasn’t seen again until England were chasing the game against Argentina in injury time. 6

Ivan Toney Sat on the bench until Lautaro Martínez’s goal in added time of the semi-final. Could not make an impact in the three minutes he was given but did well against France. 6

Ollie Watkins Largely a frustrated spectator despite his heroics in the Euro 2024 semi-final and arriving here in a rich vein of form. A half on the left flank against France and a brief appearance against Panama were scant reward. 6

Noni Madueke Some promising moments but lacked end product in his four starts and had slipped down the pecking order by the semi-final. Needs to be much more clinical at this level. 5

Did not play: James Trafford and Kobbie Mainoo

Sports.title: Trump is right – USA deserves next World Cup after putting on biggest and best tournament ever
Sports.content:
The USA knocked the 2026 World Cup out of the park and could be a host country for the 2038 tournament, which is the next one up for grabs. Donald Trump wants a new World Cup 'immediately.'

Trump is right – USA deserves next World Cup after putting on biggest and best tournament ever

England continues to show no interest in hosting the World Cup, despite being one of the greatest football countries in the world.

The United States of America just successfully pulled off the biggest sports tournament in history – and President Donald Trump already wants another USA World Cup.



7 The USA could be next in line to host the World Cup Credit: getty

"Based on the numbers, we will be requesting it again immediately,” Trump told FOX Sports.

Of course, Mexico and Canada also deserve credit for co-hosting a 2026 World Cup that set an all-time attendance record with 6,810,966 fans packing stadiums from Seattle and Miami to Monterrey and Toronto.

But the massive 104-team, six-week tourney was heavily American from the start, and that point was hammered during Sunday’s final as a Super Bowl-like halftime show was inserted into the middle of Spain’s 1-0 victory over Argentina.



“The American dream, Mr. President, came to reality," said FIFA President Gianni Infantino, while standing next to Trump. "We united the world."

Football is always the winner

There were several major controversies, and Infantino should never again allow FIFA to overturn a red-card suspension after a friendly phone call from a host nation.



But I’ll go back to what I said early in Group Stage play: You’d have to be a serious hater to still be hating on the 2026 World Cup.

The matches were fantastic from Mexico vs South Africa on June 11 to Spain making a bitter Argentina cry on Sunday at New York New Jersey Stadium.



Even that NFL venue passed its World Cup test, overcoming initial concerns about a dry playing surface to produce more than 120 minutes of sharp international football that temporarily turned soccer into America’s biggest sport this summer.

"FIFA was incredible," Trump said. "There has never been anything like it in terms of an event, let alone soccer or football. ...We're very proud of our country. We're very proud of the job that was done by everybody."

It will take years to process the financial impact of a tournament that could allow FIFA to make $9 billion on ticket sales and another $1bn in TV rights, with a projected $13bn in total revenue.

7 Donald Trump wants America to 'immediately' host another global tournament Credit: getty



7 Lionel Messi showed the passion of the World Cup Credit: Getty

But facts are facts, and all of the predictions of disaster or embarrassment that preceded the 2026 World Cup were answered with stadiums filled to almost 100 percent capacity and a reassuring lack of off-the-pitch problems.

“We have to do this again, and we have to do it while I’m around,” Trump said. “You hear that, Gianni?”

The next World Cup in 2030 will primarily bounce between Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay also hosting matches as the World Cup celebrates its 100th birthday.



The 2034 World Cup has already been awarded to Saudi Arabia.

Then we get to 2038, and that’s where it immediately gets interesting for the USA.

Trump is 80-years-old, so simple math has the current US President at 92 when the next potential American World Cup rolls around.

7 Cape Verde helped make the 2026 World Cup a two-month success Credit: Getty

7 England is focused on winning the 2028 Euros on home soil Credit: Getty



No matter what you think about Trump or the huge country that he represents, securing the hosting rights to two World Cups would give Trump a big-picture sporting legacy unmatched by all past US presidents.

Nothing is bigger than the World Cup, and the World Cup keeps getting bigger -- an expansion to 64 teams could be on the agenda.

The USA will also host the Summer Olympics in 2028 in Los Angeles.

Acting like the United States doesn’t ‘deserve’ another World Cup is laughable, especially when you remember that Qatar was shadowed by human rights questions before the 2022 World Cup – which was praised upon completion – and the 2018 tournament was held in Russia.

Yes, ticket prices were too high this summer.

But that’s much more of a FIFA issue than a USA problem.

By the end of the biggest sports tourney in the history of planet Earth, there was far more negativity surrounding Argentina’s ‘dirty’ play than the United States as a host notion.



From NFL stadiums and new grass playing surfaces to fan safety and a worldwide buzz, the USA knocked the 2026 World Cup out of the park.

7 Ticket prices were sky high but thousands of fans still turned out to support their country Credit: AFP

7 Even the halftime show wasn't that bad Credit: Getty

The real question right now is what we're all going to do now that this wonderful, crazy and must-watch World Cup is finally over?



I'll be catching up on lost sleep, shedding a few extra beer pounds and trying to remember who's supposed to win the Super Bowl next February.

England should be raising its hand and yelling ‘Next!’ after watching Los Angeles, Kansas City, Miami, Boston and Philadelphia be proudly taken over by football fans from across the globe.

Europe already has dibs on 2030, and the thought of bouncing between Spain and Portugal for potential Round of 16 matches is already making me drool.

It’s impossible to host a perfect World Cup, especially in our social media age where negativity so often reigns supreme.



But the USA wanted the World Cup back on home soil after a 32-year drought, and the United States made the initial success of 1994 look like the foundation of a skyscraper in midtown Manhattan.

The 2026 World Cup brought out the best in the United States of America, from California to New York, while a country founded on freedom and independence celebrated its 250th anniversary on the world’s stage.

The haters can hate.

But there’s really nowhere better in the world to host the World Cup than the USA, and 2038 isn’t that far away.

Sports.title: Where is World Cup 2030? Host countries, stadiums and final location for next showpiece event
Sports.content:
Where is World Cup 2030? Host countries, stadiums and final location for next showpiece event

Preparations are already underway to celebrate the World Cup's 100th anniversary across three continents in 2030.

FIFA announced in 2023 that Spain, Portugal and Morocco will co-host the 2030 men's football World Cup.



10 Majority of the tournament will be held in Spain, Morocco and Portugal Credit: Getty

However, the opening three matches of the tournament will take place in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.

This summer's event has been a tester for the tournament to be spread across multiple hosts, with Canada, America and Mexico all putting on games in North America.

The only other time it has happened was in 2002 with South Korea and Japan.



Four South American nations initially submitted a joint bid early in 2023 but FIFA confirmed a few months later that they were only considering Morocco, Portugal and Spain.

Spain will host the next World Cup as reigning champions following their win over Argentina in New York.



Why are the first games being played in South America?

The 2030 World Cup will be held from Saturday, June 8 to Sunday, July 21 and will include 48 teams at 21 venues.

It has been 100 years since the first World Cup and FIFA is commemorating the anniversary.



The first ever tournament was hosted in Uruguay in 1930 with the nation winning the Jules Rimet as the first time winners.

Argentina was the beaten finalists in the competition while Paraguay is where CONMEBOL, the South American football confederation is based.

10 Fans have suggested that Infantino and FIFA included the South American countries in this edition in order to give the World Cup 2034 to Saudi Arabia Credit: AFP

It is the oldest confederation in the world and the only existing one at the inaugural tournament.



At the announcement, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said: "In today’s divided world, where it seems that nobody can agree any more on anything, to be able to agree on something like that is definitely an incredible message of unity and positivity.

"And we need these messages today.

"The FIFA World Cup is unique, and it is a unique catalyst as well for positive social change and unity because these tournaments, 2030, the celebration, 2034.

"They are tournaments to unite, not to divide. They are tournaments, of course, to discuss, to debate and to act.

"But most importantly, today, today is a day of unity and a day of celebration.



"Seven countries have won their World Cup today. Congratulations to Uruguay, Argentina, Paraguay, Morocco, Portugal, Spain and Saudi Arabia.

10 Lionel Messi and Argentina lifted the World Cup Trophy the last time out Credit: GETTY

"This is your day. So you should celebrate and we, we celebrate, of course, with you.

"And you, the 211 FIFA Member Associations that I can see on a giant screen in front of me, you are uniting the world.



"You are uniting the world truly, through football, because, of course, football unites the world."

Which stadiums are hosting the World Cup in 2030?

The opening three games are being staged in South America.

The Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, Argentina, which has a capacity of 100,000 people, will host as will the Montevideo in Uruguay and the Estadio Osvaldo Dominguez Dibb which will be brand new in Paraguay.

When the tournament moves to the northern hemisphere, there will be 18 stadiums between the three countries, with Spain staging the most with nine.

Madrid is home to Atletico Madrid and Real Madrid's stadiums, the iconic Bernabeu and Metropolitano Stadium.



Stadiums will span to the Canary Islands, with Las Palmas Estadio Gran Canaria also another option.

10 The Nou Camp will eventually host 105,000 people after construction Credit: AFP

10 Benfica's home has the highest capacity out of all of Portugal's stadiums, hosting 80,000 after construction. Credit: Getty

10 The 115,000 seater stadium, Hassan II Stadium, is currently under contruction and set to open in 2028 - it will become Morocco's men's team new home Credit: AFP



World Cup 2030 stadiums Morocco Adrar Stadium, Agadir - Capacity: 46,000

Hassan II Stadium, Casablanca - Capacity: 115,000

Fez Stadium, Fez - Capacity: 55,800

Marrakesh Stadium, Marrakesh - Capacity: 45,860

Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Rabat - Capacity: 69,500

Tangier Grand Stadium, Tangier - Capacity: 75,500 Portugal Estadio da Luz, Lisbon - Capacity: 80,000

Estadio Jose Alvalade, Lisbon - Capacity: 52,095

Estadio do Dragao, Porto - Capacity: 50,033 Spain Camp Nou, Barcelona - Capacity: 105,000

RCDE Stadium, Barcelona - Capacity: 40,500

San Mames, Bilbao - Capacity: 53,331

Estadio Gran Canaria, Las Palmas - Capacity: 44,500

Bernabeu, Madrid - Capacity: 83,186

Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid - Capacity: 70,692

Anoeta Stadium, San Sebastian - Capacity: 42,300

Estadio de La Cartuja, Seville - Capacity: 70,000

Nueva Romareda, Zaragoza - Capacity: 43,110

Barcelona's newly renovated Camp Nou is also an option which seats 105,000 people.

In comparison, Portugal have two host cities with Lisbon and Porto.

Sporting Lisbon, Benfica and Porto's grounds will all be used throughout the tournament.

In the proposal, Morocco listed six stadiums that included Hassan II Stadium which is currently under construction and will hold 115,000 people - the biggest stadium in the tournament and eventually the world.

How will the tournament work?

The format replicates 2026 and will feature 48 teams again, split up into 12 groups of four and the top two, plus the eight best third-placed teams all progress to the knockout stages.



The expansion that happened for this year's tournament means 104 matches will be played at the World Cup.

10 Marketing has already began despite the tournament being four years away

FIFA have said they will take into consideration that the teams playing in the opening games in South America will need a different match schedule in order to travel, rest and prepare.

However, there has been controversies surrounding the Centenary Matches with many concerned about the environmental impact caused by the high amounts of pollution due to construction and air travel.



The football organisation defended themselves and said the majority of the tournament is spent in neighbouring countries.

What will the weather be like?

In total, 14 of the 16 host cities are expected to be subject to extreme heat conditions.

FIFA has suggested scheduling kick-off times to evenings rather than throughout the day due to the weather.

About the weather at the event, Infantino said: "We are discussing all the time, and I think it's not just about one World Cup - I think it's a general reflection.



"Even to play in some European countries in July, it's very, very hot. So maybe we have to think.

"There are ways we can optimise the calendar. But we are discussing it and we will see when we come to some conclusion.

"We just have to have an open mind."

10 Heat exhaustion could affect the athletes and the fans Credit: Getty

10 Kick-off times ranged across 11 hours in a day, from 1pm to 10pm



10 Curacao are set to make history at the World Cup this summer as the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament Credit: AFP

Who has qualified for the 2030 World Cup

Six countries have automatically qualified already with the six home nations all gaining a place - Morocco, Spain, Portugal, Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.

The other places are earned through qualifier games in each continental confederation.

Each continent receives a different amount of places with UEFA (Europe) receiving the most with 16.



After that, it is the Confederation of African football with the second most at nine, followed by the Asian Football Confederation with eight.

Concacaf and Conmebol both have six places, while the Oceania Football Confederation only have one place.

The final two spots will be decided through a play-off tournament featuring six teams.

Sports.title: When is Euro 2028? Location, stadiums and dates as tournament breaks records across multiple countries
Sports.content:
When is Euro 2028? Location, stadiums and dates as tournament breaks records across multiple countries

The 2028 UEFA European Championship will be spread across four different nations for the first time as Spain aim to defend their title.

With the World Cup now over, the next Euros is just two years away.

4 Spain triumphed at Euro 2024 by winning every game

The tournament will be returning back to a European time slot in a historic multi-nation host format.

While the previous Euros took place solely in Germany, the 2028 edition will be hosted jointly by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

World champions Spain will be hoping to defend their title after beating England 2-1 in the 2024 final in Berlin and make it three major titles in a row.

With the qualifying draw approaching in December 2026, here is everything you need to know about Euro 2028.

Euro 2028: Dates

The championship will get underway on Friday, June 9, 2028 with the final taking place Sunday, July 9, 2028.

UEFA have created a schedule around 'fan fairness' aiming to limit travel between matches for supporters and squads.

The competition will be held across 31 days of matches with three primary kick-off times at 2pm, 5pm and 8pm.

The tournament will feature a total of 51 matches.

4 Both semi-finals and the final will be held at Wembley Credit: GETTY

Euro 2028: Location

Following a similar spectacle to the World Cup, this edition of the Euros will be hosted by five different football associations across four countries - England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Northern Ireland was originally meant to be part of the host group, but the redevelopment delays at Casement Park meant it was not included in the final list.

Matches will be staged across nine stadiums in eight host cities and due to unusual high amount of host nations, this means none are guaranteed automatic qualification at this stage.

All must compete in the qualifying group stages.

The stadium list features iconic grounds and brand-new facilities, including Everton's new waterfront home and the renovated Villa Park.

Wembley Stadium is confirmed to host eight fixtures, including both semi-finals and the final on July 9.

The opening match will take place at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.

Euro 2028: Stadiums Wembley Stadium, London - Capacity: 90,000

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, London - Capacity: 62,850

Etihad Stadium, Manchester - Capacity: 61,470

Hill Dickinson Stadium, Liverpool - Capacity: 52, 769

St James' Park, Newcastle - Capacity: 52,264

Villa Park, Birmingham - Capacity: 50,000

Hampden Park, Glasgow - Capacity: 51,866

Principality Stadium, Cardiff - Capacity: 73,931

Republic of Ireland, Dublin - Capacity: 51,711

4 Ireland have only participated in three European competitions Credit: Getty

Have the UK and Ireland hosted before?

While the collaboration for 2028 is a historic first, some of the home nations are not strangers to hosting a major tournament.

England is the only host in the group to have previously staged a full European Championship on its own.

Euro 96 became a cultural milestone for the country, with the event ending in heartbreak for the hosts in a semi-final penalty shootout against Germany.

Additionally, England hosted the Women's Euros in 2022, a record-breaking tournament where the Lionesses lifted the trophy at Wembley in front of 87,000 fans.

During Euro 2020, which was held in 2021 due to the pandemic, there were 11 nations hosting the action across the continent.

Eight games were featured at Wembley including both semi-finals and the final where Italy defeated England on penalties.

In addition, Hampden Park hosted four matches in Scotland.

For Wales and Ireland, Euro 2028 will mark the first time they will host a major international tournament.

While the Principality Stadium in Cardiff has hosted Champions League finals and FA Cup finals, 2028 will be its debut on the European Championship stage.

4 All home nations will have to compete in qualifiers

Euro 2028: Schedule

Group stages: June 9 / 21

Round of 16: June 24 / 27

Quarter finals: June 30 / July 1

Semi-finals: July 4 / 5

Final: Sunday, July 9 at Wembley Stadium, London

Euro 2028: Qualifying format

Due to UEFA regulations, only two hosts can take up guaranteed automatic qualification.

The organisation decided that all four countries will enter qualifying, with two automatic spots reserved as a 'safety net' for nations that fail to qualify traditionally.

If more than two host teams fail to qualify, the spots will be decided based on qualifying ranking.

54 nations will be divided into 12 qualifying groups, with the 12 group winners and eight best runners-up will all qualify directly.

The remaining spots, depending on the host performances, will be decided via play-offs in March 2028.

Sports.title: Do England need to qualify for Euro 2028? Thomas Tuchel’s Three Lions host huge tournament
Sports.content:
Do England need to qualify for Euro 2028? Thomas Tuchel’s Three Lions host huge tournament

England's World Cup dreams may be over for another four years but they can start dreaming of European glory.

An agonising 2-1 defeat to Argentina in the semi-final saw the Three Lions' hopes of winning for the first time since 1966 ended.



3 England exited the World Cup in a 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina Credit: Getty

Thomas Tuchel's side did provide some joy with a thrilling 6-4 win over France in the third place play off but now attentions will turn to what is next.

With the World Cup officially done, it should be an automatic reminder that the next international competition is in two years' time.

The next European Championship will feature a multi-nation host format and the tournament will be held from June 9, 2028 to July 9, 2028.



While the previous Euros took place solely in Germany, the 2028 edition will be co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland.

The action will be held across 31 days with three primary kick-off times at 2pm, 5pm and 8pm, and will have feature a total of 51 matches.



UEFA have designed the schedule around 'fan fairness', aiming to limit travel between matches for supporters and squads.

Matches will be staged across nine venues in eight host cities, including Wembley Stadium, Everton's new waterfront home, and a newly regenerated Villa Park.



England is the only host nation to have previously staged a full European Championship on their own in 1996, with the tournament becoming a cultural milestone for the country.

That campaign ended in heartbreak for the Three Lions as they went out in a semi-final penalty shootout against Germany.

Additionally, England have also hosted the Women's Euros in 2022, where the Lionesses eventually lifted the trophy at Wembley in front of 87,000 fans.

3 Wales missed out on Euro 2024 after losing on penalties to Poland at the Cardiff City Stadium Credit: Getty



Euro 2028 stadiums Wembley Stadium, London - Capacity: 90,000

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, London - Capacity: 62,850

Etihad Stadium, Manchester - Capacity: 61,470

Hill Dickinson Stadium, Liverpool - Capacity: 52, 769

St James' Park, Newcastle - Capacity: 52,264

Villa Park, Birmingham - Capacity: 50,000

Hampden Park, Glasgow - Capacity: 51,866

Principality Stadium, Cardiff - Capacity: 73,931

Aviva Stadium, Dublin - Capacity: 51,711

Scotland previously hosted four matches at Hampden Park during Euro 2020, when 11 nations shared hosting duties across the continent.

For Wales and Ireland, this will mark their first time hosting a major international tournament.

Northern Ireland will not be a host after Belfast's Casement Park was removed as an option.

Do host nations need to qualify?

Due to tournament regulations, only two host nations are able to receive automatic qualification.



UEFA has decided that all four co-hosts will enter the traditional qualifying route, with two automatic spots reserved as a 'safety net' for nations that fail to qualify the 'normal way'.

If more than two nations don't qualify, the spots will be decided based on their overall qualifying ranking.

In total, 54 nations will be divided into 12 qualifying groups, with the group winners and eight best runners-up will all qualify directly.

The remaining spots, depending on the host performances, will be decided via play-offs in March 2028.



The draw which selects the qualifying groups will be held in December 2026.

3 London will be a host city with two stadiums, including Wembley and Tottenham Hotspurs Credit: Getty

Who will be England manager?

Thomas Tuchel has taken plenty of heat for his tactical decisions in the 2-1 defeat to Argentina in the World Cup semi-final.

This has led to calls for him to either quit or be fired from the role.



talkSPORT understands, however, that the FA have no plans to relieve Tuchel of his duties.

Shortly before the World Cup, Tuchel signed a contract extension until the end of Euro 2028.

Euro 2028 schedule

There will be 51 matches involving 24 teams.

It has already been confirmed that should England qualify, they will be playing their opening match at Manchester City Stadium, followed by two games at Wembley Stadium.

The Republic of Ireland, Scotland and Wales would play their group fixtures in Dublin, Glasgow and Cardiff respectively.



The opening games will be held at the Principality Stadium, while semi-finals and the final will be at Wembley in London.

Host cities will stage a minimum of two different groups to provide local fans with a variety of teams to watch in their region.

Michael Owen said: "UEFA Euro 2028 will be an incredible moment for players and fans.

"It will be a chance to celebrate our shared love of the game on home soil in brilliant stadiums across passionate football cities."

Sports.title: What Nicolas Otamendi said to Rodri during heated altercation after World Cup final
Sports.content:
What Nicolas Otamendi said to Rodri during heated altercation after World Cup final

Former Manchester City teammates Rodri and Nicolas Otamendi were involved in a heated confrontation after the World Cup final.

Following Spain's 1-0 win over Argentina, there were violent scenes, as midfielder Leandro Paredes began throwing punches.



4 Otamendi was visibly furious with Rodri after the World Cup final Credit: Getty

Rodri was involved in that chaos before he then went on to get into an angry argument with Otamendi on the pitch.

Footage emerged after the final on Sunday of the two ex-Man City stars furiously clashing with each other.

Otamendi appeared to be the aggressor, pointing and shouting at Rodri after being approached by the Spain captain, which left the Golden Ball winner looking completely bemused.



Both players were speaking in Spanish, but the altercation has now been translated to English, with the topic revealed.

And it seems Otamendi took issue with how another of his former friends has been speaking about the World Cup referees.



"Start talking less, idiot," he said when Rodri walked towards him post-match. "You guys spent the whole week crying.

"You spent the whole week crying. You and [Aymeric] Laporte, both of you.



"That's not how it's done. You were crying to the referees all week, my friend."

Rodri looked confused as the rant continued, asking what he meant, while Spain's Mikel Oyarzabal stepped in to break things up.

"Laporte?" Otamendi added. "Didn't you see what he said this week?"

4 Otamendi pointed and shouted at Rodri after being approached by him post-match

4 The ex-teammates' confrontation got heated on the pitch



What did Laporte say to anger Otamendi?

It appeared that Otamendi had been left furious at comments from another ex-Man City teammate, Aymeric Laporte.

Laporte called for the World Cup final referee to 'do his job' to prevent an aggressive approach from Argentina.

La Albiceleste had already been embroiled in controversy at the tournament regarding their treatment from officials.

When asked by Spanish outlet MARCA ahead of the final whether he was concerned about the aggression, Laporte said: "I'm not worried at all about physical play as long as it's part of football.



"If the referee does his job, I have no problem with it. It's true that in recent matches we've seen things that have surprised us, situations that have been allowed to go unpunished.

"Especially with Argentina, which is a team that likes to leave little messages with its challenges.

4 Spain's Laporte had been speaking about the World Cup officials ahead of the final Credit: Getty

"That shouldn't be allowed in football, particularly in tournaments of this magnitude, because it can unsettle you and make you lose your composure."



He added: "It's the referee's job to keep those situations under control so the match doesn't get away from him.

"If one or two players are allowed to do whatever they want, the game will become chaotic. Since the beginning of the tournament, we've been a very fair team in that regard.

"We don't go around kicking opponents or making reckless fouls, and I think that's the approach we have to maintain in this match.

"But, of course, a lot will depend on the officiating."

Spain went on to beat Argentina 1-0 in the World Cup final, with Enzo Fernandez sent off for two yellow cards before extra time.

Sports.title: Tottenham star Cristian Romero appears to snub Donald Trump during World Cup final presentation
Sports.content:
Cristian Romero appeared to avoid shaking Donald Trump's hand when collecting his World Cup runners-up medal.

The Tottenham captain was on the losing side on Sunday, as the defending champions lost 1-0 to Spain after extra time, courtesy of Ferran Torres' 106th-minute winner.

5 Romero joined Lionel Messi and the rest of his heartbroken Argentina teammates after losing to Spain Credit: AFP

La Roja dominated a one-sided game, and had a man advantage following Enzo Fernandez's red card late on in normal time.

Victory for the European nation was their second World Cup triumph, having first tasted glory in the 2010 edition in South Africa.

Meanwhile, Argentina were left heartbroken as they missed their chance to become the first nation in 64 years to repeat as world champions.

Awkward?

After giving up their title, a tearful Lionel Messi led his team onto the podium to collect their runners-up medals.

The medals were presented by FIFA president Gianni Infantino and the three leaders of the host nations - including US president Trump.

While most players shook the hand of Infantino and Trump - who were stood side-by-side - Romero seemed to have other ideas.

After having his silver medal put over his shoulders by Infantino, the 28-year-old walked straight past Trump without acknowledging him.

Romero looked like he was about to snub Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum too after he shook the hand of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, before remembering and turning back.

'Pure chaos merchant'

While it was not clear if Romero had deliberately ignored Trump, footage of the incident quickly began to circulate online.

One user commented: "Romero really dodged President Trump like he wasn’t there."

5 Romero was presented with his runners-up medal by Infantino Credit: ITV

5 But the Argentina defender then walked straight past US president Trump Credit: ITV

With the Spurs man known for having a questionable disciplinary record, another wrote: “Romero is a pure chaos merchant.”

Meanwhile, a third suggested this may not have been a deliberate move from Romero, given he had already received his medal and acknowledged Infantino for it.

They commented: “Hang on, he already had his medal from the other dude and shook his hand. Didn’t look like he intentionally tried to diss Trump?”

Trump did not appear to notice the snub, as he carried on passing the medals over to Infantino to present, and shook hands with the rest of Romero's teammates.

And the president later took centre stage, as he was on hand to present the World Cup trophy to Spain.

At the Club World Cup final last year, Trump made the headlines as he joined Chelsea in their celebrations on the podium.

5 Trump was in shot as Spain lifted the World Cup for the second time in their history Credit: Getty

5 Romero cut a lonely figure as he missed out on back-to-back World Cup wins Credit: Getty

This time, after presenting the trophy to Spain, Trump moved towards the edge of the group for the initial lift, before Infantino appeared to usher him away.

Romero and his Argentina teammates weren't on hand to witness any of this though, as they turned their backs to the trophy lift.

The Tottenham centre-back endured a disappointing afternoon altogether, as he exited the field on 70-minute mark after appearing to suffer an injury.

Argentina put up a fight to defend their World Cup title, but they were ultimately outclassed by Spain.

Lionel Scaloni's side defended doggedly in the 90 minutes of regulation time, before Fernandez was sent off after receiving a second yellow card for a foul on Pau Cubarsi.

But their resolve was broken by Torres in the second-half of extra time, with Argentina only registering their first shot on goal after this, as they tried in vain to find an equaliser late on.

Sports.title: When is the 2030 World Cup? Six teams get automatic qualification immediately after 2026 final as hosts
Sports.content:
When is the 2030 World Cup? Six teams get automatic qualification immediately after 2026 final as hosts

Spain have been crowned champions of the world in New York, and will now look to defend their title on home soil in four years' time.

La Roja were victorious as Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the 106th minute against Argentina.



3 Spain will defend their title in front of the home fans Credit: Getty

The defeat meant no second fairytale for the 39-year-old Lionel Messi, raising the question of whether the icon will feature at the 2030 World Cup?

When is the next World Cup?

The next edition in 2030 will be held from Saturday, June 8 to Sunday, July 21.

FIFA will be celebrating 100 years since the first World Cup, and the event will be spread across six different nations.



While Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-host the tournament, the opening three matches of the tournament will take place in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.

These initial fixtures are being played in South America to commemorate the centenary of the first ever competition, which was hosted and won by Uruguay in 1930.



Argentina were the beaten finalists in the inaugural edition while Paraguay is where CONMEBOL, the South American football confederation is based.

It is the oldest confederation in the world and the only existing one at the first tournament.



The hosts

The opening game will be held at the iconic Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, Argentina, which boasts a capacity of 100,000 people.

A brand new venue in Paraguay called Estadio Osvaldo Dominguez Dibb and the historic Montevideo in Uruguay will also host opening matches.

However, after those three matches, the World Cup will shift entirely to the Northern Hemisphere in 18 stadiums across Spain, Morocco and Portugal.

Spain will be using iconic homes of football, including Real Madrid's Bernabeu and Barcelona's Camp Nou.

It's set to hold 115,000 people and is in the process of becoming the biggest stadium in the world.



Will all six nations automatically qualify?

All six host nations have automatically qualified for the tournament - Morocco, Spain, Portugal, Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.
