World.title: Spain crowned world champions with 1-0 extra-time win over Argentina in the final
World.content:
Spain crowned world champions with 1-0 extra-time win over Argentina in the final

20th Monday, July 2026 - 00:47 UTC Full article

Photo: EPA/EFE/RONALD WITTEK

Spain were crowned world champions for the second time in their history by beating Argentina 1-0 in extra time in the final played on Sunday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The winning goal came in the 106th minute, after a cross from Pedro Porro that Nico Williams headed on and that, according to the match report, Ferran Torres finished to settle a game clearly dominated by the Spanish side.

The run of play reflected Spain's superiority, with 68% possession and twenty shots, eleven of them on target, against Argentina's three attempts, none on goal. The defending champions, who had reached the final hoping to repeat their Qatar 2022 triumph, barely troubled goalkeeper Unai Simón and sat back for much of the match.

The game had two decisive incidents. In the second half, the referee disallowed a Spanish goal for a foul flagged earlier in the move, with the score at 0-0. Near the end of regulation time, Argentina's Enzo Fernández was sent off for a second bookable offense after a hard challenge on Spanish defender Pau Cubarsí, leaving Argentina with ten players for extra time. The South American side finished the match with five bookings and one dismissal.

With this result, Spain claim their second World Cup, sixteen years after the one won in South Africa in 2010, when they beat the Netherlands, also in extra time, through a goal by Andrés Iniesta. The title adds to Euro 2024 and cements the generation led by coach Luis de la Fuente, who called for the achievement to be “valued.” Midfielder Rodri was named the tournament's best player.

“Destiny was written. Every final is difficult, we had Messi in front of us, but we have always relied on ourselves, playing our game,” Ferran Torres said after the match. For Argentina, the defeat dashed their bid to become the first national team to win two consecutive World Cups since Brazil, champions in 1958 and 1962.

The final closed a World Cup hosted by the United States, Mexico, and Canada, whose decisive stages were played on US soil. The tournament was marked, in its closing stretch, by the controversy surrounding Argentina, after its players displayed a banner about the Falklands following the semifinal against England, an episode FIFA is assessing for a possible breach of rules barring political messages. Argentina played the final while awaiting that decision.

World.title: Trump takes center stage at the World Cup final, presenting Spain's trophy and holding it beforehand
World.content:
Trump takes center stage at the World Cup final, presenting Spain's trophy and holding it beforehand

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 23:05 UTC Full article

The episode fits into the close relationship between Trump and Infantino, which has run through much of the tournament

US President Donald Trump was one of the central figures off the pitch at the 2026 World Cup final, co-hosting alongside FIFA President Gianni Infantino the trophy presentation to Spain, champions after beating Argentina 1-0 in extra time at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Trump, who watched the match from the VIP box with his wife, Melania, also held the original trophy before kickoff, in images that circulated widely on social media.

Trump's role in the ceremony marked a change from the tournament's two previous editions. At Russia 2018 and Qatar 2022, Infantino presented the trophy alone. FIFA had announced before the final that the two would do so jointly. The handover by the host country's head of state is, however, a practice with historical precedent at the World Cup: Queen Elizabeth II presented the trophy to England captain Bobby Moore in 1966, and King Juan Carlos I did so with Italy's Dino Zoff in 1982.

Trump entregando la Copa del Mundial de Futbol del 2026 a la selección española. pic.twitter.com/u0IoU3LK6a — Orlando Avendaño (@OrlvndoA) July 19, 2026

Before the match, the trophy was brought up to the presidential box, where Trump took it and patted it before returning it to the area set aside for the ceremony. The scene drew attention for taking place outside the official on-field act, in which the cup is usually kept under guard until its presentation to the champions. While players from both teams walked past the trophy without touching it, following a football tradition, the president approached it.

The episode fits into the close relationship between Trump and Infantino, which has run through much of the tournament. During an earlier White House visit, Infantino had already let Trump hold the cup and told him the trophy is “for winners.” FIFA also opened an office in Trump Tower in New York, and at the 2025 Club World Cup final, played at the same stadium, Trump remained at the center of champions Chelsea's photograph.

The final closed a World Cup hosted by the United States, Mexico, and Canada, whose decisive stages were played on US soil and in which Trump's role was a recurring feature, from the build-up to the closing ceremony. The tournament also introduced other US-inspired novelties, such as a halftime show and the award of championship rings to the winning team. Spain won their second world title, sixteen years after the one achieved in South Africa in 2010.

World.title: ICE kills a Colombian and a Mexican in operations where they weren't the target, officials say
World.content:
ICE kills a Colombian and a Mexican in operations where they weren't the target, officials say

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 23:00 UTC Full article

Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, who had lived in Houston for three decades, had died on July 7, at a traffic stop in that city

Two Latin American migrants were shot dead by agents of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) within a week, in operations in which, as federal authorities and lawmakers acknowledged, neither was the intended target. The deaths revived protests and calls for accountability over President Donald Trump's immigration policy.

Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 26, died on July 13 in Biddeford, Maine, when an agent fired at the vehicle he was driving. Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, who had lived in Houston for three decades, had died six days earlier, on July 7, at a traffic stop in that city. Migrant-rights groups said Durán Guerrero was authorized to work in the country; the embassies of Colombia and Mexico are providing consular assistance to the families.

The circumstances of the Maine death are the subject of conflicting accounts. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said the driver tried to flee and that, “fearing for public safety,” the agent fired. Senator Angus King, after speaking with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, gave shifting accounts of whether the man was the target of the operation, and noted that the agents were not wearing body cameras. In Houston, the Harris County District Attorney's Office opened its own investigation and issued nearly twenty subpoenas, saying the federal government was not sharing evidence.

Following the two shootings, Mullin suspended most ICE traffic stops, at the request of Republican Senator Susan Collins, who said the Biddeford case raised “critical questions.” The pause, however, lasted hours: border czar Tom Homan played it down, and the measure was reversed by government decision.

The deaths come amid a sharp increase in immigration arrests. Democratic lawmakers and former officials linked the incidents to pressure to meet arrest quotas. “When there is that relentless pressure to do more, more and more, agents make mistakes,” Deborah Fleischaker, a former ICE deputy policy director, told CNN. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticized the administration for deploying thousands of agents “without making sure they were trained.”

DHS has repeatedly defended its agents' conduct. Mullin said in May that agents “sacrifice” themselves for the country's safety and that ICE had been “demonized.” Approval of Trump's immigration policy has fallen: about 60% of Americans disapprove of it, according to an Ipsos and Washington Post poll. Various media tallies, in the absence of official figures, put at several dozen the number of people who have died in ICE shootings or in custody since the start of Trump's second term.

World.title: Lula asks Trump to explain 25% tariffs on Brazil, speaks of a "war of truth"
World.content:
Lula asks Trump to explain 25% tariffs on Brazil, speaks of a “war of truth”

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 17:43 UTC Full article

“The war I want to wage with him is a war of narrative, a war of truth. I want to show the world who is telling the truth in this tariff war between Brazil and the United States,” Lula said

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva publicly called on his US counterpart, Donald Trump, to explain the reasons behind the 25% tariffs he imposed on most Brazilian products, a measure Brasília attributes to political rather than commercial motives. The levies, announced on July 15 by the Office of the US Trade Representative, will take effect on July 22.

“The war I want to wage with him is a war of narrative, a war of truth. I want to show the world who is telling the truth in this tariff war between Brazil and the United States,” Lula said on Friday during a visit in Rio de Janeiro. The president, who is seeking reelection in the October 4 vote, said his country was “a peaceful people” and that Washington would not manage to deceive Brazilian society.

The tariffs are applied under Section 301 of US trade law, following a yearlong investigation that concluded Brazil engaged in unfair trade practices. Washington cited the treatment of US technology companies, barriers to ethanol, intellectual-property protection, the PIX payment system, and illegal deforestation linked to agribusiness. The measure includes broad exemptions, among them coffee, beef, oranges, some energy products, and aerospace parts. A parallel investigation into forced labor, concluding next week, could add a further 12.5%.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio blamed Lula for the outcome of the negotiations and said he had not negotiated “in good faith,” arguing that the president had put his “ego” ahead of a deal. Lula rejected Washington's arguments: he said his government has reduced deforestation, that 76% of the US products Brazil imports pay no duties, and defended his country's right to regulate digital platforms and to keep PIX, which he described as “a heritage” of the Brazilian people.

The dispute moved to the center of the election campaign. Lula's main rival, right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, rejected the government's accusations that his family had promoted the levies in Washington and attributed the measure to Lula's own handling of the matter. He and his brother, former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, met with Trump at the White House in May.

The tariffs come on top of the 50% ones Trump had imposed in 2025, explicitly tied to the trial of former president Jair Bolsonaro — a Trump ally — sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. Brazil's government estimates the new levies could affect 18% of its exports to the United States, some $7.4 billion, and is weighing reciprocity measures and support for affected sectors.

World.title: Andy Burnham is the Labour leader, third time lucky for the UK’s prime ministerinwaiting
World.content:
Andy Burnham is the Labour leader, third time lucky for the UK’s prime minister in waiting

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 01:35 UTC Full article

Andy Burnham sworn is as MP fom Makerfield

By Eric Shaw, Honorary Research Fellow in Politics, University of Stirling. Mr. Shaw is alzo a member of the Labour Party - A brief introduction, Andy Burnham officially becomes UK Prime Minister next Monday and can be expected to announce plans for new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, as reported by BBC.

However the Labour Party's 2024 manifesto - which the new leader said he would follow - had pledged to not issue new licenses but to honor existing ones.

At the heart of the debate are two oil and gas fields in Scotland - Rosebank and Jackdaw - which regulators approved in 2022 and 2023 under the then Conservative government, but were overturned in 2025 after a legal challenge..

The announcement will form part of a flurry of measures from Burnham including plans to take water and energy companies under public control and a new council house-building program.

He is also expected to outline new measures that will give “people breathing space on the cost of living” and intends to make a “dynamic start... focused on delivering tangible change to people's lives as soon as possible”.

However on oil and gas, BBC reports that a source close to the incoming PM said no final decisions in the area had yet been made and would be unveiled at a later date instead.

Andy Burnham has won on his third attempt to be Labor’s leader. In a wide-ranging speech to Labour MPs at a special conference in London, a jubilant Burnham pledged to “bring back hope” and promised to be a leader for all nations of the UK. But it has taken him well over a decade to get here. In 2010, as a rising star associated with the Blairite wing, he made his first bid for the leadership.

In truth, back then he had little prospect of success: he was merely placing a marker. Five years later, he stood again but could do little to derail the Jeremy Corbyn bandwagon. Yet fast-forward 11 years and his ascent seemed unstoppable. Next Monday, he will become the UK’s 59th prime minister.

To understand why and how this happened, the circumstances that created this opportunity for Burnham are key. In 2024 Labour returned to power with a thumping majority, but with little more than a third of the total vote. Within months the new government was lurching from crisis to crisis; its standing in the polls collapsed and Keir Starmer became the most unpopular Prime Minister since modern records began.

At the same time, the party faced powerful challenges from opposite ends of the political spectrum – the radical-right Reform UK and the left-wing Greens. Labor’s electorate was visibly disintegrating, its plight made stark by the disastrous local and devolved parliamentary elections of May 2026 when it shed huge numbers of local councillorsand los Wales for the first time in over a century. The message for the parliamentary Labour Party (PLP) was stark: virtually all of them were at risk of losing their seats.

In these circumstances speculation around a challenge to Starmer mounted. But why should a man twice rejected by the party so rapidly emerge as the sole contender for the crown? The key (though not sole) factors are Labor’s system for electing its leader, the balance of internal party alignments, the structure of competition and the personal factor.

In terms of the election procedures, in 2010 Labor’s leader was selected by an electoral college divided into three sections: MPs, party members and trade union political levy-payers.

This was replaced in 2013 by direct membership voting, with three categories of members – ordinary members, affiliated (trade union) members and registered supporters. (This is discussed in detail in my book, Order and Rebellion: Labor’s Managerial Politics from Miliband to Starmer, co-authored with Emmanuelle Avril.) This was the system in 2015 when Corbyn swept the board across all three categories.

But by 2026 there had been two significant changes. First, the class of registered supporters had been abolished. Second, the nominations threshold for leadership contenders had been raised from 12.5% to 20% of the PLP. It is unlikely the former had much effect but the latter certainly did, by effectively blocking anyone from the hard left from entering. This benefited the soft left, where Burnham positions himself.

Soft-left membership

There are no really reliable estimates of the shifting balance of alignments within Labor’s membership. Gauging this is difficult because of massive turnovers in membership between 2010 and 2026. Most observers would agree that membership shifted after 2015 and then to the right after 2020.

Paradoxically, the center of gravity among the rank and file did not change dramatically. Close observers of the party agreed that the mean party members tended to be soft left. This is why Starmer contested the 2020 race on a soft left platform (soon abandoned). If Burnham had done likewise in 2015, he might have won.

The structure of competition in Burnham’s three contests differed considerably. In 2010 he was not a serious contender, with the race effectively between the Miliband brothers Ed and David Ed and David. In 2015 there were four contestants: Burnham, Corbyn from the hard left, and Liz Kendall and Yvette Cooper from the right.

As a member of the shadow cabinet under Ed Miliband, Burnham had shifted to the left and was initially seen as the frontrunner. However, he made a fatal miscalculation in assuming that in response to the 2015 election defeat the party would move to the right and so he did so himself.

In fact, the party swung left and Corbyn was able to sweep up the leftwing vote – including those broadly on the soft left.

Burnham learned his lesson. After quitting parliament and winning the newly created post of mayor of Greater Manchester, he increasingly adopted a soft left posture. In the race to succeed Starmer, there were only three other plausible candidates: Angela Rayner and Ed Miliband from the soft left, and Wes Streeting from the right.

Here, chance intervened on Burnham’s side. The popular Rayner was forced to resign as deputy prime minister and deputy leader over a tax issue. Otherwise, she would probably have been in pole position. Like Rayner, Miliband, who worked closely with Burnham, was unwilling to stand against him since both shared his soft left stance. This left Streeting. His problem was simple: even if he mustered the 81 nominations he required, as a right-winger he had no chance of beating Burnham in a leadership contest. Streeting new this, so opted not to stand.

Finally, among Burnham’s personal qualities, two are worth noting. The first is his undoubted popularity among those who know him best – his Greater Manchester constituents. More broadly, he normally receives a better net rating than any other Labor politician.

The second is his willingness to take a major risk by standing for a constituency, Makerfield, that he could easily have lost. Every one of its wards were won bt Reform in the local elections and its demographics rendered it a top target for the party.

But Burnham’s unexpectedly decisive victory in the by-election demonstrated his mass appeal. For hundreds of beleaguered Labour MPs fearful of losing their seats, he was seen as their one and only lifeline. Burnham had staked his career on Makerfield and won.

World.title: Argentina-England match drove a surge in online Falklands talk, consultancy Ad Hoc says
World.content:
Argentina-England match drove a surge in online Falklands talk, consultancy Ad Hoc says

18th Saturday, July 2026 - 00:38 UTC Full article

The day of the match saw some 660,000 mentions, nearly double the volume recorded on the most recent April 2 — the date on which Argentina commemorates those killed in the 1982 war

Argentina's victory over England in the World Cup semifinal was not confined to the sporting arena on social media. According to an analysis by the Argentine consultancy Ad Hoc, digital conversation about the Falklands surpassed two million mentions over five days around the match, in an episode that revived the sovereignty claim following the banner displayed by the Argentine players.

According to the measurement, the day of the match saw some 660,000 mentions, nearly double the volume recorded on the most recent April 2 — the date on which Argentina commemorates those killed in the 1982 war — when about 373,000 were logged. The consultancy identified several peaks in the conversation between July 10 and 16: the moment Argentina's opponent became known, statements by Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva, the day of the match itself, and the subsequent remarks by President Javier Milei, which drew reaction in the United Kingdom.

The figure the consultancy highlighted was the marked predominance of the Spanish-language term. According to Ad Hoc, “the Argentine framing prevailed in the conversation,” as “Falklands” — the British name for the islands — accounted for just 9% of mentions over the past five days, against “Malvinas,” which reached a volume roughly ten times higher: around two million mentions versus 210,000.

El encuadre argentino predominó en la conversación, ya que el término “Falklands” (la denominación que los británicos le dan a las islas) representó apenas el 9% de las menciones registradas en los últimos 5 días, frente a “Malvinas” que alcanzó un volumen 10 veces superior. pic.twitter.com/HjrYejj915 — Ad Hoc (@AdHocOK) July 17, 2026

The analysis also measured the sentiment in the digital conversation toward Milei in relation to the islands and to the figure of Margaret Thatcher, on July 15 and 16. According to the consultancy, 66.7% of those mentions carried a negative charge, against 19.9% positive and 13.4% neutral, a result it attributed to the president's statements after the win and to the government's position on the issue. This is a measurement of social-media conversation, not a representative public-opinion poll.

The data offer a quantitative dimension of the episode that dominated the agenda between Argentina and the United Kingdom during the week. After the match, Argentine players posed with a banner reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” (“The Falklands are Argentine”), which prompted a protest from the British government and FIFA's assessment of possible sanctions. Milei called the gesture “valid and lawful,” though he asked that football not be mixed with the diplomatic dispute.

The Falklands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute with Argentina. Argentina manager Lionel Scaloni had asked before the match not to confuse the two spheres: “It's a football match,” he said. The final will be played on Sunday against Spain.

World.title: “The Falklands cannot remain British for ever,” a Guardian column argues
World.content:
“The Falklands cannot remain British for ever,” a Guardian column argues

17th Friday, July 2026 - 23:08 UTC Full article

The columnist reviewed the negotiations that preceded the 1982 war

In an opinion column published in the British newspaper The Guardian, writer Simon Jenkins argued that the Falklands “cannot remain British for ever” and called for London to eventually reopen sovereignty negotiations with Argentina. The piece is the columnist's personal opinion and does not represent the newspaper's editorial position.

Jenkins took as his starting point two recent developments: the agreement reached this week between the United Kingdom and Spain to dismantle the Gibraltar border, and the “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” banner that Argentine players displayed after knocking England out of the World Cup semifinal. Drawing on that contrast, the author argued that none of Britain's imperial-era territories has an eternal right to remain as it is, and noted that defending the islands costs the British taxpayer more than £60 million a year.

The columnist reviewed the negotiations that preceded the 1982 war. In 1980, then-minister Nicholas Ridley presented islanders with a “leaseback” formula, under which the United Kingdom would cede sovereignty to Argentina and then lease the islands back for a lengthy period while retaining administration. The historical record confirms that the proposal was rejected by the islanders themselves, hostile to ceding sovereignty to a country then ruled by a military junta, and that the British government had pledged not to proceed without their consent. Jenkins argued that Argentina's invasion in April 1982, while talks were under way, collapsed that path and froze any discussion of the islands' future for more than four decades.

In one of the most contentious passages, the author held that Britain's staunch defense of the archipelago is partly explained by the fact that the islanders were, in his words, white and British, unlike other populations of territories London relinquished. This is the columnist's personal thesis, not an established fact, and it contrasts with the official British position, which grounds its sovereignty in the principle of the inhabitants' self-determination.

That position rests on the 2013 referendum, cited in the column itself, in which 99.8% of 1,517 voters chose to remain a British overseas territory. There has been no resumption of sovereignty negotiations since, and successive British governments maintain that the question cannot be discussed without the islanders' consent. Argentina, for its part, maintains its claim and has on various occasions asked to reopen talks.

Jenkins concluded that, sooner or later, a British government will find the courage to reopen negotiations, though he was skeptical that a banner unfurled at a US stadium could drive such a change. The Falklands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute with Argentina. The 74-day war of 1982, begun with the invasion by General Leopoldo Galtieri's military junta, left 649 Argentine servicemen, 255 British servicemen, and three islanders dead.

World.title: Venezuela raises official death toll from June double earthquake above 5,000
World.content:
Venezuela raises official death toll from June double earthquake above 5,000

17th Friday, July 2026 - 22:25 UTC Full article

The true scale of the disaster remains surrounded by uncertainty

The official death toll from the double earthquake that struck northern Venezuela on June 24 rose on Friday to 5,069, after 139 new fatalities were added, according to the president of Parliament, Jorge Rodríguez. The tally, released via Telegram, keeps the number of injured at 16,740 and of people left homeless at 17,907. Authorities present these figures as provisional, more than three weeks after the disaster.

The two quakes, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, struck barely 39 seconds apart, with epicenters in the country's northwest. The larger one was the most powerful recorded in Venezuela in more than a century. La Guaira state, on the central coast, was the hardest hit, with numerous buildings collapsing; damage was also reported in Caracas and other parts of the north.

The true scale of the disaster remains surrounded by uncertainty. The US Geological Survey had estimated a high probability that the death toll would exceed 10,000, and international organizations and media have warned that the figure could be considerably higher than the official one, with tens of thousands of people still missing. Efforts to verify the disaster's magnitude have been hampered by information restrictions in the country, where numerous websites remain blocked; the UN urged authorities to fully restore access to media and social networks.

According to the official report, authorities have assisted 128,324 affected families, while 21,235 people remain in 107 temporary camps. Since June 24, some 1,331 aftershocks have been recorded; the most recent sizeable one, a week ago, caused panic and precautionary building evacuations in La Guaira.

The government launched a biometric census to determine the number of homes needed, which it estimates at around 25,000. On Tuesday, the National Assembly approved on first reading a reform of the Law against Real Estate Fraud to speed up reconstruction. The first vice-president of Parliament, Pedro Infante, said the amendment — pending a second debate — seeks to provide legal certainty and financing so the private sector can begin an accelerated home-building process.

The disaster strikes a country going through a prolonged institutional crisis. The government is led by acting President Delcy Rodríguez — sister of Jorge Rodríguez — following the capture in January of President Nicolás Maduro, currently held in New York awaiting trial on drug-trafficking charges. Rebuilding La Guaira and the affected areas is shaping up as one of the administration's main challenges in the months ahead.

World.title: A White-Knuckle Taxi Trip Through the Mountains of Costa Rica
World.content:
With my car doing what it does best– sitting idly in the carport awaiting a part– I walked twenty minutes in the dark down the long incline of the main street of the barrio to line up for the 5 am bus to Quepos. A red taxi pulled up. The driver stepped out and said, “Quepos! Dominical!” The going rate from Perez Zeledon to Quepos is 25 to 30 thousand colones. Not worth it as after 35 years here, I live happily on Tico time. Then he quoted his price. Mil to Dominical, mil quinientos to Quepos. Me and 2 other guys stepped forward. He loaded our gear in the trunk and off we went.

You pay your money and you take your chances. The first thing I noticed about my driver was that he liked to drive fast. The radio was tuned to a local station. Between latin dance songs,I heard an ad for a Tico restaurant in New Jersey. We crossed the Rio Pacuar bridge, recently expanded to two lanes, and began the ascent toward the 1,200 meter (3,900 feet) El Alto.

My back seat partner wore a head and neck cover and dark glasses. He reeked of garlic. I assumed he was a construction worker and not a terrorist. We passed a meat truck going up the mountain. The early morning hour meant fewer slow vehicles and we made good time. At the top of the mountain, a small pack of young men on motorcycles passed us in a swarm.

The downhill descent takes 16km (10 miles) to reach sea level. My driver wanted to cover this distance in record time. He tailgated slower traffic. Every curve felt like a carnival ride. I grabbed the overhead handle. It was broken, hanging by a screw. On a short straightaway, he breezed past a couple trucks and flew through the curve. I thought about Buddy Holly, Richie Valens and the Big Bopper, skipping the slow bus ride to catch a plane to their next destination.

We were also a trio who decided to skip the bus and save time. Death comes in threes. A long time ago, a guy I knew drove off the side of this same mountain in the fog. The smell of burning brakes lingered in the air. I was about to tell our driver that I wanted to arrive in Quepos, but not in a body bag. Then we hit the village of Platanillo, where I lived over thirty years before. We got behind a solid line of cars that descended the final mountain at a steady, unpassable pace.

We reached the costanera and were soon flying along at 120 kph. This is 75mph, the average speed on an interstate highway in the states. If I am in a car going this speed, I prefer to be in the driver’s seat. But my driver was a robust middle aged man and who knows how many tens of thousands of kilometers he had sped over the challenging roads of Costa Rica. I relaxed and went back to word games on my phone.

Twenty minutes outside Quepos our driver decided there was room for one more. An elderly woman at the bus stop climbed in. We were barely back to top speed when she began talking of her beliefs. In a loud slow voice the words streamed out. Yehova, Jesucristo, Gloria a Dios, gracias al señor. The car windows were down and a rush of wind through the car muffled a lot of what she said, which was fine with me. At one point the guy in the dark glasses said something about servidores de Satanas. I couldn’t hear enough to know if he was pro or anti Satan.

We got to Quepos and I paid the driver and found out he had an appointment in Quepos. He had covered the 80 kilometers in an hour fifteen. The money he collected went into his gas tank. A bargain is a bargain, and It’s not often you find a bargain while waiting for a bus at five in the morning.

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Route 27 Goes One-Way at 2 p.m. and the Weather Turns with It
World.content:
If you spent the mid-year break at the beach, today is the day most people head home — and two things will shape your afternoon drive. Route 27 turns all its lanes toward San José for four hours, and the weather turns wet and windy from the middle of the day. Plan around both and you’ll skip the worst of it.

Between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m., every lane on Route 27 runs one way, toward the capital. The highway does this on the busiest return days to clear the flood of cars coming off the coast at once, so traffic keeps moving instead of stacking up at the tolls. Crews start closing and setting up the road at 1 p.m., and normal two-way traffic is back by 7 p.m.

The part to watch is speed and direction. While the lanes are flipped, the limit drops to 60 km/h (37 mph), and traffic officers will be checking — the lower speed is what keeps a road full of redirected lanes safe. And if you need to go the other way, toward Caldera or the coast, you can’t use Route 27 at all during those hours. Take an alternate instead: Route 3 through Atenas, Aguacate and Orotina; Route 1 over Cambronero; or Route 239 through Ciudad Colón, Puriscal, San Pablo, Turrubares and Orotina.

The weather gives you a reason to leave earlier rather than later. Rain and wind both build through the afternoon and into the night — exactly when the road will be busiest.

Mornings are the calmer window. Expect scattered showers over the Caribbean and the Northern Zone and some drizzle across the eastern and northern edges of the Central Valley, but nothing that should slow a drive. By afternoon, rain picks up over the Central and South Pacific — the coast most people are driving home from — and spreads to Limón and its lowlands by evening.

Wind is the part to respect. Gusts will reach 40 to 65 km/h (25 to 40 mph) in the lowlands and 70 to 95 km/h (43 to 59 mph) in the mountains, so the climb over the hills between the coast and the Central Valley will be blustery. Ease off on exposed stretches, leave more room behind the car ahead on wet pavement, and watch for standing water where the afternoon downpours pool.

In San José, look for 19 to 24 °C (66 to 76 °F) with wind from early morning. Out on the Nicoya Peninsula, Nicoya swings from about 22 to nearly 36 °C (72 to 96 °F). You can check conditions for your own route on our regional weather forecast before you set off.

The wet stretch doesn’t end today. Forecasters expect next week to open with another round of Caribbean rain as a new tropical wave moves through, so if your drive slips to Monday, the same advice holds.

In short: if you can, be on the road before the lanes flip at 2 p.m. and before the afternoon rain sets in. If you’re leaving later, hold to 60 km/h on Route 27, give yourself extra time, and take it slow through the wind and water on the way up.

World.title: Wildfire Smoke From Canada Casts Shadow Over World Cup Final
World.content:
Smoke from hundreds of Canadian wildfires has added an unexpected health and weather concern to Sunday’s World Cup final between Argentina and Spain, although improving forecasts suggest the match should go ahead without major disruption.The haze spread across the northeastern United States during the week, pushing air quality into unhealthy ranges in parts of New York and New Jersey.

More than 80,000 spectators are expected at MetLife Stadium, known during the tournament as New York New Jersey Stadium, for the 3 p.m. kickoff on July 19.The open-air venue has no roof or enclosed climate-controlled environment to protect players and fans from smoke, heat or direct sunlight.

Conditions around the stadium remained unsettled Saturday. Heavy thunderstorms, damaging winds and flash flooding moved through the area, forcing Spain to cancel its final outdoor training session. Argentina’s practice was delayed by about 45 minutes before the defending champions were able to take the field.

The storms caused immediate disruption but were also expected to help clear the thickest wildfire smoke before the final. Forecasters said the weather system should push much of the pollution away from northern New Jersey, leaving only light haze or a lingering smell of smoke by Sunday afternoon.

Air quality in East Rutherford is expected to improve from levels considered unhealthy for sensitive groups on Saturday to the moderate range Sunday. That would mean little risk for most spectators, although people with asthma or existing heart and lung conditions could still experience symptoms. Sunday’s forecast calls for mostly sunny skies, lower humidity and a high near 83 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius).

The smoke has already affected professional sports elsewhere in North America.A Major League Soccer match between the Chicago Fire and Vancouver Whitecaps was postponed because of poor air quality, while a Canadian Premier League match in Hamilton, Ontario, was also called off.

Toronto canceled an official World Cup fan festival and public screening of the Argentina-England semifinal after an air-quality warning was issued. A National Women’s Soccer League match between Gotham FC and the Washington Spirit went ahead at Citi Field in New York, but officials introduced hydration breaks roughly every 15 minutes.

United States midfielder Trinity Rodman later described the conditions as difficult and questioned whether the match should have been played under circumstances requiring so many stoppages. The risk is greater for players than for most fans because intense exercise increases breathing rates and the amount of fine particulate matter drawn deep into the lungs.

A World Cup final could require more than two hours of outdoor exertion when warmups, halftime and possible extra time are included. Wildfire smoke can cause sore throats, coughing, headaches, irritated eyes and fatigue even among healthy adults. Prolonged exposure can also create greater problems for people with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions.

Health officials generally recommend reducing strenuous outdoor activity when smoke is present. People who need additional protection should use a properly fitted N95 respirator rather than a cloth mask. Air-quality monitors at the stadium have been recording conditions at 10-minute intervals, and tournament organizers remain in contact with local authorities.

No delay, relocation or change to the scheduled kickoff has been announced. The outlook is considerably better than it appeared earlier in the week. Forecasters now expect the most dangerous smoke to move away before Argentina and Spain take the field, though sensitive spectators have been advised to check local air-quality readings Sunday morning.

After a tournament repeatedly interrupted by heat and thunderstorms, the final now faces one last environmental concern. Barring another sudden shift in the winds, however, the smoke is expected to remain a troubling backdrop rather than an obstacle to crowning the 2026 world champion.

World.title: Belize basks in sunshine while a depression may form up north
World.content:
Belize basks in sunshine while a depression may form up north

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize gets the Sunday it hoped for. Mostly sunny skies, warm temperatures, and calm seas set the stage for World Cup final day, while forecasters keep a distant eye on a system taking shape far to the north in the Gulf of Mexico.

According to the National Meteorological Service, a light, warm, and mostly dry easterly airflow prevails. Skies will be mostly sunny today, turning clear to partly cloudy tonight, with any showers staying isolated, ideal conditions for wherever you plan to watch Spain and Argentina contest the final at 1:00 p.m.

The tropical outlook carries a new note, though not one for Belizean alarm. A broad surface low located over the northeastern Gulf of Mexico has a high chance of becoming a tropical depression later today or tomorrow. That system sits far to Belize’s north, well away from our shores, and the Met Service confirms that elsewhere in the region, including our area, tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the next 48 hours. It is a development worth following, nothing more for now.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 82 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will be hot, climbing to 94 degrees Fahrenheit (34 Celsius) and dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius).

At sea, conditions stay gentle, with easterly winds of 5 to 15 knots, a light chop, and waves of 2 to 4 feet, another fine day on the water.

Looking ahead to Monday and Monday night, the fair and warm pattern continues, with shower activity, if any, remaining isolated.

Today’s low tides are at 7:54 AM and 8:10 PM, with a high tide at 1:42 PM and another high at 2:11 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:27 AM and will set at 6:30 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Catherine Cumberbatch.

World.title: Spain vs Argentina today: the final of dreams, who wins it?
World.content:
Spain vs Argentina today: the final of dreams, who wins it?

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): This is the one. Spain and Argentina, the number two and number one ranked teams on the planet, meet today at 1:00 p.m. Belize time at MetLife Stadium to decide the World Cup, and across the Jewel, a nation painted in blue and white holds its breath.

The stakes could not be written any larger. Argentina, the defending champions, stand ninety minutes from back-to-back World Cup titles, a feat achieved only twice in history.

And at the centre of it all is Lionel Messi, playing what is expected to be the final World Cup match of the greatest career football has known. The golden boot picture shifted on Saturday, when Kylian Mbappé struck twice in France’s wild 6-4 third-place defeat to England, taking his tournament tally to ten, two clear of Messi’s eight, and claiming the all-time World Cup scoring record with 22. To snatch the boot back today, Messi needs nothing less than a hat trick, or two goals and an assist. A second straight crown, though, requires only a win, and back-to-back titles would complete a legacy no scoring chart can measure.

But standing in the way is the most formidable obstacle this tournament could offer. Spain, the European champions, have conceded exactly one goal in seven matches, a defensive record that borders on unreal. They dismantled France 2-0 in the semi-final with a team goal, the Porro and Olmo one-two, already being hailed among the tournament’s finest, and they arrive as the bookmakers’ favourite, with the numbers giving La Roja roughly a 41 percent chance to Argentina’s 27, and a meaningful chance this goes the distance to extra time.

Argentina’s answer is written in scar tissue. The champions have stared down elimination repeatedly, storming back from 2-0 down against Egypt with three late goals, outlasting Switzerland in extra time, and then, in Wednesday’s semi-final, beating England 2-1 to end a forty-year wait against their fiercest rival. This team does not know when it is beaten, and in Messi it carries the one player on Earth capable of deciding any match alone.

So the question is the oldest one in sport: does the immovable object or the unstoppable story win? Spain’s control, discipline, and near-perfect machine, or Argentina’s champions’ heart and the destiny of the greatest of all time?

A projected 1.8 billion people worldwide will watch it decided, and few places will live it more intensely than Belize, where the Albiceleste’s army has waited all tournament for this day. At 1:00 p.m., the country stops.

So make your call, Belize, and make it loud: Spain or Argentina, who lifts the World Cup today? Drop your prediction and your final score in the comments.

World.title: Ten goals of madness: England beat France 6-4 for third place
World.content:
Ten goals of madness: England beat France 6-4 for third place

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): They call the third-place match the game nobody wants to play. Somebody forgot to tell England and France, who produced one of the most extraordinary matches in World Cup history on Saturday, a ten-goal spectacle that England won 6-4 to claim the bronze, while Kylian Mbappé rewrote the record books even in defeat.

The numbers alone belong in a museum. As the Associated Press reported, it was the highest-scoring World Cup game since Hungary beat El Salvador 10-1 back in 1982, and the ten goals were the most ever scored in a third-place match.

England did the early demolition. Declan Rice opened in just the third minute, Ezri Konsa doubled the lead, and Bukayo Saka struck twice, in the 37th minute and in first-half stoppage time, to send the Three Lions in at half-time an astonishing 4-0 up. With France facing humiliation in coach Didier Deschamps’ final game in charge, the rout looked on.

Then came the fightback. France roared out after the break, with Mbappé scoring twice either side of a Bradley Barcola goal to claw it back to 4-3 and set up a frantic finish. Les Bleus pushed for the equaliser, but Saka completed his hat trick from the penalty spot in the 87th minute, and though Ousmane Dembélé pulled another back in the dying moments, England struck once more at the death to seal a 6-4 win and their best World Cup finish since lifting the trophy in 1966. Notably, England did it all without captain Harry Kane, who did not feature, ending his tournament on six goals.

Mbappé’s consolation was historic. His brace took his tournament tally to ten goals and, as Euronews reported, carried him past Lionel Messi on the all-time World Cup scoring list with 22 career goals to Messi’s 21. It also stretched his golden boot lead to two, ten goals to Messi’s eight, meaning, per ESPN’s breakdown of FIFA’s tiebreakers, Messi needs a hat trick, or two goals and an assist, in today’s final against Spain to snatch the award back.

And that is the beauty of it: even the consolation game ended up pouring fuel on today’s main event. The bronze is England’s. The records are Mbappé’s. The stage, at 1:00 p.m. Belize time, belongs to Messi, Argentina, and Spain.

Did you catch the ten-goal madness, Belize? And can Messi answer Mbappé today? Comment below.

World.title: More traffic headache coming for motorists in Liguanea
World.content:
Sewer upgrade work underway on Retreat Avenue off Old Hope Road on Saturday. The work will shortly be extended on Old Hope Road to its intersection with Wellington Drive. Naphtali Junior

MOTORISTS in the Liguanea area of St Andrew should brace for major traffic disruptions this summer as the National Water Commission (NWC) undertakes the renovation of sewage infrastructure along Old Hope Road

Speaking during a recent meeting of the Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s headquarters in St Andrew, Minister of Water Matthew Samuda said the work forms part of the Government’s ongoing programme to strengthen resilience through upgrading the county’s water and sewage network.

He explained that work on Munroe Road and Wellington Drive, which led to traffic snarls in the area for weeks, is now complete, allowing work to begin on the stretch of Old Hope Road that runs through Liguanea, Matilda’s Corner, and Seymour Avenue.

Samuda told Observer editors and reporters that work along that corridor was deliberately postponed to avoid disrupting students travelling to sit their various examinations.

“We didn’t start last month because we didn’t want to run the risk of a child being stuck in traffic trying to get to their PEP [Primary Exit Profile] exams at St Peter and Paul, or a child trying to get to Campion to do their CXC [Caribbean Examination Council] exams along that particular space. We expect to start in the coming week or so,” said the minister.

World.title: Puzzling double murder in Mandeville
World.content:
An undated photo of murder victim Deneekia Pounall, 24, Knox Community College nursing student and resident of Heartease district in Manchester .

BY KASEY WILLIAMS Observer staff reporter kaseyw@jamaicaobserver.com

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Even as police here have launched a manhunt for a gunman who posed as a passenger in a taxi before disembarking the vehicle and killing two passengers on Saturday, detectives are struggling to make sense of the incident as up to press time they had not determined a motive for the attack.

“It is senseless…He paid his fare and got his change and the vehicle drove off and he just fired shots on it. The motive is not clear, because why would you shoot up a vehicle with seven people,” a senior police source told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

Police identified those killed as Deneekia Pounall, 24, a nursing student at Knox Community College, a resident of Heartease in the parish, and her neighbour 21-year-old Sadefa Henry.

According to the police, about 7:30 pm on Saturday, Pounall and Henry were seated in a Toyota Voxy operated as a public passenger vehicle on the Mandeville to Royal Flat route when a man, who was a passenger in the vehicle, disembarked at a section of Caledonia Road commonly referred to as Horseshoe Curve.

The man reportedly opened fire on the seven occupants of the taxi, hitting the two who were seated at the back of the vehicle.

They were taken to the Mandeville Regional Hospital where Pounall was pronounced dead on arrival, while Henry later succumbed to his injuries.

Residents of Heartease told the

Observer on Sunday that Pounall and Henry lived in neighbouring apartments at a property in the community.

“She was such a calm girl. She nuh talk, and the guy was quiet and humble, so this incident is quite puzzling,” said a resident who requested anonymity.

The double murder has increased the number of homicides reported in Manchester to 20 since the start of the year.

Just last week acting head of the police’s Area Three, Senior Superintendent Shane McCalla, predicted that fewer than 94 murders will be recorded across Manchester, Clarendon, and St Elizabeth by year end, following the launch of Operation Reset last month.

“We are trending upwards in the murder and aggravated assaults, so Operation Reset was primarily designed to address this…and in terms of the acquisitive crimes, we are trending down by 104. This is our commitment to the High Command that Area Three will deliver in December,” he told the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s High Command last Wednesday at the Mandeville police station.

McCalla gave a breakdown of murders statistics down the years in Area Three. He said in 2023 there were 189 murders, in 2024 there were 150 murders, while 94 murders were recorded last year.

“Year to date we have 58 [murders]. Despite seeing some issues where St Elizabeth is concerned… I am convinced and I am committing to you that we will end under the 94 [in December],” he vowed.

World.title: Sumfest history
World.content:
Mavado (left) and Vybz Kartel share the Sumfest stage. (Garfield Robinson)

For 18 years it remained one of dancehall’s biggest unanswered questions: Could the music that once divided a nation ever become the force that united it?

Shortly after 2:00 am on Sunday that question was answered inside Plantation Cove as a Taste of Reggae Sumfest delivered an experience of history-making proportions.

Vybz Kartel and Mavado stood shoulder to shoulder on the festival’s grand stage, writing a new chapter in one of the most defining narratives in dancehall culture. The showdown was far more than an exhibition of hit songs. It was the closing of a circle that began during the combative Gully/Gaza era — a rivalry that shaped an entire generation of dancehall fans and forever altered the genre’s landscape.

Dressed for battle, but performing in brotherhood, both deejays were ready to give fans exactly what they asked for.

Without hesitation, they reached back into the catalogue that made them icons. Serving up songs such as

The Real McKoy, Real Deal, Send A Hell, the entertainers elicited loud cheers of approval from the sold-out crowd.

The tension that once defined the rivalry had given way to celebration.

“This a history innu,” Mavado declared.

“Memba dat,” Kartel responded before embracing his long-time rival.

“We ago gi unnu supm unnu never see yet,” Kartel continued.

For two hours they spewed hit after hit from their arsenal of songs.

For Professor Donna Hope, one of Jamaica’s foremost authorities on dancehall culture, the significance of the moment extended well beyond nostalgia.

“Eighteen years later… We have been through many things, they’ve been in exile in different ways, they lost things, they gained things, and so the energy was different,” she reflected after the performance. “Gaza/Gully in 2008 was a very combative energy but Reggae Sumfest 2026, it was different. Their performance reminded people that dancehall culture is alive and well and Vybz Kartel and Mavado are powerful artistes that have matured and now understand the mission and are carrying it out.”

Even while revisiting songs born from lyrical warfare, the two men frequently completed each other’s lyrics, laughed together, and embraced the shared legacy they helped create. Records that once encouraged fans to choose sides became reminders of just how deeply both artistes have shaped modern dancehall.

Mavado confidently held his own with crowd favourites, including Weh Dem A Do, Top Shatta Nah Miss, Chat Too Much, Warn Dem, and Amazing Grace.

Kartel answered with equal force, unleashing anthem after anthem through Gaza Army, Broad Daylight, Kill Dem All, Done, Weh Dem A Go, Murder Informa, and Never Scared.

Female fans were delighted with selections including Love Dem, Picture Me & You, Beg You (A Touch), and Come Home, while Mavado countered with Squeeze Breast, Bicycle, Ever Blessed, When You Feel Lonely, and Never Believe You.

The surprises continued as Mavado invited Stacious to recreate their hit Come Into My Room, while Kartel called on Gaza Hindu to perform Spice’s verses on Ramping Shop and Virginity.

“It’s a good feeling to be back on a Sumfest stage,” said Stacious. “Tonight I’m here not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall who lived through the era where Gully/Gaza did a run road… Mavado hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while so I was happy to witness that return and be a part of it… [I]t’s always fun when we connect…” As they got ready to draw the curtains on their historic set, the clash songs and romance anthems gave way to messages of gratitude and faith as the deejays delivered Hope and Pray, God Is the Greatest, The Messiah, and Thank Yuh Jah. Then came the perfect ending. Their first collaboration, Happiest Days. “This a the first song me and him ever do,” Kartel reminded the audience. “Listen to it good and see how everything come full circle.” Few closing songs could carry greater symbolism — history, legacy secured!

World.title: Rastafari ganja rights review
World.content:
From left: Sancia Bennett Templer, permanent secretary, Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce; Delano Seiveright, minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and chairman of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce; Delroy Chuck, minister of justice and constitutional affairs; and Olivia “Babsy” Grange, minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport, engage meeting attendees (out of picture) following Thursday’s high-level ministerial consultation on Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis framework at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

THE Government on Thursday opened consultations on the country’s sacramental cannabis framework during a high-level policy meeting at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

Justice Minister Delroy Chuck; Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia “Babsy” Grange; minister of state in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Marisa Dalrymple-Philibert; and minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright led the talks with senior technocrats from the ministries.

The discussions were convened following recommendations of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce, chaired by Seiveright, which identified the need for a coordinated consultation on policy and operational issues affecting Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis regime.

The meeting considered the existing legal and administrative framework with the objective of providing greater clarity, consistency, and certainty while safeguarding the religious freedoms provided under Section 7C(2)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, which makes provision for members of the Rastafarian community to possess ganja.

The meeting discussed matters relating to the recognition and oversight of sacramental organisations, approved cultivation lands and spaces, cultivation and possession limits, transportation arrangements, enforcement protocols, and the need to clearly distinguish sacramental cannabis activities from Jamaica’s regulated, commercial cannabis industry.

Jamaica’s commercial cannabis industry is regulated exclusively by the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) under the Dangerous Drugs Act and its Regulations, with no other entity having legal authority to license or regulate commercial cannabis activities.

There have been growing concerns surrounding the misuse of the sacramental framework to facilitate unlawful activities, as well as persistent confusion about what the law permits.

In recent times there have been repeated allegations from Rastafarians about facing prosecution over their use of ganja, despite the provision in law for its sacramental use.

Recently the

Jamaica Observer reported the case of Westmoreland resident Troy Harrison who had charges of possession of ganja and dealing in ganja against him dropped in the Westmoreland Parish Court.

The Crown offered no evidence on both charges on the basis that Harrison is a member of the Rastafarian community and therefore entitled to possess and use ganja for sacramental purposes.

“Some police continue to want to interpret the law how they want to,” attorney-at-law Marcus Goffe, who represented Harrison, told the

Observer.

“The Rastafari community is fed up with the continual targeting and unfair prosecution of members of the community for ganja, despite the 2015 amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act intended to recognise and protect the community’s rights. It is clear that the narcotics police are not fully aware of the extent of Rastafari’s ganja rights or how they are to approach, investigate, determine, and resolve the rights of Rastafari in relation to ganja,” charged Goffe, who was then on a mission to have the seized ganja returned to Harrison.

Against charges such as the ones made by Goffe, the high-level meeting led by the Government ministers also explored mechanisms to strengthen coordination among the various ministries, the CLA, and the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

A significant part of the discussions focused on the possible transfer of responsibility for the operational governance and administration of sacramental cannabis matters to the Ministry of Culture, recognising the fundamentally religious and cultural character of the sacramental regime.

Ministers agreed that the proposal should form part of the ongoing consultation process as the Government works to strengthen governance; improve inter-ministerial coordination; and provide a clearer, more effective framework that protects legitimate sacramental rights while preserving public confidence, public safety, and the rule of law.

World.title: US Customs seizes over US$50,000 from passenger headed to Jamaica
World.content:
FORT LAUDERDALE, USA (CMC) — United States Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agency says officers at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Miami seized more than US$53,800 (approximately $8.5 million) in undeclared currency from an outbound traveller headed to Jamaica.



According to CBP, the traveller was arrested July 1 on federal money laundering charges.

“CBP officers were inspecting passengers departing on a flight destined for Kingston, Jamaica,” CBP said. “Although the traveller declared they were not carrying currency, officers discovered and verified US$53,800 in US currency.

“Homeland Security Investigations responded to the scene, and the individual was arrested. Federal prosecutors accepted charges for money laundering under Title 18, US Code, Section 1956,” CBP added.

Daniel Alonso, director of Field Operations for CBP’s Miami and Tampa Field Office, said, “Criminal organisations often rely on bulk cash smuggling to move illicit proceeds across international borders.

“CBP officers remain vigilant in identifying these violations and work closely with our law enforcement partners to disrupt transnational criminal activity while protecting the integrity of our nation’s borders,” he added.

CBP said there is no limit to the amount of currency or other monetary instruments travellers may transport into or out of the United States.

However, it said anyone transporting more than US$10,000 in currency or monetary instruments into or out of the country must report the funds by filing a FinCEN Form 105, Report of International Transportation of Currency, or Monetary Instruments.

“Failure to report currency or filing a false report may result in the seizure of the currency and could lead to civil or criminal penalties,” CBP said.

It added that its outbound enforcement mission targets illicit bulk cash smuggling, narcotics trafficking, weapons smuggling, and other transnational criminal activity while facilitating lawful international travel and trade.

The identity of the passenger has not been released.

World.title: MoBay businessman urges colleagues to make walls available for murals
World.content:
The mural at the Hilton and Hilton building was officially opened last Wednesday by (from left) lead artist Anthony Smith; Mayor of Montego Bay Richard Vernon; vice-chairman Doctor’s Cave Bathing Club, Kathryn May; executive director Kingston Creative, Andrea Dempster Chung; and co-owner of Hilton’s Pharmacy Anthony Tavares. .

MONTEGO BAY,St James — Anthony Tavares, a director at Hilton and Hilton, owners of the building that houses Hilton’s Pharmacy and Henderson’s Bookstore, and now home to a mural, says he will be encouraging fellow members of the business community to make their buildings available for similar public art projects across Montego Bay.

“I am trying to get other business owners around Montego Bay interested,” Tavares told the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

Starting with his friends, he will ask more businesses to support the initiative by offering prominent wall spaces for murals, helping to enhance the city’s aesthetics and provide it with a boost.

The mural on the Hilton and Hilton-owned building is the third in a series being created by Kingston Creative, with funding support from Doctor’s Cave Bathing Club.

Two earlier murals, funded by TUI Care Foundation, were unveiled in February at the Scotiabank branch on St James Street and on St Clavers Avenue.

The latest work adorns the left side of the Hilton Pharmacy building on St James Street, offering a striking view to people entering the area.

“I feel very positive about it because we need to uplift the conscience of Montegonian people, civic pride,” said Tavares.

Describing the painting as stunning, he explained that the mural came at no cost to the company, with the owners of the building willing to work with its partners to ensure it remains in excellent condition.

“We’ll probably get in touch with Kingston Creative and have the artist come in and do some work,” added Tavares as he pointed out that Kingston Creative approached the business with a request to use the wall, to which the company readily agreed.

“This one is mural number three, we have another one coming soon, and the plan is continue working with the city of Montego Bay, Mayor Richard Vernon, and funders like the TUI Care Foundation and Doctor’s Cave Bathing Club,” executive director of Kingston Creative, Andrea Dempster Chung, told the Observer.

While remaining tight-lipped about the next project in Montego Bay, Dempster Chung said the initiative forms part of a wider effort to strengthen the city’s cultural and creative ecosystem.

“It’s important also for cultural tourism because it helps us to diversify that product from sun, sea, and sand and give tourists a reason to come further into the cities and the towns and really explore the real Jamaica and touch base with the real people, the vendors on the street, etc,” she said.

Dempster Chung explained that the long-term vision is for the murals to become attractions, following a model already established in Kingston.

“The intention is to have a self-guided tour where people can walk around the centre from murals one, two, three, four, five, six, stop at the vendors, buy coconut water, buy some things at the craft market, and work their way back around the course to the Montego Bay Cultural Centre, which is where we have our National Gallery West and our National Museum West,” said Dempster Chung.

She pointed out that responsibility for maintaining the murals will rest with the municipal corporation.

“These murals are gifts to the city, every municipality has to look after the assets whether they put the assets in place or whether they were gifted the assets.

“We fully respect that the city of Montego Bay will realise that this is their asset and they will work to take care of it just as if they were given a bench, just as if they were given a park,” added Dempster Chung.

The mayor assured that the St James Municipal Corporation will play its part in ensuring the murals remain in good condition by setting up regular cleaning and repairs when needed.

“However, I’m urging our community to help care for them. This way the murals will stay bright, visible, and welcoming for residents and visitors, and remain a proud part of the city’s transformation,” added Vernon.

He said the murals form part of the corporation’s urban renewal programme under MoBay STEP-UP, in partnership with Kingston Creative, which aims to bring life and colour to Montego Bay while showcasing its culture and creativity.

The latest piece was painted by Anthony Smith, who works under the moniker Taoszen, with assistance from fellow artist Joel Cameron.

The mural shows a woodcarver at work, representing the artisans who preserve Jamaica’s craft tradition.

Taoszen also painted the murals at S Hotel and several pieces along the Reggae Wall of Fame at the Catherine Hall Entertainment Centre.

He said it took eight days to complete the latest mural.

“When I am focused on the work, when I lock in and Joel Cameron is here and assisting me — and he wasn’t in the way, he’s there providing me with whatever assistance I need — that helped me,” added Taoszen.

World.title: EU hits China’s Alibaba with €550M record fine over illegal products
World.content:
The finding that AliExpress failed to check and tackle these risks "is very dangerous for our consumers, but it’s also unfair for those companies that are complying with all our rules," Virkkunen said.

The record fine is the third one imposed under the Digital Services Act so far. It comes two months after Brussels hit rival marketplace Temu with a €200 million bill over similar breaches. “We were looking at the duration and the seriousness of these failures when deciding the size of the fine," Virkkunen said, recalling that Temu had so far only been sanctioned for failing to check its service for illegal products sold in Europe properly.

The Commission opened a probe into AliExpress in March 2024 over suspected breaches of the DSA, including also on the platform's transparency on advertising and recommender systems. Many of these suspected breaches were already settled in a series of commitments in June 2025.

In its new findings, the EU assessed that AliExpress failed to "evaluate whether it had sufficient staff to review potentially illegal products," leading to "overcharged" moderators having "only like 10 or 20 seconds to review the illegal product," a senior Commission official said in a briefing ahead of the announcement. It also failed to assess how its recommender and advertising systems "exacerbate" the spread of illegal products and relied on compliance checks that "could easily be circumvented through mis-categorization."

AliExpress has until Oct. 20 to come up with an "action plan" to address the infringements, which lasted at least until June 2025, or face additional penalties.

A spokesperson for AliExpress called the fine "disproportionate" in a statement on Monday and said the company "has been, and continues to be, firmly committed to meeting our obligations and we have invested substantial resources in risk assessment and mitigation, product safety and consumer protection."

The spokesperson added that AliExpress is "carefully reviewing the decision and considering all available options."

This article was updated to include a comment from AliExpress.

World.title: America’s reassurance mission at Farnborough
World.content:
Europe’s biggest airshow of the year is set to open this week under the specter of two wars, with the Pentagon facing doubts it can hit a trillion-dollar budget topline and if it will play nice with NATO nations increasingly confident about going it alone.

The show that spans more than five million square feet — enough to fit 78 football pitches or 1,350 Concordes stacked wing to wing — has been running since the end of World War II and will launch tens of billions of dollars worth of deals. But with the U.S. delaying arms sales and hanging onto more weapons, the feeling is in the air that American credibility — especially their ability to clarify what they want from Europe and to meet demand — is on the line here at Farnborough.

“There's no question that the primary subtext to this air show, last year's air show, I'm sure next year's air show, is going to be the geopolitical issues and the transatlantic issue in particular, and a lot of anxiety about what that means on both sides,” said a U.S. industry official. “Europe is far from a monolith. You have European countries that would absolutely like to push full on the gas to build an organic defense industrial base. You have others that are very clear they want to continue to buy American kit.”

“We still argue that we make the best stuff in the world, and everybody wants it,” added the official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But the Europeans are worried if they can get it.”

Scar tissue: Even as top European officials acknowledge they will need America’s help rearming, some are chafing at the Trump administration’s suggestions that the continent shouldn’t try to replace the U.S. defense industry’s role — even as the Pentagon is signaling that it is removing some U.S. forces from Europe.

“The U.S. is moving the goalpost while demanding Europe take ‘primary responsibility’ for its own defense while opposing the industrial-policy tools to do it,” said Oscar Jonsson, a specialist from the Swedish Defence University. “Most European states figured that buying American won’t reverse the trend of U.S. withdrawal, and it will only prolong an overdependence on the U.S. It’s not unlikely that there will be a compromise with some more buying American, but it’s only a slight delay to the structural shift.”

World.title: Pistorius makes fresh push for Hegseth meeting after spring setback
World.content:
The plans are still being prepared and the individual meetings depend on the minister’s final schedule.

The German defense ministry declined to comment on the plans. However, it would be Pistorius’ second attempt this year to secure a dedicated meeting with Hegseth in Washington.

The German minister abandoned the U.S. leg of a planned North America trip in May after a meeting with Hegseth could not be arranged. Pistorius went ahead with the Canadian portion of the trip, while Hegseth traveled to the Shangri-La Dialogue security conference in Singapore.

The episode was a setback for Berlin as it sought direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.

Pistorius and Hegseth have met before. Most recently, both were at the NATO Summit in Ankara. And during a formal Pentagon visit in July 2025, the two discussed the future of U.S. forces in Europe and Germany's interest in the American Typhon long-range missile system as well as Tomahawk missiles.

Those questions have only become more pressing. Hegseth announced in June a six-month review of U.S. troop deployments in Europe, while Washington has already reduced some of the military capabilities it makes available to NATO. Pistorius has warned that any American withdrawal must be coordinated with European allies to avoid dangerous gaps in the alliance’s defenses.

World.title: Andy Burnham to become UK prime minister — live updates
World.content:
Former Greater Manchester mayor takes over from Keir Starmer and names his Cabinet. Follow along for all the latest news and analysis from the POLITICO team.

LONDON — Britain gets (another) new prime minister Monday: Andy Burnham.

The former mayor of Greater Manchester — who succeeded Keir Starmer as leader of the U.K.’s governing Labour Party last week — will enter No. 10 Downing Street this lunchtime and start naming his top team.

Starmer — who was ousted by his own party despite winning a landslide majority just two years go — made a farewell speech in front of No. 10 before heading to Buckingham Palace to meet King Charles III and formally resign.

Burnham gets his own audience with the king. He’ll head back to No. 10 for a speech setting out his priorities — so far focused on devolving power, tackling the cost of living, and bringing “hope” to the country — before settling in to the job and picking his Cabinet.

Expect a flurry of announcements through the day on Burnham’s picks, and some early signaling of his policy priorities. Follow the POLITICO team below for the latest.

World.title: The European Parliament’s answer to its AI worries: More AI
World.content:
“Parliament has not been immune to AI slop and misleading AI-generated content,” said Brando Benifei, the Socialists and Democrats lawmaker who led Parliament’s work on the AI Act, the EU’s landmark law governing the technology. “MEPs must lead by example as the AI Act’s transparency rules become applicable.”

The project captures the dilemma facing Parliament as generative AI becomes embedded in its daily work. Around 2,100 people use AI daily in the Parliament — around 20 percent of all staff.

Its leaders want officials to stop feeding parliamentary material into uncontrolled public platforms, but they are also concerned that the technology is degrading the quality of legislative work and introducing errors or misleading content into the democratic process. Their suspicions that lawmakers and assistants are already relying on AI have been fueled by a surge in amendments requiring translation, telltale drafting styles and occasional hallucinated references to laws that do not exist.

Committee chairs asked Parliament Secretary-General Alessandro Chiocchetti to draw up guidelines for lawmakers’ use of AI. He replied that the matter might instead fall to the Parliament’s constitutional affairs committee, which would need to amend the institution’s rules of procedure to introduce stricter rules.

MEPs are currently under no obligation to disclose whether amendments, questions or other parliamentary work were produced with the help of artificial intelligence.

Irish Renew lawmaker Barry Andrews, who chairs the Parliament’s development committee, said it was already clear that some MEPs were using AI to draft parliamentary questions, speeches and amendments.
