World.title: Emirates unveils ‘game-changing’ headrest across economy class
World.content:
Catching some Zs in economy class isn’t easy, and we’ve splashed plenty of cash on everything from eye masks to neck pillows in a bid to sleep better.

 

But for passengers flying with Emirates, there’s no need to buy anything to help in your quest for sleep because the airline has just unveiled a “game-changing” new headrest.

The U-Dream headrest, which is being rolled out across all of Emirates’ Airbus A350 aircraft and most of its Airbus A380s and Boeing 777s, features flexible side wings that mean you can sleep without your head falling forwards or sideways.

The UAE flag carrier is the first airline globally to introduce the headrest.

“Emirates never rests on its laurels when it comes to customer experience and we have found a way to significantly improve the comfort for Economy Class passengers, especially those travelling long-haul,” Sir Tim Clark, president of Emirates Airline, said.

“The U-Dream changes the game if the person wants to sleep – by supporting the neck in full. No more neck pillows needed. It’s another innovation that shows our commitment to customers and cements our Economy Class as the best.”

So far, three A350 aircraft have the headrest, and the entire fleet of A350 aircraft will have it by the end of the year.

From 2027, the headrest will also be installed on Emirates’ retrofitted A380s and 777s.

Economy class innovations

Earlier this week, US airline United announced it would be offering Economy Plus rows with no middle seat, giving customers extra elbow room and a shared table.

It comes after the airline unveiled its “relax rows”, a row of seats that convert into a bed.

Air New Zealand has just launched bunk beds on ultra long-haul flights that you can book for a four-hour window.

World.title: EU slaps €550 million fine on AliExpress over illegal and counterfeit goods
World.content:
The European Commission on Monday fined AliExpress €550 million for failing to adequately assess and mitigate risks linked to the sale of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products on its e-commerce platform.

 

The decision comes just days after the EU introduced a €3 flat duty on parcels worth less than €150, which had previously entered the bloc duty-free – a move expected to significantly affect the business models of Chinese online retail giants AliExpress, Shein and Temu.

The fine is the latest development in formal proceedings launched in 2024 over a potential breach of the EU’s Digital Services Act. The Commission found that AliExpress failed to establish an effective system to detect and remove illegal products, while underestimating the gap between the number of human moderators available and the scale of their workload.

The platform’s product compliance checks were also found to be vulnerable to abuse, with malicious traders allegedly misclassifying products to exploit less stringent requirements.

According to the Commission’s investigation, large volumes of illegal products – including unsafe toys and dangerous cosmetics – continued to circulate on AliExpress despite moderation efforts, in some cases remaining online for weeks after being flagged.

The Commission also found that AliExpress failed to properly enforce its penalty policy, allowing stores selling illegal products to remain active on the platform even after receiving sanctions.

The company’s brand authorisation system, designed to prevent the sale of counterfeit goods, was deemed ineffective and insufficiently robust to stop abuse, with sellers able to bypass safeguards and list fake products.

AliExpress now has until 20 October 2026 to submit an action plan outlining how it will address the Commission’s concerns. The EU executive will then decide within two months of receiving the plan whether further action is required.

Asked for comment by Euronews, AliExpress replied it has invested substantial resources in risk assessment and mitigation, product safety and consumer protection.

"We disagree with today’s decision and the disproportionate fine, which does not adequately reflect our established framework and the significant, proactive enhancements we have made," the company said in a statement. "We are carefully reviewing the decision and considering all available options."

World.title: After the whistle: AI videos, false quotes and the World Cup's biggest viral fakes
World.content:
The final whistle for the 2026 World Cup has blown, with Spain crowned world champions after beating Argentina 1-0 in the final which took place New Jersey.

 

Yet while the football is over, another tournament played out online with a slew of AI-generated videos, fabricated images and misleading clips spreading alongside the biggest matches, often racking up millions of views before being debunked.

The posts served a range of purposes, from humour and political messaging to criticism of players and their teams. Other publications were seemingly crafted to generate clicks and advertising revenue.

The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, took a look at some of the false and misleading content doing the rounds.

AI's favourite player: Erling Haaland

No player embodied the rise of AI-generated content in this tournament more than Norwegian striker Erling Haaland.

Perhaps the most viral was a video of him glancing up at his reflection in a restaurant and flinching. It garnered more than 30 million views in a single day, but it turned out to be a result of a face swap applied to a video originally posted by a Chinese content creator.

Fake video of Haaland Social media

However, it didn't seem to matter for fans of the player, with the video going on to gain a further 10 million views across social media.

Putting words into players' mouths

Nevertheless, not all false posts about Haaland were harmless.

One video on X showed the Manchester City striker speaking after Norway's defeat to England on 11 June, with the caption "I'm going to support Argentina because England illegally took their territory" attached to it.

Spanish subtitles in the video repeated the same statement, referring to Argentina's claim over the Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic.

This clip garnered thousands of views, but the caption is untrue.

Fake claims about Haaland Social media post from Instagram

In reality, the post-match interview of Haaland shows that when asked by the media who he would support for the rest of the tournament, he replied: "I think I have some of my [Manchester] City teammates in England, and in France, and Spain, so of course I want England to do well."

"I've been supporting ... I think I got an England national team jersey before I got a Norway jersey when I was little, so of course I want England to do well because it's a nice country and it's a nice t-shirt," he said in the clip.

Haaland is not the only player to fall victim to videos that put false claims in his mouth.

After the Norway-England match, England midfielder Jude Bellingham was quoted in viral posts as saying, "Messi is my idol" and "FIFA is rigged and corrupt." However, recordings of his post-match interviews show he made neither statement.

Claims tournament rigged for Argentina spark wave of fakes

One of the biggest conspiracy theories running throughout the World Cup alleged that the tournament was rigged for Argentina to win. It gained mass traction on social media, reaching a wide cross-generational audience.

“My two teenage boys are convinced the World Cup has been rigged for Argentina”, wrote one LinkedIn user.

The narrative intensified after Argentina's game against Egypt on 7 July, in which they won 3-2.

During the match, a series of referee decisions were viewed as controversial, in turn leading Egypt's Football Association to file a formal complaint with FIFA — accusing the match's referee, François Letexier, and his team of making "serious refereeing mistakes".

Debunked World Cup images Social media images on X

From there, theories began to spread beyond refereeing decisions, with social media users tying in unrelated events and public figures to argue that Argentina was receiving external support.

One of these alleged external backers was Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In an interview on The Mojo Podcast, Netanyahu described Argentina as a "very good team", stating that it was not Argentinian forward Lionel Messi, but in fact the country's President Javier Milei who had swayed his support. He described Milei as a "great friend" of Israel.

An AI-generated image of Netanyahu wearing an Argentinian shirt during the side's match against Austria was used to support this claim. It gained thousands of views on X but was ultimately AI-generated. Netanyahu did not attend the match.

Other posts focused on Messi himself, with users framing his reported ties to Israel as further evidence of rigging.

"Why did Messi visit Israel twice in 2022, the SAME YEAR that Argentina won the World Cup?", claimed one user in an X post with more than 80,000 views.

On social media, claims that the World Cup was rigged in favour of Argentina went viral Social media posts on X

Despite this, these claims were not backed up by any publicly available official sources, while accounts relaying them provided no concrete evidence.

Fabricated evidence instead emerged, such as an AI-generated image of FIFA President Gianni Infantino injecting performance-enhancing drugs into Messi's arm.

Another image, which gained thousands of views on X, alleges that the referee for the Argentina-England game, Ismail Elfath, had asked for a photo with Messi after the match.

But the image is actually from 2022, showcasing a moment which took place before a match between Argentina and France.

Another viral clip, which gained 8 million views on X alone, appeared to show Messi feigning injury against Switzerland.

However, visual inconsistencies, such as Swiss players' incorrect kits revealed that the video was in fact AI-generated.

World.title: Ukraine fires 400 drones at Moscow as Russia steps up ballistic missile attacks
World.content:
Ukraine launched over 400 drones toward Moscow overnight on Monday, reportedly hitting an oil depot and a logistics centre.

 

Ukrainian President Volodmyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also struck two shadow fleet tankers and four cargo ships in the Black Sea.

The attacks followed a weekend of escalating exchanges between the two sides, with Russia targeting Kyiv with ballistic missiles on Sunday and Ukraine hitting warehouses belonging to one of Russia's largest online marketplaces—Wildberries—outside of Moscow on Saturday.

On Saturday, the Ukrainian military struck two Wildberries warehouses. Local media reported that another fire was reported at a warehouse belonging to the Russian online retailer in Ukraine's latest attack.

Out of the 400 Ukrainian drones launched, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said most were downed away from the capital and 85 were intercepted near Moscow.

Ten people, including a child, were wounded and several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were damaged, the head of the region around Moscow Andrei Vorobyov reported.

Vorobyov listed damage in the towns of Podolsk, Domodedovo and Odintsovo.

A day earlier, Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, killing one person and injuring 16 others. In recent weeks, Moscow has intensified its use of ballistic missiles.

“Russian forces have launched more ballistic missiles against Ukraine thus far in July than Russia reportedly produces each month,” the Institute for the Study of War said on Sunday.

“Russia appears to be dipping into its stockpiles to continue increasing the number of ballistic missiles it launches against Ukraine, as these missiles have a higher success rate than drones and cruise missiles,” it added.

A residential building is seen in fire following a Russian air attack in Kramatorsk, Donetsk region, Ukraine, Monday, 20 July, 2026. Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP/Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP

According to Ukraine's air force, Russia launched 94 long-range strike drones at Ukraine overnight, of which Ukrainian air defences jammed or intercepted 81. Nine drones and a missile caused damage at nine locations.

The growing escalation indicates an agreement between the two sides remains distant, but Kyiv has said its strikes on the Russian capital are intended to damage Russia's offensive capabilities and pressure the Kremlin to negotiate.

"We are justly responding to every Russian strike on our cities and communities," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X. "This war must be ended, and that is possible only by intensifying pressure on the sole cause of this war".

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said he would hold "key talks" on Monday as he grapples with a domestic political crisis after announcing a cabinet reshuffle last week.

What began as anger over the dismissal of the reformist defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has swelled into public outrage over Zelenskyy's management of the military, and sparked protests demanding radical changes at the top command.

World.title: Oil prices rise as fighting between US and Iran intensifies
World.content:
Oil prices jumped in early trading as the US announced further attacks for a ninth consecutive night. Iran has responded to the strikes by targeting US allies across the Middle East.

 

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 3.2% to $90.95 per barrel, while US benchmark crude climbed 2.8% to $84.04 per barrel.

“The US and Iran continue to exchange strikes, which are proving to be deadly for both sides,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary on Monday.

"If this escalation goes unchecked, we could return to an environment of widespread attacks across the Persian Gulf," they added.

Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global oil transport, has nearly ground to a halt, adding to pressure on supplies, they noted.

Elsewhere, AI-related shares including chipmaking stocks declined on Friday, pulling world markets lower. Pledges of huge spending on AI are fuelling worries the sector may be in a bubble, and many investors have opted to sell to lock in profits from recent big gains.

“The return to war in the Strait of Hormuz may start to weigh more heavily on financial markets before too long, especially if even strong tech earnings reports continue to be met with scepticism,” Jonas Goltermann, chief markets economist at Capital Economics wrote in a note Monday.

Markets were also shaken by the rollout of another powerful Chinese AI model, this time by Beijing-based Moonshot AI.

The impact of the new Kimi K3 open-source AI model was similar to when China’s “ DeepSeek moment” rattled world markets in early 2025. It was viewed as another sign of how lower-cost, capable Chinese AI models are increasingly challenging rivals like Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT.

World.title: Hungary's PM Péter Magyar: 'It would be great honour if Judit Polgár accepted the presidency'
World.content:
Péter Magyar, the prime minister, has invited Judit Polgár, the most successful female chess player the world has ever seen, to become Hungary’s president. Polgár is the only woman in the history of chess to have broken the 2700 Elo rating barrier for super-grandmasters. She led the women’s world rankings for 26 consecutive years, achieved a career-best of eighth place on the overall world list, and is a two-time women’s Chess Olympiad champion. The widely respected athlete has not previously taken on any political role.

 

“Our country needs unity, peace and a president in whom every Hungarian can be proud. The presidency is not a profession, not a job, but the highest form of service. The president’s duty is to serve and to represent every Hungarian.

"The Judit Polgár put forward today as president by recognised figures of Hungarian public life is such a person, which is why I will meet her on Monday and ask whether, until the adoption of the new constitution, she is prepared to serve our country in a new role," the prime minister wrote in his Sunday evening Facebook post (source in Hungarian).

"For decades, Judit Polgár's name has been synonymous with talent and perseverance. As the most successful female player in chess history, she led the women's world rankings uninterrupted for 26 years, while also breaking into the top ten of the overall world list.

"A five-time Chess Olympiad champion, international grandmaster and recipient of the Order of Saint Stephen of Hungary, her extraordinary life story was recently presented in the documentary film The Queen of Chess.

"A few weeks ago, Christ’s College at the University of Cambridge elected her to its fellowship. Judit Polgár's career to date has always been about performance. The esteem in which she is held is not due to political loyalties or connections, but to her exceptional talent, diligence, extraordinary stamina and integrity.

"She is a Hungarian whose achievements inspire respect and admiration at home and across the world", Magyar continued in his post.

At the beginning of July, the prime minister posted a photo on his social media accounts showing him playing chess with Judit Polgár. Since then there has been lively speculation as to whether Magyar is considering her as his candidate for head of state.

On Saturday evening, President Tamás Sulyok announced that he would sign the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law. His mandate will end on the day after the law is promulgated, meaning that from midnight on Sunday he is no longer Hungary’s president. For one month, the office will be held by the Speaker of the National Assembly, Ágnes Forsthoffer.

On Sunday, sixteen leading figures from science, culture and sport wrote a letter to Forsthoffer, proposing chess player Judit Polgár for the presidency. The Ügyvédkör lawyers’ group, meanwhile, announced it is putting forward Péter Bárándy as its candidate for president.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: How 'blue dot fever' is affecting concerts
World.content:
Live music remains popular, but many concerts are struggling with unsold tickets and cancellations. While superstars fill stadiums, smaller venues and acts are facing a crisis.

The term "blue dot fever" has been circulating in the media for some time now. "Blue dots" refer to available seats on US ticket sales platform Ticketmaster. Lots of empty seats right before a concert can spell trouble for both artists and organizers — including cancelled shows. With more and more concerts afflicted by this "illness," is the future of the concert scene uncertain?

The economy of superstars

The situation is quite different for big name stars. Leading musicians like Beyonce, Oasis and Coldplay still easily fill large stadiums.

According to official Pollstar charts, Beyonce had the most successful music tour in 2025, generating over $400 million (Є359 million) in revenue. The Oasis Live '25 tour was one of the biggest box office successes in recent years. Coldplay also remains a strong crowd-pleaser, with many concerts on their current world tour selling out instantly.

Yet all big concerts share a common challenge: rising costs, as points out Johannes Everke from Germany's Federal Association of the Concert and Event Industry: "Due to increasing personnel costs, rising technical costs, energy and inflation, we have soaring production costs in comparison with 2019." As a result, tickets are becoming more expensive, meaning fewer fans can afford them.

However, the impact of these rising costs are not evenly experienced across the board. Stephan Thanscheidt from FKP Scorpio, one of the largest concert and festival promoters in Europe, confirms this. "Several factors are in play here, such as some megastars having huge legions of fans who’d never miss their idols for anything. And if they need to keep an eye on their spending, many people would choose to go for a large concert, perceived to be a major event, over several smaller ones if they need to keep an eye on their spending."

Beyonce topped the list of the highest-grossing tours of 2025 with her 'Cowboy Carter Tour' Image: Cover-Images/IMAGO

The late US economist Alan B. Krueger called this "the economics of superstars," in which only a few superstars generate most of the revenue.

What about the stars of tomorrow?

Johannes Everke believes the live music market is under significant strain. Typically, organizers rely on revenue generated from large concerts to fund smaller, lesser-known acts. However, this model is at risk of collapsing if the profit margins are reduced.

Everke says that while large ticket sales at mega-events guarantee high revenue, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the promoters are gaining big profits due to ticket prices rising at a slower rate compared to promotion costs.

"The circle of life means supporting smaller bands for a period until they become big enough to start making money. You then take those profits in turn and reinvest in so-called product development by supporting smaller acts once again," Everke told DW.

He started out with intimate concerts and now fills stadiums: Ed Sheeran in 2011 (left) and 2024 Image: M. Harris/Capital Pictures/C. E. Junior/Fotoarena/IMAGO

One prominent example is Ed Sheeran, who, along with others, was supported by FKP Scorpio over the years before becoming a top-selling star. "Many of our current successes began as passion projects, and we couldn't always know whether they would end up being financially successful," Stephan Thanscheidt confirms. "It wouldn’t be possible without cross-financing new ideas or artists we believe in. When we succeed today, we make tomorrow’s successes more likely."

Concerts are no longer promotion tours

Another complicating factor is how the economics of concerts has changed.

Everke explains that in the past, tours served to promote new albums. "You’d play concerts and even if you lost money on them, you’d recoup the costs through album sales. So, labels would sometimes give financial contributions to concert tours." But in the age of streaming, this is no longer the case.

According to Everke, approximately half of artists’ income now comes from live performances. So, the pressure to achieve commercial success through touring is extremely high.

Additionally, many established musicians are having much longer careers now. "They’re all playing an endless series of concerts because record sales alone no longer provide enough for them to make a living," Everke says. This situation leads to a saturated market and intensified competition for audience retention.

Moving away from touring?

Some megastars have shifted away from touring and are now establishing "residencies." These are series of concerts in which artists perform at the same venue over an extended period of time.

Coming to Europe in the autumn: Shakira at the opening ceremony of the World Cup in Mexico in June Image: Kai Pfaffenbach/REUTERS

One major example of this is Shakira, who is set to play a series of 12 concerts in the second half of 2026 in Madrid. Demand has been so high that additional dates have been announced on more than one occasion. The performances will take place in the "Estadio Shakira," a built-for-purpose stadium.

Harry Styles is another such example: In June, he played 12 concerts in London's Wembley Stadium.

Johannes Everke does not see this being a sustainable model for the future of the market though, as only very few artists are able to attract fans from all over Europe, or across continents.

Why solidarity is needed — the British example

Johannes Everke remains optimistic despite the challenges and warning signals. Live music events are in demand as never before, and the market is growing.

According to the GEMA organization, around 70 million people attended concerts featuring popular music (mostly pop and rock) in Germany in 2024, which is more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Even though a select few superstars will continue to account for the majority of the market’s revenue in the near future, Everke believes that the market will still expand to a broader audience. He remains certain that "people always want to hear something new and will always be wanting to hear new music and new trends."

Mega event in London in June: The Harry Styles Residency at Wembley Stadium Image: Stephen Chung/London News Pictures/ZUMA/picture alliance

Everke maintains that it is important to continue supporting smaller events. He cites a positive example from the British LIVE Trust model — at many large concerts, one pound per ticket is voluntarily contributed to a fund that supports small venues and the grassroots music scene.

Harry Styles supported this effort during his London residency, which Everke says is a "fantastic sign of solidarity within the industry."

Perhaps the many "blue dots" are not a sign of waning interest in live music, but instead show a market in transition. The challenge now is to preserve and nurture smaller venues and artists.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: DRC neighbors boost preparedness as Ebola cases surge
World.content:
Uganda, Rwanda and Zambia are strengthening border screening, disease surveillance and emergency response measures. The growing Ebola outbreak in the DRC is raising concerns about cross-border spread.

Countries bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have stepped up screening at border crossings, trained frontline health workers, and activated emergency plans to reduce the risk of imported cases as the DRC battles a growing Ebola outbreak.

The country's health ministry said on Monday that at least 930 people have died due to the illness. The country has recorded 2,344 cases of the Bundibugyo strain. The outbreak, which started on May 15, 2026, is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently warned that the number of cases could be 2-4 times higher than what is known.

In Zambia, authorities have stepped up screening at points of entry despite recording no confirmed Ebola cases. Dr. Naeem Dalal, assistant director for preparedness and response at the Zambia National Public Health Institute (ZNPHI), told DW that infection prevention measures had been reinforced nationwide.

The Ebola survivors of DR Congo To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Infection prevention and control is currently being activated, where a lot of disinfection will be taking place, and face masks and washing of hands with soap and water will become mandatory," Dalal said.

He added that provincial public health emergency response centers had been activated to coordinate a rapid response if suspected cases are detected.

Uganda, which has successfully contained previous Ebola outbreaks, has also increased surveillance along its border with the DRC. Speaking on Uganda National Television, Dr. Beda Senkware of Kabale Referral Hospital said three western districts remain particularly vulnerable.

"The risk of getting this disease, Ebola, is very high. We have three districts that border the DRC — Kisoro, Kanungu and Rukungiri. These three districts have been put at the highest risk of getting Ebola," Senkware said.

The WHO and the Africa CDC have urged neighboring DRC countries to remain vigilant Image: Hajarah Nalwadda/AP Photo/picture alliance

Rwanda has likewise strengthened health screening at border crossings, expanded disease surveillance and prepared rapid response teams to investigate suspected cases.

The East African Community's response to Ebola

Regional cooperation is also increasing. The East African Community (EAC) has agreed on a coordinated response to improve preparedness and reduce the risk of cross-border transmission.

EAC Secretary General Stephen Mbundi said partner states are working with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), the World Health Organization (WHO) and other partners to expand surveillance, laboratory testing and emergency response capacity.

"We are mobilizing regional mechanisms and working closely with Partner States, Africa CDC, WHO and development partners to strengthen surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, risk communication and rapid response capacities," Mbundi emphasized.

The heightened preparedness follows a warning from the WHO that the outbreak may be significantly larger than official figures indicate because many infections are going undetected in conflict-affected areas of eastern DRC.

Speaking during a virtual news conference in Geneva, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the outbreak had become "the third largest Ebola outbreak on record" and had "expanded faster than any previous outbreak" over the past month.

Tedros also called on international donors to help close a funding gap of more than $400 million (€344 million) for the joint WHO-Africa CDC preparedness and response plan.

The conflict in eastern DRC coupled with skepticism and rumors are complicating the fight against the epidemic Image: Arlette Bashizi/REUTERS

The outbreak is centered in eastern DRC, where conflict, insecurity and population displacement have complicated efforts to identify cases, trace contacts and contain the virus. The DRC has experienced several Ebola outbreaks since the virus was first identified there in 1976, but health experts say insecurity has made the current outbreak especially difficult to contain. There is currently no known vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain.

Africa CDC urges countries to focus on early Ebola detection

Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya urged neighboring countries to strengthen surveillance and laboratory capacity to improve early detection.

"This outbreak started in Ituri. Now it's moved to Uganda and to other parts of the DRC. That is putting countries neighboring the DRC at risk," Kaseya said, adding that timely detection remains critical to preventing wider transmission.

What makes this Ebola outbreak different To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"If countries do not increase capacity to detect, they are really at risk. This is the message we are giving to countries: if you are near the DRC, please increase your capacity to detect."

Professor Aileen Marty, an infectious disease specialist at Florida International University, said the ongoing violence continues to undermine containment efforts.

"The cases have continued to rise because it's a highly inflamed area where there has been ongoing conflict for over a decade," Marty said.

"A few of our treatment centers have been burnt down. That discourages health workers from going there to manage patients and increases the number of people who travel elsewhere while infected. That is also making it extraordinarily challenging."

Marty said the situation underscores the importance of preparedness in neighboring countries, where surveillance, rapid diagnosis and coordinated public health responses remain the best defense against regional spread.

Apart from Uganda, no other neighboring country has linked a confirmed case to the current outbreak, but health officials say vigilance remains essential until transmission in the DRC is brought under control. They warn that sustained investment in surveillance, laboratory capacity and regional cooperation will be critical to preventing the virus from spreading across borders.

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

World.title: Germany news: Resistance to Nazi terror commemorated
World.content:
07/20/2026 July 20, 2026 German housing rental up 4%

The cost of rent has risen 4% year-on year in the second quarter, according to figures from the German Economic Institute (IW).

The IW said that rent continued a significant nationwide rise as it provided statistics on rental prices and stagnating purchase prices.

"Rents rose particularly sharply in Cologne (+7.9%), followed by Hamburg (+5.5%) and Leipzig (+5.4%)," the IW said in a new report.

The IW said that the supply of rental apartments remained below the level seen in 2022 in most major cities.

The IW said that the rental market was battling with a shortage of available units with dramatic declines seen in a number of cities.

"In Hamburg, the number of rental listings has more than halved, by 57%. Frankfurt am Main has seen a 43% decrease in listings, and Leipzig a 40% drop," the IW said.

The exception was Berlin, where there was a 43% increase when compared to 2022.

World.title: Taking stock of 2026 World Cup: Football's biggest show yet
World.content:
A worthy world champion, a call from the US president, security concerns and a few pleasant surprises. The 2026 World Cup is over. So what will we remember about global football's biggest World Cup ever?

Football didn't have it easy at the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada.

There were questionable decisions by FIFA, the sport's governing body, as well as a lot of spectacle and a final in which only one team actually played football.

After a total of 104 games in this biggest-ever World Cup, Spain were deservedly crowned champions and for the first time, a country's men's and women's teams are both world champions at the same time.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino described the tournament as the "greatest sporting, social and cultural event in humanity," while US President Donald Trump congratulated FIFA on what he called "one of the all-time greatest sporting events in history."

But was it really? Here's what will be remembered.

How was the biggest-ever tournament received by viewers?

Fears of empty stadiums — especially in the US, where football isn't the number one sport — proved unfounded. According to FIFA, 6,810,966 fans attended the tournament, the first to be co-hosted by three countries. This set a new record for World Cup attendance.

Given that the schedule featured 104 matches, instead of 64 at previous tournaments, a record attendance figure is no surprise. The average attendance was around 65,000, and according to FIFA, 99.7% of all available seats were filled. However, many empty seats were visible in stadiums, especially during the group stage.

Hydration breaks draw criticism

Fans criticized the newly introduced hydration breaks. Most coaches, however, supported the breaks — or, at least, did not complain about them.

Uruguay’s now-former coach, Marcelo Bielsa, on the other hand, criticized the additional opportunity to influence the game.

"Playing four halves instead of two changes the culturally shaped perception of football," he said. "These breaks add nothing to the game, but take a lot away from it."

Germany felt both the advantages and disadvantages of the hydration breaks Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

Were there any surprises at this World Cup?

World Cup newcomer Cape Verde caused quite a stir. The small African nation held eventual world champions Spain to a 0-0 draw and narrowly lost to defending champions Argentina in extra time in the round of 32.

The Democratic Republic of Congo celebrated a 1-1 draw against Portugal and its superstar, Cristiano Ronaldo. Paraguay knocked Germany out of the tournament in the round of 32. Curacao, the smallest World Cup participant, made history by scoring their first-ever World Cup goal against Germany and earned their first-ever World Cup point against Ecuador.

Price madness at World Cup

This World Cup was expensive. Fans had to dig deep into their pockets for tickets, hotels, parking fees or flights. However, prices inside the stadiums caused additional frustration. In the US, visitors had to pay up to €20 ($22) for a beer, more than €17 for French fries or about €7 for a bottle of water.

In Mexico, too, food and drinks were significantly more expensive than usual. At the Azteca Stadium, where the opening match took place, a beer cost the equivalent of about €15.50 — almost as much as the country's minimum daily wage.

Tickets for the final were unaffordable and unattainable for most people Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

What role did Trump play at the World Cup?

There was widespread concern that Trump might use the World Cup to advance his political agenda. After all, the US president had repeatedly declared the tournament to be his personal prestige project. Yet Trump didn’t show up at the stadium until the final and largely kept a low profile during the tournament.

Nevertheless, the 80-year-old sparked the biggest scandal of the tournament. After US forward Folarin Balogun was shown a red card, he successfully lobbied FIFA President Infantino to review the automatic ban for the next game.

Balogun was allowed to play in the round-of-16 match against Belgium, but couldn't stop America from losing to Belgium.

"The current FIFA president has bowed to Donald Trump," said former FIFA boss Joseph Blatter. However, the criticism of Infantino is reportedly unlikely to jeopardize his potential reelection as FIFA president in March 2027.

How safe was the World Cup?

The war in the Middle East and unrest in Mexico had raised significant security concerns in the run-up to the tournament. While the games in Canada and the US went off largely without a hitch, there were several incidents in Mexico. Fans stormed an already overcrowded fan zone in Guadalajara; after a victory by the co-hosts, a car plowed into a celebrating crowd; and several people died during victory celebrations in Mexico City.

In addition to numerous fans, particularly from African countries, Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry into the US despite having a valid visa. The authorities cited security concerns over alleged ties to a terrorist organization in his home country as the reason. The Somali FIFA referee is still expected to receive his salary due from the World Cup.

Many fans of African nations were not allowed to travel to the US for games Image: John E Sokolowski/IMAGN IMAGES/REUTERS

What was the human rights situation like?

Many human rights organizations have given FIFA an extremely poor rating.

"This World Cup has been played against a backdrop of the U.S. government’s abusive immigration crackdown," said Minky Worden of Human Rights Watch.

She also pointed to a "failure by FIFA to uphold its own human rights standards."

This seems to contradict any claim of this being the "most inclusive World Cup in history."

"FIFA had promised that everyone could feel safe. The truth is different. ICE, for example, has doubled the number of arrests," said Daniel Norona of Amnesty International USA.

Ronan Evain of the fan organization "Football Supporters Europe" criticized the opaque process for issuing visas to fans, particularly those from non-European countries.

"Our observations have revealed little or no evidence that ticket holders from Africa and Asia actually received visas to enter the US," Evain said.

What's next after the World Cup?

For Infantino, further expanding the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams is certainly conceivable. Instead of the current 104, there would then be 128 matches.

"That is definitely an issue that will be examined after this World Cup and discussed within the committees," the FIFA president told Swiss broadcaster "blue Sport."

Despite the widespread criticism of Infantino, his position as FIFA president is not in jeopardy. On the contrary: More games mean more money that he can distribute to the member nations. Next year, Infantino is expected to be re-elected to his post for the third time.

If reelected, Infantino would be in charge until 2031, a year after the next World Cup, which is to be spread over three continents. A total of three games will be played in Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina before the tournament moves to Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: UK: Andy Burnham to take office as seventh PM in 10 years
World.content:
After securing the leadership of the ruling Labour Party last week, Burnham will be invited to form a government by King Charles III.

Newly-minted Labour Party leader Andy Burnham is set to meet with the UK's King Charles III on Monday, the traditional final step in becoming the country's head of government.

Burnham will be the seventh British prime minister in the last 10 years since the UK voted to leave the European Union.

His predecessor Keir Starmer announced that he was stepping aside in June after several Cabinet ministers resigned amid plummeting poll numbers and questions about his leadership.

Former mayor of Greater Manchester Burnham managed to win a risky special election in June in order to re-enter parliament.

What is expected today?

For Burnham to officially become prime minister, Starmer will formally tender his resignation to King Charles III.

In prepared remarks as he left 10 Downing Street, the outgoing leader highlighted his role in taking Labour from slumping poll numbers to a "landslide victory" two years ago.

"Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago," he said, claiming a better economy, shorter NHS wait times, and decreasing immigration.

He wished his successor "every success" and said offered his full support.

Later today, Burnham will also meet with the King, who will then call on the Labour leader to form a government.

He is then expected to give a short speech before heading into the Downing Street offices.

World.title: Guyana: Dozens feared dead after ferry capsizes
World.content:
Rescuers have been able to save 67 passengers so far. It is unknown exactly how many people were on board as authorities said the passengers' list is inaccurate.

Several people were feared dead after a ferry carrying more than 100 people capsized off the coast of Guyana, authorities said.

The ferry MV Barima left Guyana at the northeast corner of South America on Saturday afternoon, carrying at least 133 people for a trip from the capital Georgetown to Port Kaituma.

Public Works Minister Juan Edghill said that the list of people on board was not "a true reflection of the occupants on board," asking family members and loved ones to reach out to officials to create an official tally of those missing.

The inaccuracy in the list of passengers has created an additional challenge as authorities do not know how many people they are searching for.

Rescue operations underway

The rescue operations were launched after air traffic control received a distress call from the ferry around 11 p.m. local time on Saturday.

Rescue teams have so far saved 67 people. The rescued victims include 41 men, 11 women, six boys and nine girls, Prime Minister Mark Phillips said in a statement Sunday.

"The families of those rescued, as well as the relatives of all recorded passengers and crew members, have been engaged," Phillips said, adding that "the captain and mate of the vessel, who were among those rescued, have returned to the area to assist with the search and rescue operation."

However, no survivors have been found since Sunday afternoon.

"Search and rescue is still in progress," Public Works Minister ‌Edghill said. "So to the families that are out there wondering about their loved ones, we are doing everything that is humanly possible to find them."

Rescuers have found 67 survivors so far Image: Bishop Juan Edghill/Handout/REUTERS

What do we know about the cause of the incident?

Prime Minister Mark Phillips said investigators are looking into the incident, adding that two crew members were found to have tested positive for cannabis.

Phillips said that the vessel, which had had maintenance in 2024 and was due for an inspection later this year, reported a cargo weight of 268 tons out of a 284-ton-capacity.

It was licensed to carry more than 300 passengers and it was equipped with 250 life jackets, six inflatable life rafts and two rigid life rafts, according to the prime minister.

"Let me be absolutely clear: where negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing is established, those responsible will face the full force of the law," Phillips said in a Sunday evening press conference.

World.content:

US motorists are in for more pain at the pump Image: Brandon Bell/Getty Images/AFP

The average price in the US for a gallon of gasoline rose to $4 a gallon (€3.50) again on Monday amid renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, up from $3.14 a gallon one year ago, according to motor club federation AAA.

The average gas price in the US first exceeded $4 a gallon at the end of March, falling in mid-June as crude oil prices dropped after Washington and Tehran reached an interim deal.

People around the world, including in Germany, are seeing higher prices at the pump as a result of the war, which has drastically reduced global oil supply through the virtual closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

As the US and Iran move closer to resuming an all-out war, oil prices have risen again, with Brent crude, the international standard, climbing 3.2% to $90.95 per barrel and benchmark US crude creeping up 2.8% to $84.04 per barrel on Monday.

World.title: España habita la eternidad
World.content:
La Roja consigue su segundo Mundial con un gol de Ferran Torres en la prórroga después de reducir a la Argentina de Messi, que no tiró ni una vez hasta el minuto 117

Imposible no recordar Sudáfrica, a Iniesta, a Cesc, la prórroga, el abismo, la gloria. Imposible no verlo en este instante de Ferran Torres que sucedió diez minutos antes, el 106 después de años celebrando la leyenda del 116. Porro envió una pelota al área, Nico Williams la dejó atrás con la coronilla y Ferran reventó la red y provocó otro estallido inolvidable, la segunda estrella, el segundo título mundial contra la última campeona, a la que redujo casi a la nada. No tiró ni una vez hasta después del gol de la Roja, algo insólito. Ningún equipo se había pasado los 90 minutos de una final sin intentarlo. Ninguno tampoco hasta el 117. El juego de la selección de Luis de la Fuente desmanteló a la Argentina del mítico 10, la abrasó con el juego, la fue pinchando con una sucesión de tiros blandos y la acabó rematando con un zurdazo. Despidió a Messi de los mundiales con una exhibición coral.

ESP España 1 Unai Simón, Pedro Porro, Aymeric Laporte (Eric García, min. 98), Marc Cucurella, Pau Cubarsí, Dani Olmo (Mikel Merino, min. 74), Álex Baena (Nico Williams, min. 74), Rodri (Martín Zubimendi, min. 98), Lamine Yamal, Fabián Ruiz (Pedri, min. 61) y Mikel Oyarzabal (Ferran Torres, min. 61) ARG Argentina 0 Emiliano Martínez, Cristian Romero (Facundo Medina, min. 69), Gonzalo Montiel (Nahuel Molina, min. 57), Nicolás Tagliafico, Lisandro Martínez (Nicolás Otamendi, min. 43), Nico González (Leandro Paredes, min. 45), Alexis Mac Allister, Rodrigo De Paul (Giuliano Simeone, min. 69), Enzo Fernández, Julián Alvarez (Marcos Senesi, min. 101) y Lionel Messi Goles 1-0 min. 105: Ferran Arbitro Slavko Vincic

Tarjetas amarillas Lisandro Martínez (min. 40), Paredes (min. 51), Enzo Fernández (min. 81), Cristian Romero (min. 91), Scaloni (min. 103), Alexis Mac Allister (min. 110) Tarjetas rojas Enzo Fernández (min. 92)

España habita ya la eternidad. Se asomó en Sudáfrica, con la primera versión de un libreto de juego brillante y evolucionó durante algo más de una década a la fórmula prodigiosa con la que ganó la Eurocopa de 2024 y ahora el segundo Mundial. Imposible no recordar Sudáfrica, que llegó también después de un Europeo. La primera estrella es aviso al mundo, sacar la cabeza. La segunda supone instalarse en la eternidad del fútbol.

El entusiasmo por el gol de Ferran, por el juego que parecía inevitable que llevara al título mostró también algo asombroso de un país sumergido en la crispación, pero que ha encontrado algo en lo que consigue ponerse de acuerdo para producir una criatura tan hermosa como este equipo. Para producirlo y para disfrutarlo.

00:40 El gol de Ferran Torres que le ha dado su segundo Mundial a España El gol de Ferrán Torres. Foto: Seth Wenig (AP Photo) | Vídeo: VÍDEO SOLO DISPONIBLE EN ESPAÑA

Lo gigantesco de la ocasión, una final de la Copa del Mundo, no desfiguró a España. Todo lo contrario. Se ha construido para citas de este vuelo estratosférico. Salió a tejer su juego y a asfixiar al rival con lo que le saliera puntada a puntada. Argentina, como casi siempre en el Mundial, parecía querer dejarlo para más adelante, hasta los minutos en los que Messi despierta del letargo. Pero no eran ellos. Era el juego apabullante de la Roja, que los redujo como nadie.

Solo les quedaba aguantar y empezaron levantando las barricadas por el centro. Mac Allister, Enzo Fernández, De Paul y Nico González se apretaban en la zona por la que España ha desplegado sus tramos más brillantes. La encontraron sobrepoblada, pero Dani Olmo maniobra en esos callejones como un escapista que negocia con su propia trampa. Se giró, tiró una pared con Lamine y el extremo del Barcelona se vio en el área ante el Dibu Martínez. Lisandro desvió el tiro y el portero reaccionó con solvencia.

España tocaba, Argentina mantenía los equilibrios, un plan de resistencia que le funciona como a nadie. Porque nadie tiene a Messi, claro, de paseo por la hierba recién regada mientras el resto se desgasta, tomando las medidas del rival para confeccionar el traje en su cabeza. Era pronto para el 10, pero a la defensa española se le distrajo un balón y se encontró encarando a Unai Simón, que aceleró para despejar antes de que lo controlara. No reaccionó a tiempo. No era el momento.

00:19 La entrada a Cubarsí por la que ha sido expulsado Enzo Fernández Foto: JEENAH MOON | Vídeo: VÍDEO SOLO DISPONIBLE EN ESPAÑA

Tampoco era la ruta por la que se esperaba el encuentro. Aunque Unai tuvo que esprintar otra vez para desactivar una carrera de Julián Alvarez. Quedó en nada. Todavía no se había disparado la señal. La refriega iba hacia el otro lado. Argentina ponía cara de que era lo de siempre. Pero no. La señal no llegaba. No había cómo.

España insistía con una partitura en la que Rodri marcaba el tempo y Olmo tocaba la trompeta. El azulgrana pisaba el acelerador y viraba el viento. Buscaban poco a poco más a Lamine Yamal, pero Scaloni le había preparado la vigilancia de dos laterales, Tagliafico y Nico González. Le iban delimitando el territorio, indicándole hasta dónde tenían pensado permitirle avanzar. Que era poco. Enseguida se encontraba con un cuerpo que le chocaba por detrás. Igual que Oyarzabal, desconectado hasta que aparecía por el medio, pero que también iba acumulando rasguños de sus encuentros con los argentinos.

La Roja se enfrentaba a una ardua faena de desbroce, rama a rama, trampa a trampa. Pero este equipo juega con una confianza colosal en la fórmula. Solo se acelera para ir hacia delante. No se demora a contemplarse mientras acumula pases. No se exhibe. Ausculta la fortaleza para introducir una cuña, para abrir una grieta y lanzarse a través de ella.

00:21 El gol anulado a Nico Williams Foto: MATT SLOCUM | Vídeo: VÍDEO SOLO DISPONIBLE EN ESPAÑA

Argentina acumula horas de resistencia. Esta vez sin respiro, porque no acertaba con los pases. Scaloni maniobró ya en el descanso. Retiró a Nico González y metió a Paredes para seguir vigilando a Lamine, que no encontraba la manera. Messi ni aparecía. El jugador del Barça encaraba, buscaba, pero se perdía en el roce con el que lo trataban.

Después de una hora de paciencia, De la Fuente intervino para seguir empujando. Ferran entró por Oyarzabal y Pedri, por Fabián, buena compañía de Rodri. La música era la misma. Argentina no consideraba necesario nada más. Entraron en el último cuarto, después de la segunda pausa de hidratación, sin haber intentado un solo tiro. Pero con el inconveniente de que se le lesionó otro central, el Cuti Romero.

Lamine consiguió sacar un centro al área, pero Ferran le entregó la pelota de cabeza al Dibu. Pedri encontró un pasadizo desde la frontal, avanzó y tiró muy blando, también al portero. Cubarsí probó desde lejos como contra Bélgica y el Dibu con pudo quedarse con el balón. Salió también Nico Williams y le puso un centro a Laporte, a quien le salió un cabezazo sencillo para el portero.

La respuesta argentina a la tormenta fue insistir en el choque, como vía para llegar a cero a la prórroga. Y ahí les llevó el Dibu con una extraordinaria parada a un tiro libro de Lamine. Se adentraron en ese territorio límite con un futbolista menos por la doble amarilla a Enzo. Su plan entonces era más lija y menos juego. España siguió a lo suyo, con un Nico Williams eléctrico. España ganó con la academia y resistió a la calle, para una segunda estrella eterna.

World.title: El agua que hace crecer la población de toda una comarca
World.content:
Las plantas de Bezoya en Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) son un ejemplo de cómo innovación, adaptación, sostenibilidad y responsabilidad empresarial consiguen retener a vecinos de toda la zona que quieren trabajar y vivir en el mismo lugar

Carla Pardo era una niña la primera vez que pisó la embotelladora en la que hoy trabaja; fue en una excusión escolar. Desde su pueblo, San Cristóbal de Segovia, se tardan apenas cinco minutos en coche hasta la fábrica, situada en Trescasas, y esa proximidad marca la diferencia en su día a día: “Es calidad de vida, un lujo que no se compensa con otras cosas”, confiesa esta joven de 32 años, responsable de Calidad de las dos plantas de Bezoya en la provincia de Segovia. La segunda también está cerca, a unos 25 kilómetros de distancia, en Ortigosa del Monte. La combinación ha supuesto que Pardo haya podido quedarse donde se ha criado; de hecho, acaba de comprarse una casa.

Pardo no es una excepción. La mayor parte de la plantilla de estas dos embotelladoras está formada por vecinos de la zona. Su compañero Sergio Moreno (Otero de Herreros, 41 años) entró en la de Ortigosa del Monte hace 10 años por una baja, pasó a tener un contrato indefinido y escaló: “Empecé aprendiendo a manejar distintas máquinas y carretillas”, recuerda. Actualmente es jefe del equipo de Producción. “Si respondes bien, puedes ir creciendo”, explica. “Fue la mejor decisión de mi vida a nivel profesional”. Él también es de los alrededores, vive tan solo a cuatro kilómetros de su puesto de trabajo. “He nacido aquí y no me iría ni a Segovia capital. La tranquilidad, la naturaleza y la cercanía con los vecinos son fundamentales para mí”.

Sergio Moreno, jefe del equipo de Producción, sujeta la botella de agua PI (de 3,14 litros), uno de los nuevos formatos de la marca. Santi Bur

Para Carla Pardo, “cada vez más personas pueden desarrollar una carrera profesional en un entorno rural gracias a la existencia de empresas con empleo sólido”. Su testimonio refleja una de las principales apuestas de Bebidas Bezoya, como subraya su director general, Sergio Bravo (Santander, 48 años): “Tenemos en las plantas 170 empleados y en la compañía somos 230 en total; es una plantilla muy estable a la que iremos incorporando más personas”. Los tres, Pardo, Moreno y Bravo, son el ejemplo de cómo el viaje del agua del manantial a los negocios o casas retiene el talento de los pueblos.

Diseños innovadores y más sostenibles

En embotelladoras como estas se necesitan, además, personas de muy distinta cualificación. Como afirman desde Bezoya, la empresa tiene dos objetivos: la sostenibilidad y la adaptación a las demandas de sus clientes. Como explica Bravo: “La sostenibilidad es un eje clave en Bezoya, y no solo la económica y social, también la medioambiental”. Esa gestión responsable está vinculada a la innovación y a crear nuevos productos, dos pilares que se refuerzan mutuamente. Por ejemplo, han renovado los formatos pequeños y medianos para que sean más ligeros, ergonómicos y sostenibles. Su opción de bag in box (una caja de cartón con dispensador) utiliza un 70% menos de plástico que una botella convencional de capacidad similar. Además, han lanzado la botella PI de 3,14 litros, diseñada con menos material que otras alternativas equivalentes. “Permite la comodidad de una garrafa, pero es fácil de almacenar, de servir y cabe en la nevera”, describe Bravo.

Pero el objetivo de ser más responsables medioambientalmente es transversal, y empieza por el origen. “Cuidamos la diversidad del entorno del manantial”, asegura su director general. Lo hacen de la mano la Red Natura 2000, fundamental para la conservación de la naturaleza en la Unión Europea, cuyo propósito es asegurar la supervivencia a largo plazo de las especies y los tipos de hábitat. Esta red asegura la compatibilidad entre las actividades humanas y el uso adecuado del territorio.

Las fábricas de Bezoya emplean energía 100% renovable. Además, valorizan más del 90% de residuos y compensan la diferencia con reforestación, según Bravo. Toda la flota comercial es híbrida o eléctrica y las botellas están hechas en su totalidad de otras botellas recicladas.

Para trabajar en estos propósitos de forma más eficiente, en febrero la empresa matriz, Pascual, lanzó el Proyecto Aura, una reorganización que ha convertido sus distintas áreas de negocio en cinco compañías especializadas (Lácteos, Café, Distribución e Internacional, además de Hidratación). Todas mantienen un gobierno común, pero cada una cuenta ahora con un equipo propio y una hoja de ruta para adaptarse mejor a su mercado. En el caso de Bezoya, “el objetivo es trascender el agua mineral sin gas y consolidarse como una compañía centrada en la hidratación saludable”, describe Bravo, al frente de esa unidad.

Sergio Bravo, director general de Bebidas Bezoya, posa desde la embotelladora de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) con la Sierra de Guadarrama de fondo. Santi Burgos

Un agua de calidad

El consumidor es cada vez más exigente. “Su preocupación van más allá del precio, pide productos que no solo le ayuden a cuidar su salud, también quiere impactar lo mínimo en el medioambiente”, afirma Bravo. Por eso, responden con “máxima coherencia” y con mineralización muy débil (’Para vivir muy fuerte’, dice su lema). Como apunta Pardo, esta tipología “puede generar en el organismo una especie de limpieza. Las células del torrente sanguíneo están cargadas con distintos minerales y, al tener el agua una mineralización muy baja, si esa concentración es alta, la arrastra”. En cambio, si el agua tiene una mineralización media, el equilibrio se mantiene y, si es alta, aporta más electrolitos y minerales, “lo que ayuda a recuperar las sales”.

Pardo, como responsable de Calidad, se asegura de que el producto llegue al consumidor con las mismas propiedades con las que emerge del manantial. “El agua viene así de la montaña: es buena y pura, con una composición estable químicamente”, explica. La travesía hasta que llega al envase da comienzo en la sierra de Guadarrama, en un perímetro de protección al que llaman la zona de captación. Allí, la pluviometría (la lluvia o la precipitación que cae) se filtra por un terreno granítico, un tipo de suelo que deja esa mineralización tan baja.

Carla Pardo, la responsable de Calidad de las plantas de Bezoya, en el laboratorio de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia). SANTI BURGOS

El alumbramiento, la primera vez que se ve el agua, es ya dentro de la botella. Después pasa por el etiquetado, el loteado y el empaquetado, y ya queda lista para que el consumidor la beba. En todo momento, su temperatura se mantiene fría. “En invierno es aproximadamente de 9 grados y en verano puede llegar hasta los 13″, indica la experta.

En la zona de captación “no hay absolutamente nada; ni pozos ni ninguna extracción externa, porque el agua nos llega por gravedad”, describe la segoviana. Tampoco realizan intervenciones en el entorno más allá de la construcción necesaria para la planta que, en los últimos años, se ha ampliado. Sergio Moreno ha sido testigo de esta evolución: “Me motiva haber llegado desde abajo y ser parte de estos cambios; la fábrica, la línea, la formatos... Todo se ha modernizado”. Una evolución que, más allá de la adaptación a las demandas de los clientes y a la sostenibilidad, permite que el trabajo perdure, los puestos se mantengan y la comarca logre una población estable.

A Moreno el trabajo en cadena le gusta; le permite ayudar al compañero que va antes y al que va después. “He podido coordinar equipos y conocerles de primera mano. Algunas veces ayudo a personas que ya estaban cuando entré, y noto cómo he crecido. Es muy bonito”, confiesa. También se enorgullece del resultado, del producto final: “Vas de vacaciones y ves botellas de Bezoya. Además, a la gente le encanta. Es muy gratificante”, resume.

World.title: Lo que no puedes perderte si vas a Asturias de vacaciones este verano
World.content:
Varios caballos en la laguna de Sobia, en el concejo de Teverga (Asturias).

Restaurantes, pueblos, playas, naturaleza y prerrománico en un destino ideal para ver el eclipse solar del próximo 12 de agosto

Sería injusto reducir los atractivos de Asturias a su clima fresco en verano. Pero es cierto que, en los últimos años, el imparable aumento de las temperaturas ha hecho que el Principado se haya convertido en la opción elegida por muchos para pasar las vacaciones. Asturias batió en 2025 su récord de turismo rural con 304.979 visitantes, según los datos que publicó el pasado mes de febrero el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE).

Quienes elijan esta comunidad este verano, tienen muchas opciones para disfrutar de la naturaleza más allá de los Picos de Europa —aunque siempre merecen una visita— y para perderse por sus pueblos y aldeas. Además, Asturias también será un enclave estupendo para contemplar el eclipse total de sol del próximo 12 de agosto, ya que será total en toda la comunidad, como explica nuestra guía. World.title: Picnic makes first operating profit in NL
World.content:
Online supermarket Picnic made a profit in the Netherlands for the first time last year, 10 years after its launch, according to annual figures published on Monday and reported by the Financieele Dagblad.

The Dutch arm booked an underlying operating profit of €4 million, but heavy spending on new distribution centres in Germany pushed the group as a whole to a net loss of €272 million, slightly more than the year before.

The number of customers across the Netherlands, Germany and France grew by 700,000 to 3.6 million.

Picnic, which delivers in three-quarters of the Netherlands, is still in dispute with unions FNV and CNV over which collective labour agreement should cover its delivery workers. It lost a court case last year over unpaid evening and weekend supplements and is negotiating a settlement while appealing to the Supreme Court.

World.title: Asylum agency claims €185m from hotel reception middleman
World.content:
The refugee settlement agency COA is claiming €184.7 million from René Derksen and his company LCHD, which arranged emergency accommodation for asylum seekers in hotels across the Netherlands, the Financieele Dagblad reported on Monday.

The agency has secured a claim against Derksen’s farmhouse in Didam, Gelderland, blocking any sale of the property. It is is one of the largest claims ever brought by a Dutch government body against a company.

COA confirmed to the paper it has started legal proceedings against LCHD and its directors over “a dispute about the execution of the assignment by LCHD and the termination of rental agreements”, but declined to comment further while the case is before the courts.

LCHD acted as COA’s exclusive intermediary for hotel accommodation from spring 2022, when the arrival of refugees from Ukraine left the agency scrambling for beds.

Over two and a half years, COA paid the company more than €500 million to book hotel rooms nationwide. FD reported earlier that Derksen paid himself more than €40 million in dividends over the period.

Derksen has been a suspect in a criminal investigation since 2023, alongside his former business partner Bob van der Valk, a member of the hotel family.

Prosecutors and the fiscal investigation service FIOD are looking into the two men’s cooperation and the money flows between them; both are suspected of, among other things, private-sector corruption.

Derksen has denied any wrongdoing, saying his prices were transparent and everyone involved knew LCHD was a commercial party making a “logical minimum margin”. LCHD has lodged a counter-claim against COA for what it calls unjustified breaches of contract.

The agency spent €2.5 billion on emergency accommodation in hotels and on cruise ships in 2024, against €1 billion on regular reception.

World.title: Major transport disruptions over A27 bridge safety warnings
World.content:
The Merwedebrug, which carries the A27 motorway over the river Merwede near Gorinchem, has been closed to all lorries since Saturday evening.

Roads agency Rijkswaterstaat said inspections found the bridge’s steel was weaker than expected in several places, and that it could no longer guarantee the structure would hold under heavy traffic.

Cars, vans, motorbikes, buses and emergency vehicles can still use it.

Lorries are being sent on long long detours as a result. It is not clear how long the closure will last.

Transport association TLN, which represents Dutch hauliers, said the impact was enormous. “Transport operators are already facing sharply rising costs,” the group said, pointing to a new lorry levy introduced on July 1 and higher diesel prices. “Extra detour kilometres only increase the financial pressure.”

The nearby Papendrechtsebrug closed last week for nine months of maintenance, cutting off one alternative route. The Merwedebrug was last shut to lorries in 2016, when cracks were found in its beams. That closure lasted nearly three months. A replacement bridge is due to be built starting this summer.

World.title: Drugs lab find forces evacuations in The Hague
World.content:
Up to 200 residents of a street in The Hague were allowed back into their homes at 11pm on Saturday, after police finished dismantling a drugs lab found in a house in the Segbroek district.

Residents of dozens of homes on the Meidoornstraat, along with their pets, were told to leave by 1pm on Saturday and were taken in at the district office on Fahrenheitstraat while the police and and a specialist firm removed the remaining chemicals.

The city council said on Sunday there was no longer any acute danger, and that the evacuation had been a precaution against exposure while the material was being taken away. Residents have been advised to keep their windows shut because of the smell.

Police were called to the house at around 1pm on Friday after a report of a strange smell, and found a lab still in operation. Officers shut down the production process by pumping out the chemicals. A 39-year-old man from The Hague who had come into contact with the liquids was taken to hospital and arrested.

A 34-year-old man from Voorburg was arrested at around 10pm on Friday. A 44-year-old from The Hague and a 71-year-old from Leiden were also held. Police are still investigating what type of lab it was and are canvassing the neighbourhood for witnesses and camera footage.

According to NOS, barrels holding thousands of litres of chemicals were found at the property, of which 500 to 750 litres were removed on Friday. A spokesman for the regional safety board told the broadcaster that a lab of that size would not normally be found in a residential area.

World.title: Music colleges draw internationals as Dutch student share falls
World.content:
Only around two in 10 students training as performing musicians in the Netherlands are Dutch, according to figures from education agency DUO obtained by public broadcaster NOS.

The Dutch share of students at conservatoires – the country’s higher music education colleges – has fallen from 52% to 22% over the past 20 years. Nine HBO colleges teach music at degree level and seven offer a master’s in performance. Of those master’s students, 78% come from abroad.

People in the sector blame 15 years of cuts to music teaching. “Far from all schools have structural music education, where children can get to know music,” said Jan van den Eijnden, senior adviser at cultural education body LKCA and a teacher at the Tilburg conservatoire. Music lessons outside school have become fragmented, with big differences in cost and availability, he said.

The arts council Raad voor Cultuur has calculated that the culture sector, which includes music education, has lost more than €500 million a year relative to other sectors since 2005.

Many music schools and arts centres have closed, and there is less room for one-to-one tuition. “That comes at the cost of developing talent,” Van den Eijnden said.

The drop is showing up in amateur music too. At the Wereld Muziek Concours in Kerkrade, a four-yearly wind music festival with orchestras from 28 countries, no Dutch orchestra entered the youth division this year.

Van den Eijnden and WMC artistic director Björn Bus both said the government should guarantee organised, affordable music tuition, pointing to Belgium, where lessons are far cheaper, and Luxembourg, where free tuition is written into law.

International student numbers in the Netherlands fell for the first time in two decades this academic year, a decline the government has sought as it works to limit recruitment.

World.title: Save yourselves while you still can: an assimilated introduction
World.content:
Our regular columnist Molly Quell is worried that she might have gone a bit too far with her inburgering process.

“They were fine, but…” I trailed off. I couldn’t quite put my finger on why I hadn’t enjoyed meeting my husband’s colleagues after we ran into them at a pub.

My (Dutch) husband and I were out with some (Dutch) friends when several of his (non-Dutch) work acquaintances happened by the bar where we were set up with beers and bitterballen.

The group was welcomed to join us, chairs were procured from nearby tables and another round of trips was ordered.

The colleagues were jolly, with conversation running from summer holiday plans to obscure folk traditions from their various homelands.

And yet, they irked me.

As he and I walked home, my husband asked the standard, post-social-engagement debrief questions. He probed about my hesitation over his colleagues.

“They didn’t introduce themselves,” I said, finally articulating what had bugged me.

The internationals, I realised, hadn’t engaged in the Dutch ritual of introducing themselves to everyone at the table, with a firm handshake and requisite eye contact.

Ten years ago, I would have told you with great confidence that this was a silly and awkward social interaction. That it is disruptive at parties and gatherings. That you forget everyone’s name immediately and then run the risk of not knowing their name if you get into real conversation later.

I’m not here to defend the practice. But I have now become so accustomed to it that it bothers me when it’s not done.

I’ve gone too far with my integration.

I’ve integrated a lot. I swim in canals. I happily go to the nude, mixed-gendered sauna. I’ve sold stuff on King’s Day and bought plates with Albert Heijn zegels.

Those are all defensible. Jumping in a canal is really keeping me cool this summer and I still use my plates.

But mandatory group introductions at social gatherings? I should self-deport and spend some time thinking about what I’ve become.

This is more or less how all human traditions come to pass. Enough people do something enough times, it becomes normalised, and now I’m congratulating 25 people sitting in a circle on someone else’s birthday.

In general I do like Dutch Introduction Culture. Dutch teenagers are much more comfortable interacting with adults than teenagers of other nationalities, in my experience. I assume this is because they have been forced from a young age to introduce themselves to everyone.

You say hello. You acknowledge that there is another person present. You do it in all facets of human interaction. At meetings and events and, goddammit, when you run into your colleague at the pub.

But to go so far as to look down upon lovely people who have no idea it is expected of them and therefore don’t do it? Next thing you know, I’ll be carrying a “Grenzen dicht” poster at a far-right rally.

When you live amongst people, you absorb their cultures and customs. I spend most of my time around Dutch people these days and my sense of reality has been warped.

Honestly I think it’s too late for me. I’m offended by the idea of putting on a bathing suit to go to a sauna. I grow increasingly frustrated with colleagues who cannot simply say directly what they want. A few weeks ago, I teased a friend for having a “luxurious” lunch.

Reader, it was a salad.

Save yourselves, get out while you still can. But make sure you firmly introduce yourself upon arrival.

World.content:
