World.title: Joyce shouts at dog during ABC interview
World.content:
Joyce shouts at dog during ABC interview

One Nation MP and former deputy prime minister Barnaby Joyce was being interviewed by Sarah Ferguson on 7.30 when he roared at a dog off-camera.

World.title: ‘Sit down!’ Barnaby Joyce went on ABC’s flagship current affairs show ... and shouted at a dog
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘Sit down!’ Barnaby Joyce went on ABC’s flagship current affairs show ... and shouted at a dog Alexander Darling July 20, 2026 — 9:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I, I think … SIT DOWN! … Sorry, it’s a dog.” Barnaby Joyce was about to answer a question on the ABC about whether he was comfortable with where his party leader, Pauline Hanson, was taking him, when he roared at a dog off-camera. Loading It wasn’t clear how close the dog was or what it was doing to raise his ire, but the strange outburst proved the climax of a live nine-minute interview during which he claimed Channel Seven had suggested Hanson meet with British right-wing agitator Tommy Robinson, and appeared to suggest that One Nation could try to identify illegal immigrants using the medical system and parking fine data. When he composed himself, Joyce said he had changed his views the way that many other Australians had.



When journalist Sarah Ferguson asked if he had set a limit on how far he was willing to go in defence of Hanson, Joyce didn’t answer directly. “When you say set a limit, you know, I’ve heard other things today, like she supports returning to the White Australia policy. She doesn’t, and she said that quite clearly on the stage,” he said. Joyce roars at the offending dog. ABC Joyce appeared on the public broadcaster’s 7.30 program following Hanson’s highly publicised trip to Europe, in which she was seen relaxing in Italy with billionaire friend Gina Rinehart, told the Conservative Political Action Conference in London not to apologise for being white, and appeared on a podcast and Channel Seven segment with Robinson. Ferguson then asked whether he endorsed Hanson’s call to bring Robinson to Australia, and Joyce immediately claimed Seven’s program, Spotlight, had suggested Hanson and Robinson meet.



When pushed on the fact Seven denied this, Joyce said he’d read emails and had “a different opinion”. When asked if he agreed with Hanson’s remarks in the Spotlight program that Muslims bred at cost to Australian taxpayers, Joyce again defended his leader: “She also said that obviously it’s not a case of every person of the Islamic faith. There is an issue in Australia that if people go and into a form of balkanisation where you … where there’s not an assimilation, where you go into a form of an alternate culture which is at odds with the egalitarian ethos of Australia, then that creates massive problems. And we saw that in Bondi.” One Nation leader Pauline Hanson talking to Tommy Robinson. X/@TRobinsonNewEra The mysterious dog that had riled Joyce resurfaced a few minutes later: Earlier on Monday, Joyce had backed Hanson’s call for mass deportations – which she later clarified to add that this applied only to people in Australia illegally – and he was pressed on this by Ferguson. “You said today you could wait until overstayers go to see a doctor or a nurse. So will you require GPs and doctors to report visa overstayers to authorities?” Ferguson asked.



“I have to apologise for the dog,” Joyce began his answer, though there was no disturbance obvious to viewers. Related Article Updated

Political leadership ‘Do not apologise for being white’: Hanson takes aim at privilege and trans rights “Don’t worry about the dog, just answer the question,” Ferguson pressed calmly. Joyce bristled at this: “Don’t be rude, otherwise this interview will come to a grinding halt.” Ferguson asked the question again, with Joyce interrupting before she could finish.



“Oh no, Sarah that’s ridiculous, unless you want to keep illegal immigrants here, then there’s no point in calling them illegal ...” Asked a third time how One Nation would detect illegal immigrants to deport, Joyce said: “From time to time, they’re going to come across all range of things, whether it’s health issues, whether it’s parking fines, whatever it is. And when they pop up, they’re going to be sent off because otherwise the whole thing’s a farce.” Editor's pick FIFA World Cup Oops, he did it again: Trump hogs the stage, crashes World Cup trophy lift The interview ended with one more reference to the offending, unseen canine. “Thank you very much indeed for joining us. The dog was no problem,” closed Ferguson.



Joyce replied: “It was for me.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Jack’s big TED talk
World.content:
“I’d like to congratulate ABC’s Play School on its 60th anniversary,” declares Jack Dikian of Mosman. “It was the only show where choosing between the windows felt like the biggest decision of my childhood. But whichever one I picked, they ignored it anyway.”

Roger Hallett of Toowoomba (Qld) can “clearly recall a stunt for Sydney Uni Commemoration Day (C8) in the ’60s that involved publishing and distributing a broadsheet newspaper to city commuters with the masthead of the Sydney Moaning Herald, correct font, Granny column and all. The feature article included a ‘photo’ of the Sydney Harbour Bridge being towed out of the harbour on its way to New Zealand.”

“Allan Gibson noted that ‘depending on where you lived, ‘the talkies’ (C8) had different names’, ” observes Richard Payne of Urangan. “When I lived on Norfolk Island in the ’60s, we all went to Rawson Hall Talkies at Burnt Pine. I can well remember that a screening of Mutiny on The Bounty one night engendered vigorous audience participation!”

“My dad definitely didn’t go to the cinema, the pictures or the flicks,” declares Helen Lewin of Tumbi Umbi. “He only ever went to the ‘fleas and itches’ and enjoyed the looks that brought. He wasn’t Cockney either.”

This might explain why John Dawson of North Parramatta thinks “our Picture Show Palace was named ‘The Fleahouse’ by locals . Thus, the tale of the two fleas coming out after the show conferring: ‘Shall we walk, or take a dog?’”

World.title: ‘My work is done’: King Charles accepts Starmer’s resignation as Britain’s PM
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeUK politics ‘My work is done’: King Charles accepts Starmer’s resignation as Britain’s PM David Crowe Updated July 20, 2026 — 8:59pm ,first published 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A formal transfer of power is under way in Britain after Keir Starmer visited King Charles for a private meeting in which he officially resigned as prime minister. The meeting cleared the way for the next prime minister, Andy Burnham, to visit the King soon afterwards, so the monarch can invite him to form government, elevating him to the leadership. Starmer left the prime minister’s official residence, 10 Downing Street, to speak briefly before hundreds of reporters in remarks that were televised live, while a helicopter flew overhead to capture his departure. Britain’s outgoing prime minister Keir Starmer receives applause as he leaves No. 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth “My work is done. In 6½ years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024,” he said.



“Since then, it has been the privilege of my life to serve you and this great country as prime minister, and I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago.” He spoke in front of dozens of ministerial colleagues, staff and family members including his wife, Victoria. “As I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success. He has my full support,” Starmer said. “I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved.”



After being hugged by his wife, and hugging some of the supporters behind him, Starmer walked to a waiting car with Victoria and drove to Buckingham Palace to see the King. Buckingham Palace confirmed soon afterwards that Charles had met Starmer and his wife. In the standard language of these notices, it said the King was “graciously pleased to accept” Starmer’s resignation – the same wording used for the statements about the departures of previous prime ministers. King Charles welcomes Starmer to Buckingham Palace, where he officially resigned as PM. Getty Images Burnham arrived at the palace within minutes of the Starmers’ departure. The meetings at Buckingham Palace will formally conclude a long fight within the Labour Party to replace Starmer after growing discontent over his leadership, and a year of planning by Burnham and his allies to take power within the party.



In being named to the top post on Monday, Burnham will become the nation’s seventh prime minister since 2016. While he has set out broad ambitions in speeches and interviews, he is yet to name his cabinet ministers and settle disputes among his supporters about who should hold the key Treasury post of chancellor of the exchequer. Starmer and his wife, Victoria, depart Downing Street. Getty Images Starmer delivers his final address in front of dozens of ministerial colleagues, staff and family members. Getty Images Bond market investors are watching the cabinet decision closely, given the country’s net public debt is £2.9 trillion ($5.6 trillion) – equivalent to 95 per cent of annual economic output – and rising.



Burnham, who has spent the past nine years as mayor of Greater Manchester, set out broad themes about his plans in a speech three weeks ago, knowing he had the numbers within the Labour Party to lead the government. Related Article Updated

UK politics ‘Number 10 North’: PM-in-waiting vows major power shift out of London “We will create a more streamlined state with a clearer purpose to power up all parts of the country and put a laser-like focus on growth and regeneration – good growth,” he said. Burnham, however, captured attention with a related pledge to shift some of the powers of the prime minister’s office in Number 10 Downing Street in London – near the major public service departments around Whitehall – so that a new unit of government would be responsible for northern England and other areas outside the capital. Burnham called his proposed new office “Number 10 North”, and the phrase dominated media coverage of his speech, although he did not outline any details on how it would work.



Labour has 403 seats in the House of Commons, giving it a comfortable majority. The Conservative Party has 117 seats, the Liberal Democrats have 71, Reform UK has seven and the Greens have five. Small parties and independents make up the rest. Related Article UK politics Four things to know about Andy Burnham, the man likely to be the UK’s next PM But the divisions within the Labour parliamentary party have weakened the government, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has made big gains in local government elections and has soared in the public opinion polls as a potential prime minister. Burnham’s rise began in earnest on May 19 when he overcame resistance from Starmer’s allies and gained party approval to run as the Labour candidate at a byelection for the seat of Makerfield, which he won on June 19. Starmer announced on June 22 that he would resign. With Labour MPs making it clear they wanted a new leader, Starmer set up an internal party timeline to decide his replacement. When party officials called for nominations, Burnham was the sole candidate – an extraordinary development given he had become a member of the House of Commons only days earlier.



While Burnham will be the seventh prime minister in roughly a decade, he is also being described as the sixth prime minister in 10 years. Former Conservative prime minister David Cameron stepped down on July 13, 2016 – 10 years and one week ago. He was followed by Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak from the Conservative Party. They were followed by Starmer and Burnham. World.title: Carlton’s coach search narrows with three assistants among four contenders
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 Carlton’s coach search narrows with three assistants among four contenders Sam McClure July 20, 2026 — 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The race to become Carlton’s next senior coach is entering its most critical stage, with the Blues’ selection panel to meet this week after whittling the field to four contenders, including interim coach Josh Fraser, for one of football’s biggest jobs. Multiple industry sources, speaking on condition of anonymity because the process is confidential, have confirmed that St Kilda senior assistant Corey Enright, Geelong assistant James Kelly and Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham have all progressed through the opening phase of the process and remain firmly in contention for one of the AFL’s most sought-after roles. The Blues are also deliberately leaving a seat open in the process for interim coach Josh Fraser should he decide to formally put himself forward. Carlton have made allowances for Josh Fraser - giving him the chance to apply late for the role. Getty Images Fraser has not yet entered the race but has enhanced his credentials since taking over on an interim basis following Michael Voss’ departure and winning seven games from his nine in charge. Rather than shutting the door on their caretaker coach while the season is still unfolding, Carlton have opted to allow Fraser the opportunity to enter the process at a later stage if he wishes.



The coaching selection panel will meet this week to assess the remaining candidates before determining who progresses to the next round of interviews. Carlton president Rob Priestley is overseeing the search, with chief executive Graham Wright, football boss Chris Davies and Adam Simpson forming the club’s coaching selection panel. The group has spent recent weeks canvassing candidates from across the competition as the Blues seek to appoint the coach they believe can return the club to premiership contention. Simpson vehemently denied reports two weeks ago that Enright was firming as favourite for the role and that Fraser would enter the process at a later stage. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 The inside story of a coaching coup 17 years in the making The latest developments mean several experienced assistants have now fallen out of the race.



Hawthorn assistant Daniel Giansiracusa, Western Bulldogs assistant Brendan Lade and Collingwood’s head of strategy and coaching Hayden Skipworth each held preliminary discussions with Carlton during the opening stages of the process. However, competition sources confirmed the trio will not progress any further. The remaining candidates each bring contrasting coaching backgrounds. Enright has long been regarded as one of the competition’s premier assistant coaches. A three-time premiership player with Geelong, he is now Ross Lyon’s senior assistant at St Kilda and has been linked with several senior coaching vacancies over recent years without taking the final step. Kelly has also built an impressive coaching resume since retiring from a decorated playing career. After beginning his coaching career at Essendon, the former Geelong champion returned to the Cats, where he has become one of Chris Scott’s most trusted assistants. Graham is viewed across the industry as one of the AFL’s emerging senior coaching prospects. He worked under Simpson at West Coast before switching to Fremantle for the 2022 season and is regarded as one of the best football brains not to be a senior coach.



Fraser remains something of the unknown in the process. While he has not formally entered the race, his work stabilising the Blues during a turbulent period has earned respect internally, prompting the club to leave the door ajar rather than finalise the next stage of the process without him. Carlton have not publicly committed to a timeline for appointing Voss’ successor, but the search is gathering momentum as the selection panel prepares to trim the field further.

World.title: Buckley at a ‘fork in the road’ after Tasmania’s coach call on Hinkley
World.content:
In today’s AFL briefing: Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold on Saturday night.

The Magpies and premiership forward Bobby Hill are set to part ways.

Essendon star Nate Caddy has been discharged from hospital and is expected to play this week. Nathan Buckley has opened up about his extreme disappointment on missing out on the gig as the inaugural senior coach of the Tasmania Devils and says the situation has left him at a “fork in the road”. Buckley, who coached Collingwood to the 2018 grand final, has cast strong doubt that he’ll throw his hat in the ring for two other vacant coaching jobs in the AFL – the next senior coaches at Carlton and Essendon. “I haven’t really reflected on where those roles sit,” a candid Buckley said on Fox Footy on Monday night. “And I don’t think I will enter those processes.



Nathan Buckley says he will stay focused on immediate priorities at Geelong. via Getty Images “I’m absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks [as an assistant coach] with Geelong and how that plays out. “I was committed to that [the Tasmania job]. And that [ambition] ended a day ago.” As the dramatic events unfolded in Tasmania on the weekend, the Devils settled on Ken Hinkley with news of his appointment filtering out late on Sunday. Buckley said he was told by Devils CEO Brendon Gale that he had been unsuccessful.



“I texted back [to Gale] that ‘I’m disappointed, but thanks for letting me know’. And I’ll come back around and touch base in time [with Tasmania, for some feedback] because it’s obviously a busy time for the Devils.” “Obviously Kenny is the right fit for Tassie. Good luck to them all, and I hope that that goes really well. “I’m sure that they’ll be a great fit.” Buckley described his situation as a “fork in the road”. “The future there [at the Cats] for me will inform my next step in footy. I’ve probably wouldn’t have come back in unless I’d looked at Tassie, so it’s a fork in the road,” he said.



“And I’m really grateful for where I’m at, rather than maybe just being on the couch, five years in media, without really knowing what I was doing with footy. “But now that I’m back in a club - I don’t know what’s next.” Blues seek clarity from prominent commentator over McKay injury Jon Pierik Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold when the star forward went off injured in Saturday’s loss to Collingwood at the MCG.



King, a dual North Melbourne premiership player and Fox Footy analyst, said on his breakfast radio show on SEN on Monday that the Blues had called him on Sunday to discuss his comments. “I took the call from Carlton [on Sunday] … and had a lot of [public] feedback about it [his commentary]. Look, my thoughts are my thoughts. I am not necessarily going to back over it too much,” King said. Out of the game: Carlton lost Harry McKay to a knee injury in the opening term against Collingwood on Saturday. AFL Photos “I think we have spoken about players that go off a little bit easy in the past. I am not saying that’s Harry on this occasion. Clearly, he has got an issue, and they are telling me he will miss two weeks. I was basically referring to an old Denis Paganism which you will know if you listened to what I said earlier.” Asked to elaborate, King said: “All good. They [Blues] disagree with what the discussion was about, which is fine. That’s footy. I am happy to move on from that.”





In commentary, King had said: “It looks to me like the docs are saying it’s a pain management issue,” he said. “‘We know you’re under difficulty and there is some discomfort there, but this is AFL footy, we need you out there’.” When it became clear McKay would take no further part in the game, King said: “Looks like he’s put a line through himself, putting the jacket on, that’s it, night over. Incredible disappointment. You wonder whether there’s any structural issue there or is it just a pain tolerance discussion?” In the box: Fox Footy commentator David King. Getty Images “This Harry McKay discussion will rage. There’s nothing worse than when a player of that significance is not there. It changes the whole game.”



In reference to his former coaches, including premiership great Denis Pagan, King said: “My old coaches would say: ‘I hope that’s a two or three-week [injury]. If that’s a 15-20 minute [injury], you lose a lot of respect’.” Carlton said on the night that McKay had been ruled out by club doctors. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 The inside story of a coaching coup 17 years in the making King added at half-time: “If that’s just a bit of pain management then you’ve got a lot more to answer for. I hope that’s not the case with Harry and time will tell.” McKay, the 2021 Coleman medallist, has battled mental health problems through his career.



In the AFL Players Association’s annual insights and impact report released last week, 34 per cent of players said they felt a level of disrespect by broadcast media. This included concerns about a focus on negativity and hyperbole. After seven-straight wins under caretaker coach Josh Fraser, the Blues have lost their past two games, against Hawthorn and Collingwood, but remain in contention for a wildcard berth. They host the Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium on Saturday. Magpies and star premiership forward preparing to split Jon Pierik



Collingwood are working towards parting ways with premiership star Bobby Hill. The 2023 Norm Smith medallist is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal reportedly worth about $750,000 a season. Industry sources have confirmed conversations between the Magpies and Hill’s management at Mac’s Sports Promotions are ongoing. The Magpies and Mac’s Sports Management were contacted for comment. Uncertain future: Bobby Hill and Collingwood are working towards a split. Getty Images Hill has not played a senior game since round 21 last year, largely because of personal issues.



He had an extended break over summer but was welcomed back into the fold earlier this season. He had been training at suburban grounds with a trainer before returning to the club. The dynamic small forward has played three VFL games, but has not been a consistent presence at the club. Coach Craig McRae has repeatedly said he was excited about Hill’s potential return, but there was always the caveat of the unknown. McRae said in June that Hill was still working through his personal issues. “Truthfully, battling,” McRae replied when asked about Hill.



Loading “He has a bit going on, let’s be really clear. He has a lot going on. He’s a work in progress, but it’s nice to have him in the building. “He’s a long way away from playing footy ... but again, when he’s in our building, at least we get some opportunities to make him feel that he’s loved and appreciated.” Hill and his partner Georgia Devlin welcomed their third child in May. Seven reported on Monday that Hill was keen for a move to the Brisbane Lions, Gold Coast or Port Adelaide.



Hill was originally drafted by Greater Western Sydney with pick No.24 in 2018. He has played 102 senior games across eight seasons. Bombers confident Caddy will face Hawks Jon Pierik



Essendon are confident Nate Caddy will be available for selection this week after he was hospitalised with an irregular heart rate during Sunday’s three-point win over Greater Western Sydney. Caddy was taken to hospital for assessment, having collapsed to the turf when he got to the interchange bench in the first quarter. He had further tests but was given the all clear and discharged on Sunday night. Ready to go: Essendon star Nate Caddy is expected to be available to face the Hawks on Saturday. AFL Photos via Getty Images Essendon’s general manager of football Daniel McPherson said he expected Caddy to train this week ahead of a clash against arch-rival Hawthorn on Saturday. “There was some concern in the first quarter when Nate’s heart rate became elevated,” McPherson said on Monday.



“He was removed from the game, and our medical team assessed him at the ground before sending him to hospital for further assessment. He was discharged last night and is back at home. “He is expected to be able to train and play without concern this week.” Caddy recently signed a contract extension until the end of 2031 in a huge boost for the battling Bombers, who no longer sit in last spot on the ladder. Wingman Xavier Duursma (hamstring) has been ruled out for the rest of the season. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom



The Bombers were able to sing the club song for only the second time in 31 games after edging the shocked Giants. It was their first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they had not tasted victory in Victoria since May last year. It was Dean Solomon’s first win as caretaker coach since replacing Brad Scott in May. While only 14,601 fans attended the game, the scenes of joy for the Bombers were palpable. “It’s a bloody good feeling. Our footy club’s been on its knees for a period of time, and the footy world’s jumped on that, and they enjoy us sitting at the bottom,” Solomon said. “We’ve felt that, and we don’t like that, so to push back a little bit and get one win, albeit one win, I’m just really happy for these players.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Residents push back against another plan for new pickleball courts
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Residents push back against another plan for new pickleball courts William Davis July 20, 2026 — 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Plans for new pickleball facilities at a quiet suburban park in Brisbane have attracted the ire of some residents, who believe they will be disruptive and potentially unsafe. A large concrete slab with painted lines marking out four courts is set to be installed at the south end of Cox Park in Lota from Monday, July 27, at a cost of about $250,000. About 40 residents turned up at Cox Park in Lota on Sunday to discuss and protest the plans for new Pickleball courts. William Davis Nearby netball courts will be torn out. Pickleball is a racquet sport that uses a hard, hollow plastic ball known for making a loud “pop” sound when hit. It is one of the fastest growing recreational activities in Australia.



It’s the second time in as many months plans for new courts caused heated dispute in the Brisbane suburbs, after construction shelved at a park in Holland Park West following similar community pushback. About 40 residents of Lota and surrounds turned up at Cox Park on Sunday to discuss the proposal, which is backed and funded by local LNP representative Alex Givney. The vast majority expressed concerns it was being built in an unsuitable spot, with some arguing the councillor had not meaningfully consulted them. Alan McFadyen lives next to the park on Bethania Street. He said he’s not against pickleball courts being built in the area, but Cox Park was too small, swampy and close to family homes.



“I think they need to abandon this site … this is just the strangest location to put it,” McFadyen told this masthead. Registered nurse Vivienne Treagus lives opposite on Richard Street, and said it was close enough to her home to disrupt her sleep during the day when working shifts. “I would also like to not have to be constantly living on eggshells thinking that someone is potentially going to be hurt, especially a little kid,” she added. Nurse Vivienne Treagus lives next door to Cox Park and said she was worried the Pickleball court could impact her ability to sleep when doing shiftwork. William Davis Both also said the existing netball courts were frequently used – primarily by young children on bikes and scooters – and they should be retained.



Many houses surrounding the park had erected signs calling for further consultation over the weekend. Related Article Queensland councils Council caves on divisive pickleball courts, blaming NIMBYs In emails from February seen by this masthead, councillor Givney apologised to residents for failing to effectively communicate the plan but said the project would go ahead regardless. “I did not anticipate that replacing the old netball courts with new courts would raise community concern,” she told opponents. “I always endeavour to be transparent and communicate effectively, and I apologise that I did not do that well enough in this instance.



“The courts will be proceeding.” She did meet with some residents in March at the park, and Brisbane City Council said these discussions shaped the final plan. Dispute over plans for a new pickleball court at Cox Park in the Brisbane Suburb of Lota. William Davis Susan Norman was one of a handful of pickleball players who attended the Sunday meeting. She explained the sport was a great way for older residents to stay active, with half of all local participants over 50 years old and one club member almost 90.



Norman said a designated court was desperately needed for the area, though she did understand why some residents had concerns about the chosen location. “I mean if it was in my backyard and I wasn’t getting consulted, I’d probably have an axe to grind.” Susan Norman plays pickleball through the Wynnum Pickleball cub and said the area needed its own court. William Davis Members of her club Pickleball Wynnum presently play at a nearby school when it is available. While some residents questioned how the courts could be built without a development application, council said its zoning for sport and recreation meant one was not necessary.



The office of Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the process had been transparent, and many of those opposing it were politically motivated. In a statement, councillor Givney said: “The new pickleball courts will breathe new life into an underused part of Cox Park. Many homes surrounding Cox Park had erected signs calling for further consultation on Sunday. William Davis “We’re turning damaged courts that have not supported a netball club for more than a decade into a community space people will use. “I represent the entire community and I’m determined to deliver improvements that benefit as many local residents as possible.”



Opponents of the Cox Park plan were set to meet on Tuesday morning to protest and call for the upcoming works to be put on hold. The dispute comes a month after another controversial plan for new pickleball courts at Joachim Park in Holland Park West was scuppered by residents. The existing netball courts at Cox Park in the Brisbane Suburb of Lota will be removed. William Davis LNP councillor Krista Adams similarly suggested the opposition had been manufactured by her political enemies, and attributed the decision to “a sustained campaign by Labor and Green-aligned NIMBYs. “I am bitterly disappointed residents of all ages will now miss out because a vocal minority was determined to block, delay and disrupt a project designed for the wider community,” she added.

World.title: The public servants nervously awaiting their estimates grilling
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: The top bureaucrats under the gun in estimates, the Public Sector Commissioner offloads his uranium shares, and the watchdog stopping short of barking. A number of top public servants are likely to face an awkward grilling during the Crisafulli government’s second block of estimates kicking off this week. The process of scrutinising how the state’s money is spent, and the figures behind the scenes managing departments and agencies, has a knack for being a fiery yet anticlimactic affair. Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm along with her DG Belinda Drew. Julius Dennis But there are a few public servants who can expect to be zeroed-in on, as others have lucrative pay cheques to lose auditioning for roles they’re now serving in an acting capacity.



Government ministers have stumbled over questions about domestic violence prevention funding and undelivered recommendations following the alleged murder of a Toowoomba mother. Those issues will likely stay under the microscope when domestic and family violence minister Amanda Camm fronts estimates alongside director-general Belinda Drew. There will surely be some heated questions over the bungled rollout of IT program Unify as well as revelations vulnerable children in state care were sleeping on mattresses in government offices. Department of Racing boss Andrew Hopper will likely face some curly questions after the deputy commissioner of the Queensland Racing Integrity Commission, Kim Kelly, quit and published a scathing criticism of its independence due to government regulations.



Some have speculated estimates may be a pseudo job interview for Queensland Police Commissioner Brett Pointing, who is serving in the role on a 12-month interim basis. Related Article Exclusive

Queensland government Taskforce chair worries LNP has ‘abandoned’ key DV recommendations Meanwhile, some fresh faces will be feeling the nerves, including John Sosso’s acting replacement as director-general at state development Shaun Ferris, and Energy Queensland chief executive Craig McCabe, who has only been in the role for a week. Mackie offloads last shares as LNP ducks uranium talk It was the kind of announcement the Crisafulli LNP has been all over: a federal agreement with a major foreign export market for riches the state’s mining sector could send in spades.



Just look at the focus on critical minerals – which has gathered enough steam to warrant audit office scrutiny. Let alone Mines Minister Dale Last’s “I’ll sign, you drill” catchcry. But on the latest opportunity for the state to tap into its vast uranium reserves to feed into a new export deal between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi, Queensland isn’t so quick off the mark. Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and Public Sector Commissioner David Mackie at the latter’s wedding in April, in which Bleijie acted as a celebrant in a “private capacity”. Facebook / Jarrod Bleijie Australia has the world’s largest uranium reserves – almost a third of the global total. Queensland is one of the states laying claim to some of this, but a politically see-sawing position on its mining is at present planted on the ban side. This is a position the Crisafulli LNP has repeated since coming to power, despite the efforts of industry to change its mind – as it did last time it held power, despite initial denials it would. “Our position remains unchanged,” Last told us last week.



Time will tell whether that remains the case. One thing which has changed is Public Sector Commissioner David Mackie’s share portfolio. An update to his declaration of interests late last month shows he has offloaded shares in a third uranium miner this year. Related Article Public service The names being floated for the role of Bleijie’s next right-hand man Mackie’s sell-off of Peninsula Energy shares now leaves his disclosed interest in public and private companies at nil. Probably not a bad place to be for the current tip to replace John Sosso as Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie’s department chief in State Development. For a while this term, both Mackie and Sosso had money in three uranium firms, including one with interests – and the largest reserves – in Queensland: Paladin Energy. Sosso still does, despite conflict concerns. One thing Circus didn’t spot on Mackie’s updated interest declaration? Bleijie’s wedding celebrant services.



New watchdog stops short of barking at LNP bill – again Almost six months into the tenure of new human rights boss Debbie Platz, and we’ve got another glimpse of what the less “combative” course being charted looks like. After not engaging in the parliamentary process for the government’s controversial bill to further expand “adult time” youth sentencing, unwind three-strike drug diversion and give police new powers to search and move people on, Platz’s office has bowed out again. Queensland Human Rights Commissioner Debbie Platz APM in her Brisbane office earlier this year. Matt Dennien This time, it’s the government’s “circuit breaker” sentencing bill, compared by a number of major stakeholder submissions to the contentious Newman-era “bootcamps”. The program is apparently due to be up and running this year. We’ll see.



The plan will create an alternative to detention for the courts of up to six months in a remote location with a service provider. Documents tabled alongside the bill say some may only be open to boys – and will likely hit First Nations kids harder than others. Related Article Exclusive

Public service Inside the human rights office planning day that left staff in tears After Circus spotted the conspicuous – and before Platz, unheard of – absence of a human rights commission submission, we reached out to the team to check there hadn’t been a mix-up or technical glitch. Nope. The watchdog first reiterated that evidence shows broader diversion, early intervention, education and housing support, healthcare, disability services and targeted support for kids at risk of reoffending work to address cycles of crime and long-term community safety. “We are continually looking to identify how we can make the best use of our resources to meet our statutory responsibilities and contribute positively to the lives of all Queenslanders,” Platz said in a statement, echoing her comments from back in March, before getting to the kicker.



“When considering whether to make a submission on a Bill, we consider a range of factors, including the impact a submission may have. On this occasion, we have not provided a submission to government about the Bill. “Submissions to parliament, which occur at the final stages of policy development, are just one way that we contribute to the development of policy and legislation.” This is true. But it’s also one of the few ways watchdogs like the commission can do so in a way that the public can see – and to date, it hasn’t seen much else. Review of pilot DV program caught in a government spin As flagged above, there are plenty of unanswered questions currently swirling around the government’s efforts at domestic and family violence prevention and reform.



One of the biggest is just what progress has been made on the outstanding recommendations of the landmark Women’s Safety and Justice Taskforce for almost a year since this masthead revealed the scrapping of an oversight role the taskforce chair has now spoken up about. Former Queensland Court of Appeal president Margaret McMurdo, had – until last week – refrained from wading back into public debate about the work of her taskforce. Another is why a pilot program with federal funding and seemingly positive anecdotal reviews recently came to a halt. The Housing Connectors crisis accommodation model received $4.95 million across 2023-26 as part of a national partnership agreement, with providers picked to deliver services in Toowoomba, Moreton Bay and Brisbane. A federal social services department website notes this would be subject to a review, a final report of which was due in mid-2025.



Given that, you’d think a question to under-pressure minister Camm about whether the review was completed, and what this found and recommended, would be a simple affair. You’d be wrong. Related Article Queensland government Bleijie claims taskforce chair worked more ‘enthusiastically’ with Labor After fobbing us with some lines about Labor not having funded the program for more than two years (the “pilot” label might have given this away!), Camm was only interested in talking up other initiatives. Thankfully, word has reached the Circus tent from more open parts of government to suggest the review was, in fact, done. Pushed on the matter, Camm’s emailed response pivoted to saying Labor “should be ashamed for blaming others” for only funding the pilot program for two years.



On why her government decided not to continue said funding, which had been delivered through the Department of Justice? Nothing. Of course, we wouldn’t want to speculate about the reasons a government might want to circle the wagons about a review of a trial program it decided not to keep funding. Have a curiosity for the Public Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com.
