World.title: Asbestos found in Timaru's Theatre Royal during redevelopment
World.content:
Asbestos has been discovered at Timaru's Theatre Royal, which is undergoing a multi-million-dollar redevelopment.

The Timaru District Council said the ground floor auditorium and stagehouse have been closed and isolated after testing last week found asbestos in plaster in the auditorium.

The council is redeveloping the historic Theatre Royal and constructing a new museum on an adjacent site at a cost of $25.8 million.

Project director Paul Haggath said the asbestos discovery was not unusual for a building of this age and appropriate measures had been put in place to deal with it.

"The asbestos within the plasterwork is inert and harmless while it remains encapsulated. We are undertaking checks and measures to ensure that all areas with potential asbestos are properly sealed and encapsulated before any further work proceeds," he said.

"There is no risk to the public, and we will provide updates as the issue is resolved."

Haggath said WorkSafe had been notified.

Work across other areas of the project, including the roof, lobby, back of house, front of house, and Te Kura Marumaru South Canterbury Museum construction, was continuing unaffected, he said.

World.title: Voter enrolment changes 'an indictment' on coalition - Hipkins
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins has promised to reverse the changes to electoral enrolments that would disqualify votes made by people who enrol on election day.

The justice minister who got the changes passed has dismissed the comments as speculation.

The coalition government passed legislation in December making a range of changes to voter enrolments and the way elections are run.

That included putting an end to same-day enrolment, banning prisoners from voting, allowing for larger anonymous political donations, and clarifying the ban on providing food, drink or entertainment at voting places - also known as "treating".

Speaking to reporters after the post-Cabinet briefing on Monday, Hipkins was fending off questions about whether he might do an electorate deal with the Opportunity Party in Mt Albert, and on Te Pāti Māori not ruling out a one-tick campaign for its seats in an effort to intentionally create an overhang.

"We just don't do electorate deals," Hipkins said.

"I'm backing all of our candidates to win the seats that they're campaigning in," he said. "Ultimately, voters deserve a rigourous contest, they deserve a choice... we're campaigning for two ticks for Labour and all of the seats across the country."

He was then asked if MMP was doing what it aimed to - revealing he had voted to keep MMP at the last referendum - and whether Labour would look again at the changes recommended by the independent review of the last election.

"Any significant changes to the electoral system, you do either want to have broad public support through a referendum, or a good degree of bipartisan support," he said.

"I don't think that any individual government or party should gerrymander the electoral system to suit their own preferences."

He said the Electoral Commission had not in his view "done well on voter enrolment for several elections now".

"As a local MP, I'm still dealing with people all of the time who are not on the electoral roll and don't know that they're not," he said, "and that is a failing by the Electoral Commission."

"People will show up to vote on election day only to find that their vote will not be counted because they're not on the roll, and that's new because previously they could show up and vote and fix their enrolment when they showed up to vote.

"They won't be able to do that anymore, and that is because of this government's decisions."

He immediately committed to reversing that. He was pushed on whether changes like that should require a supermajority, or 75 percent of Parliament, to pass.

"Something that potentially disenfranchises tens of thousands of New Zealanders is not the sort of change that an individual government should make - but this government have been quite happy to do that on a number of fronts."

He said he was "not Donald Trump" and would not claim the election was being stolen if those discounted votes affected the election result.

"But if tens of thousands of people go to cast their votes and have their votes disqualified, it will be an indictment on the track record of this government."

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith dismissed Hipkins' claims as "just speculation".

"It seems odd for him to suggest his own voters are inherently more disorganised," he said. "Late enrolments have placed too much strain on the system. The final vote count used to take two weeks, last election it took three. If we left things as they were, it would likely take even longer."

Goldsmith said the coalition's changes meant people would need to ensure they enrolled or updated their details by midnight on the Sunday before advance voting began.

"This is a significant, but necessary change, and New Zealanders have plenty of time to get organised and enrolled. Automatic enrolment updates will also now be allowed and postal requirements will be removed, helping to keep people contactable and participating in democracy.

"It will take a concerted effort to turn the ship around and address the trends of later enrolments and more special votes. Unlike Mr Hipkins, I have every confidence in the Electoral Commission to deliver."

The changes made by the government followed the independent review of the 2023 election, but explicitly went against some of the recommendations which urged a voting age of 16, allowing all prisoners to vote and stand for Parliament, freezing the ratio of electorate and list seats, and repealing treating as an offence.

The review included 117 recommendations, one of which was to consider a four-year term.

World.title: Auckland planning chair says proposed changes will remove density around local centres
World.content:
The chair of Auckland Council's planning committee Richard Hills says proposed changes to new intensification rules will remove density around local centres and focus it near frequent transport services.

On Tuesday, councillors will decide whether to make changes to the proposed Plan Change 120 (PC120) before it goes out to public consultation for a second time.

Auckland Council is required by central government to enable development capacity for 1.4 million new dwellings in the city.

In June, councillors agreed to send two versions of PC120 to local boards and iwi authorities for feedback - Plan A and Plan B, which provided for 1.4-1.6 million dwellings and 1.5-1.7 million dwellings respectively.

The feedback from local boards was largely that "about a third wanted A, about a third wanted B, and about a third wanted a mix of both or didn't say", Hills said.

The big change most local boards wanted was to remove density around local centres, "those are smaller centres in their communities, not the town centres, not the metro centres".

"There were other local boards who asked for things that can't be changed, so a change to a walkable catchment or a change to a town centre that's required under the law to stay."

The chair of Auckland Council's planning committee Richard Hills. Alexia Russell

The proposed changes to go before councillors on Tuesday were a blend of Plan A and Plan B, and focus housing density where infrastructure was already in place, he said.

"...we're largely landing in the place where we're doing all the legal requirements, but adding density, so that's six-storey developments around frequent transport corridors - the really, really busy bus routes, mostly heading into the city."

Building heights would also lift to 10- to 15- stories around most train stations on all lines within 10km of the city centre, not just specific Western line stations specified in law, Hills said.

The exception is Meadowbank train station, where it's proposed to reduce building heights to a maximum of six stories due to its valley location and poor access.

Other proposed amendments include reducing building height limits on the southern end of Takapuna Metropolitan Centre from 15 to six stories, and extending the walkable catchments around Akoranga and Smales Farm bus stations so they join up.

It is also proposed to further reducing the development potential for properties at risk of natural hazards, based on updated data, Hills said.

A law change in April, has enabled the council make changes to the overall plan, or withdraw parts of it.

Hills said removing local centres from the proposed intensification plan would leave just 15 percent of urban Auckland impacted by the plan change.

The plan to intensify in areas with existing infrastructure was in contrast to what's been happening with fast track consenting where 1000- to 2000-home developments have been given the go-ahead in areas with no infrastructure, he said.

"I think for most Aucklanders I hear, we should only be putting housing where there is good transport, water, community infrastructure like libraries and that's what the plan shows.

"It remains to be seen what councillors and iwi representatives will make of the proposed changes tomorrow," Hills said.

North Shore councillor John Gillon has proposed a separate amendment, largely based on Plan A.

World.title: 'Stop selling anything to do with methamphetamine' - Far North mayor
World.content:
Meth pipes available at shops across the country Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Far North Mayor Moko Tepania has a blunt message for shop owners selling pipes for smoking meth - stop it now.

While methamphetamine is a banned class A drug with stiff penalties for dealing and possession, meth pipes are sold openly in vape stores, $2 shops and dairies around the country.

Wastewater test results - showing the Far North had some of the highest meth consumption rates in New Zealand - prompted Tepania to personally visit shops selling the pipes.

That included dairies in Kaikohe and Ōpononi, whose owners had agreed to pull drug utensils from their shelves.

"There's no place whatsoever for glass pipes to be sold anywhere in the Far North. The damaging effects across communities, inter-generationally as well, from methamphetamine, is something that we can't stand for. So I'd be urging any retailers in the Far North to stop selling glass pipes."

Glass meth pipes like this, sometimes with an attachment so they can double as cannabis pipes, are sold at vape store, $2 shops and dairies around the country. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Under current New Zealand law, possession of meth pipes is not illegal - unless they are actually being used for smoking the drug - but importing and selling them is prohibited.

Customs told RNZ it had seized 31,000 drug utensils, including meth pipes, so far this year, and had taken some of the importers to court.

Despite that, an RNZ survey found most vape stores and $2 shops in Kaikohe and Kerikeri sold the pipes. Even some dairies stocked the distinctive glass pipes.

Few shops had an age restriction on drug utensils and some displayed them on the counter next to children's novelty items.

Customs says it has seized 31,000 drug utensils, including meth pipes, so far this year. Supplied / Customs

Feedback from listeners made it clear it was an issue around the country, not just in Northland.

RNZ asked police, Health NZ, Crown Law and councils how meth pipes could be sold so openly, including at shops frequented by children.

RNZ was told selling the pipes was not illegal, or the questions were referred to other agencies.

During a visit to Whangārei last week, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party - if it formed part of the next government - would do whatever it took to get the pipes out of shops.

"There is a very real problem here. Either the law isn't being fully enforced as it is now or there's a gap in the law that's preventing that law enforcement from taking place effectively. It's something that we've got to have a look at," he said.

"People shouldn't be able to buy meth pipes across the counter for, in some cases, as little as a couple of dollars. It's leading to a bigger problem. We've got to get on top of that."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says either the existing law isn't beng enforced, or there's a gap in the law that needs to be fixed. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

While getting rid of glass pipes would not stop people using meth, Hipkins said selling them alongside milk or toys normalised the drug.

"Having meth pipes available ready across the counter sends a message that it's legitimate and that it's okay. It's not. Methamphetamine use destroys people's lives and we should be doing everything we can to combat it."

Tepania said it was not clear if councils had any power to stop the sale of meth pipes.

"This is something that I'd like to explore. If not us, then who can get the regulatory compliance powers to be able to stop it? But my plea to Far North retailers right now is to stop selling anything to do with methamphetamine."

Today, however, the government said the sale of meth pipes had in fact been illegal all along, and told RNZ the problem was one of enforcement.

Northland MP Grant McCallum said that was the conclusion of a briefing paper prepared for Health Minister Simeon Brown this morning.

"What has emerged from this briefing is that ultimately it's about police enforcement, and there will be discussions now with the police to actually get them to focus on enforcing the law. They have got options here to remove these pipes from shops," he said.

The paper would now be referred to Police Minister Mark Mitchell.

Northland MP Grant McCallum says the problem comes down to enforcement. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

But McCallum said it was up to shop owners too, not just police, to fix the problem.

"And I would like to commend Mayor Moko for his efforts and I would also challenge those selling what are obviously meth pipes to desist because we're all responsible for the community we live in. And I think that the shop owners need to reflect on what they're doing."

Jodie Rameka, a Whangārei 25-year-old who has led a campaign to get meth pipes out of the city's $2 shops, welcomed the news.

Her reaction, when told authorities now concede selling drug utensils is illegal, was blunt.

"No shit, you know what I mean? Why has it taken them this long?"

Jodie Rameka, 25, has been leading a campaign to get meth pipes out of Whangārei's $2 shops. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Rameka said the pipes were sold in every $2 shop she had visited.

She was concerned their easy availability in shops popular with families and children could lead to drug use becoming normalised, and was pleased her campaign finally seemed to be paying off.

"I definitely feel hopeful now that we will see something put into place that will actually change how things are at the moment. It comes back to the young people in our communities," she said.

RNZ carried out a survey in June of all vape stores and $2 shops, and several dairies, in the Far North towns of Kaikohe and Kerikeri

In Kaikohe, one out of three vape stores, two out of three $2 shops, and one in two dairies sold glass pipes for smoking meth, ranging in price from $14 to $25.

The pipes were even easier to find in Kerikeri.

All three $2 shops, a vape store and a combined dairy/vape shop sold glass meth pipes, with prices starting from $11.

All shop assistants, bar one, claimed they did not know what the pipes were for.

World.title: Coromandel venue calls out 'disgraceful' behaviour from  local rugby club members
World.content:
Coromandel venue owners are calling for change after "disgraceful and disrespectful" behaviour from local rugby club members that they say is a symptom of a culture where men think they can get away with anything.

Monkey House Lounge and Cabaret owner operator Kaspur Franke said it was a slow night at their small Whitianga venue when at around 12.30am a group of boys wearing the Mercury Bay Rugby Club logo came into the bar.

"There were several of them that absolutely were disgraceful and disrespectful. They got on the stage, they were trying to get on the microphone and eventually one of them threw a drink that got into the equipment as well.

He said they asked the men to leave verbally, but they resisted, and had to be physically removed. He said that's where a "melee" happened involving about six of the men, where a performer was injured.

"There really seems to be quite a culture of misogynistic men thinking that they'll be all right because there are no consequences," co-owner and operator Molly Molloy said.

"I feel like we're in the middle of something that is much broader, which is men, and particularly sporting organisations, feeling that there's not going to be any consequences and therefore their behaviour doesn't change."

They'd trespassed the men for two years and would like to see a culture change, but said that required the community to step up.

"Hopefully this can affect some change, because society should be such that you shouldn't expect violence when you go out."

DJ Amber White, known as Slaps, said she physically removed a man after she asked him to leave and he refused, instead standing over her.

"He didn't like that. I'm a 5 foot tall woman and he just got tossed out in front of all his boys and so he thought that would be the perfect time to try fight me."

White said her partner stepped in and it turned into a fight, where her arm got smashed into a wall.

"I don't really remember much after my arm got smashed in, it was just searing pain."

"I'm okay now. You know, we're all safe, the equipment is safe, but women aren't from this kind of behaviour, from microaggressions when men are celebrating in town, when we lose the rugby or when teams lose or win, to be honest, at the hands of just alcohol.

"It gets a lot more ugly in Aotearoa than it does at Whitianga on Saturday night, so I just really wanted to make an example of this whole situation and just say that if you see something, if you see anything, like whether it's just a small comment or whether it's racist comments or your bro's doing something that's a little bit sketchy, just say something, you're not the weirdo for calling it out. They're the weirdo for being the weirdo.

"It was shocking to me to see two men being so abusive and the rest of the boys there, bar one, just laugh and find it incredibly funny. Like it is not funny."

Mercury Bay Rugby and Sports Club chairman Mike Skeen said it was aware of an incident at the Monkey House on Saturday night involving a few members of its Rugby Club.

"We understand that a complaint has been made to the police and we will fully support them in any investigation.

"As this is now a police matter, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage. Once this investigation is complete we will be better informed and will take any appropriate action as a club.

"We strongly condemn all forms of harassment or violence, particularly against women. The alleged behaviour does not reflect the values of our club."

World.title: Inquiry into fatal Mount Maunganui landslides asks public for information
World.content:
The government inquiry looking into the fatal landslides in Tauranga this year, is asking the public to share any information they have about it.

Six people lost their lives in January, including two teenagers, when severe storms and record rainfall sent mud and debris from a landslide at Mt Maunganu Mauao slamming onto the campsite below.

A landslide also fell onto three properties in Welcome Bay killing another two people, a grandmother and her grandson.

The inquiry chair Sir Mark O'Regan said video and drone footage, photos, rain gauge measurements and information relevant to the Inquiry's terms of reference could be uploaded to a portal.

He said the board wanted information about how the landslides occurred and whether agencies took appropriate steps to manage any risks immediately before the two fatal landslides, including any efforts to warn and evacuate people.

RNZ/Nick Monro

Sir Mark said the Inquiry recognised the significant impact the landslides have had on the families and friends of the victims, iwi and communities across Tauranga and beyond.

"Our thoughts remain with everyone who has experienced loss as a result of these tragic events," he said.

"This submissions process is an important opportunity for the public to share their experiences and perspectives."

The Inquiry is one of four investigations into the landslides.

A police and coronial process is underway and the Tauranga City Council and WorkSafe have also commissioned investigations.

World.title: Government moves to keep cement production in NZ with up to $60m in financial support
World.content:
The government is providing up to $60 million in financial support to Golden Bay Cement to ensure its Northland operations can continue.

The move was announced in a release to the NZX on Monday morning by Golden Bay Cement's owner, Fletcher Building.

Fletcher Building said the support reflects a specific, one-time response to an exceptional set of circumstances.

The release states the government has granted Golden Bay Cement up to $60m, but does not go into detail about the terms of the support or the form it will take.

Fletcher Building said the agreement recognises the strategic importance of domestic cement manufacturing to New Zealand's infrastructure supply chain and national resilience, and addresses the carbon cost disadvantage Golden Bay Cement faces relative to imported cement.

Golden Bay Cement's operations in Northland are the country's only domestic cement manufacturing facility, supplying about 60 percent of the cement used in New Zealand.

The financial support follows an independent assessment, which Fletcher Building said confirmed that without support, rising costs, including carbon costs, would force the plant to close and result in a shift to an import-only model from 2030.

Earlier this month, the Employers and Manufacturers Association issued a pre-election policy wish list calling on the government to consider financial incentives for industries deemed critical to the country's economic future.

Fletcher Building chief executive and managing director Andrew Reding said: "Without government support, increasing costs, including carbon emission costs that our competitors importing cement from overseas do not currently incur at the same level, would likely have required us to close the plant and move to an import-only model from 2030.

"Domestic cement production matters for New Zealand's resilience as much as for its economics."

As part of the announcement, Golden Bay Cement has agreed to invest $150m through to 2040 in continued operations, optimisation, resilience and decarbonisation initiatives at its Northland plant.

The investment will be phased over time and remains subject to Fletcher Building's normal capital governance and approval processes, with the specific programme to be agreed with the government.

In a separate statement, Economic Growth Minister Nicola Willis said the government "did not take this decision lightly" and undertook "rigorous" analysis of the situation, including the risk of setting a new precedent.

"Ultimately, we concluded that this is an exceptional case, which meets the very high bar needed to justify taxpayer support."

She said the country would have been left "massively exposed" to global supply disruptions if the Golden Bay factory shut down, as it was New Zealand's only fully integrated cement manufacturing plant.

"Cement has no practical substitutes. It is needed for the building of homes, hospitals, schools, roads, and other nationally significant infrastructure. Any reductions in its availability could bring essential construction and infrastructure development, and the economic activity they support, to a standstill."

Cabinet ministers considered the case in May and included a "limited envelope of funds" in the Budget's operating allowance as a "tagged contingency". They have since been in negotiations with Fletcher over the size of the grant and the conditions attached.

Willis said Cabinet also considered "alternative forms of regulatory relief" to the costs imposed by the Emissions Trading Scheme, but ultimately decided against that so not to undermine the scheme's integrity.

"In an uncertain world, the government has acted to secure New Zealand's national economic resilience," Willis said.

The ACT party - which has long bemoaned "corporate welfare" - said it supported keeping New Zealand's biggest cement plant operating.

But ACT's climate change spokesperson Simon Court said the need for taxpayer intervention proved the country's climate settings were not working.

"The government has loaded emissions costs onto local production, put it at a disadvantage against imported cement, and then handed Fletcher Building $60 million to keep the plant open.

"This is why ACT is campaigning to reset New Zealand's climate targets, so they work for New Zealand, rather than driving jobs and production offshore."

Fletcher Building said Golden Bay Cement directly employs more than 150 people and supports a further 450 jobs across the Whangārei district, underpinning the country's ability to build homes, hospitals, roads and infrastructure with locally sourced materials.

The Employers and Manufacturers Association said the grant to keep cement made in New Zealand should open discussions on other crucial industries.

Alan McDonald from the EMA said he did not want to pick favourites, but there were other industries the country needed for resilience, including steel, food and plastics production.

He said resilience gave New Zealand a buffer against overseas turmoil.

"If you're making grants or if you're doing things like changing the regulations, you need to make it explicitly clear why you're doing that and I think the prime minister did that when he said, look, this is an issue around national security, national resilience and it is a critical industry.

"And it's got a big role to play in the Northland economy as well as the New Zealand economy, because that's where all the product goes, 95 percent of it goes into New Zealand businesses and 60 percent of New Zealand domestic concrete use, is from that Fletcher's plant. So it's got a pretty key role. The other option is imports which aren't subject to our ETS (Emissions Trading Scheme)" he says.

World.title: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon speaks on Resource Management Act reforms
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says Resource Management Act reforms will make building infrastructure easier, faster and more affordable.

But opposition parties warn the changes could make the system more unworkable, and dilute environmental protections.

The select committee reports also pointed to an independent report finding the regulatory relief scheme it sets up could costs up to about $2b.

The reports detail 142 pages of changes to the government's proposed reforms to the Resource Management Act which includes a "regulatory relief" scheme that would see landowners compensated by councils for changes that affect them.

This included the removal of a clause requiring that use and development of the environment must be kept "within environmental limits".

Changes agreed by Cabinet would also mean existing agreements between councils and iwi - known as Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements - would be scrapped and replaced with "new narrowly scoped iwi participation agreements".

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop pointed to independent analysis showing that by 2050, the changes were expected to increase GDP annually by 0.56 percent.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. (File photo) RNZ / Calvin Samuel

"A cost benefit analysis estimates $13.3 billion in savings over 30 years through reduced administrative and compliance costs."

He said the removal of the existing iwi agreements had been because of the government's concern about the growing number of agreements, with the legislation previously allowing for existing agreements to continue but preventing new ones.

"Eight [agreements] existed when the Bills were introduced late last year. Since then, several dozen more have been agreed or initiated," he said.

"Instead, councils will have the option of entering into new narrowly scoped iwi participation agreements to record how iwi authorities will participate in statutory planning processes and processes required to give effect to Treaty settlement redress. Clear guardrails will be included in the legislation to prevent scope creep."

Changes to the purpose and goals of the legislation would "give stronger recognition to people's enjoyment of their land and the importance of food and fibre production", he said.

Bishop said the current Resource Management Act was too slow, too expensive and too unpredictable, and his overhaul would reduce unnecessary consenting, improve certainty, and make it easier for projects to get started.

He said changes recommended by the committee kept the basic concepts and architecture of the bills in place, while also ensuring stronger recognition of food and fibre production, "more workable" environmental limits, and put tighter safeguards around natural resource levies.

Asked about the cycle of repeal-and-replace or revision of resource management legislation, Bishop said National had "worked quite hard" with Labour and the Greens to find common ground, but "they just have a fundamentally different view about a range of things".

"It probably would have been possible to kind of find a bunch of things which everyone could kind of compromise on and create a bit of a muddle. I'm not about creating muddle. I'm about creating good law that serves New Zealand and and is in the national interest, and that's what we're doing."

He said the government was committed to getting the legislation passed before the election.

Labour in its minority report raised a number of concerns, saying the party supported the legislation - which somewhat resembled the bills it passed in the last Parliament - through its first reading in the hope that improvements could be made.

"Unfortunately, almost all policy decisions made during the select committee process have made the bills even more unpalatable and unworkable," the party said.

"The bills are an embarrassment-National could have worked with us to amend Labour's legislation but instead they chose to start again with something full of campaign slogans that will end up costing all New Zealanders and the environment."

Labour has pulled its support for the legislation.

The Greens and Te Pāti Māori raised similar concerns, particularly over what they said was the dismantling of environmental protections and the erosion of Māori rights and interests.

Regulatory relief

The regulatory relief scheme would see councils paying out to landowners where their property was

The reports show a ministry-commissioned report by consultancy Martin Jenkins puts the cost of that scheme at between $7 million and $1.99 billion - the huge range reflecting "that local authorities may take a range of approaches".

Labour said councils had told the committee the regulatory relief scheme would be expensive and they were "unlikely to be able to afford the cost of compensation, particularly in light of other government work that will further restrict councils' ability to raise funds," referring to the proposed rates cap of between 2-4 percent a year.

"Ratepayers would have to pay landowners for protecting something that is not their land - that is, biodiversity," Labour said.

The party said this was likely to result in a cottage industry of valuers

The Greens said they opposed the regulatory relief regime "in its entirety".

"We were deeply concerned that despite the only report the committee received on the matter outlining the novelty, uncertainty and potential for crippling costs to local councils and ratepayers of up to two billion dollars, that the committee proceeded to retain regulatory relief."

Green Party environment spokesperson Lan Pham singled out the regulatory relief framework as particularly irresponsible.

"This is not only going to cause a chilling effect in terms of councils simply not being able to meet these costs and therefore unable to protect things that matter to the community like biodiversity, but the costs could actually be much greater."

Bishop said regulatory relief was a "bottom line" for the government and the opposition parties disagreed with that idea.

"That hasn't been part of New Zealand law, but that's my point: we are deliberately changing the system. There's a range of other things they don't agree with either."

Green Party environment spokesperson Lan Pham. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Environmental protections

Labour's previous legislation aimed to set system-wide bottom limits for the degradation of the environment - for things like air pollution or water quality - based on scientific assessment.

The party said that although the legislation looked to retain that approach, the methods used would rely on national standards which "must not determine an ecosystem health limit itself".

"This does not make much sense and presumably comes from a desire to appease lobbyists who do not want nationally applied limits - yet they will likely get them through all the methodologies and minimum acceptable levels."

They also raised concern about the removal of the environmental limit clause.

"The Natural Environment Bill's goal of 'no net loss' of indigenous biodiversity is unworkable and lacks ambition. There is no definition of or baseline for measuring 'no net loss'," the party said of the replacement.

The Greens said this was dismantling the environmental protections under the current system.

They said the Minister now had discretion over whether developments needed to be within environmental limits or not, and another clause requiring caution when the science was uncertain had also been removed.

"The ecosystem health limits do not even have to be set at a level that would 'prevent significant or irreversible harm', in the way that human health limits must be," the party said.

The Greens also raised concern about timeframes for achieving interim limits had been shortened to five years, that Freshwater Farm plans were set to become self-certified, and mechanisms to address the overallocation of freshwater had been scrapped.

Pham said the changes to environmental limits were "beyond a joke".

"For the government to insist this is going to be an enduring framework, it's absolutely laughable," she said.

"They've not only removed the environmental limit thing, but they've also put in place essentially a shout-out to their favourite lobby groups - you know, big agriculture and aquaculture - and they've inserted them in the goals instead.

"This is an outrage and it certainly has no standing for a decent future for the country."

Te Pāti Māori said the bills appeared set to lead to poorer environmental outcomes, and environmental limits would be watered down.

"We disagree with the committee's view that 'measures to protect the natural environment remain the same or similar to the RMA'. Instead, the way the proposed system is configured, as two distinct bills, will affect levels of protection."

The party also said it rejected the idea of the new system providing more flexibility for the minister "and which relies on the Minister to set the appropriate amount of protection through national instruments".

Bishop agreed the changes moved away from environmental limits towards more of a cost-benefit approach.

"The setting of limits, on one level it's a scientific exercise obviously and you've got to be grounded in the science and the data and the evidence ... but the science and the data also has to be weighed against what the impact of setting those limits might be on society and the economy that we live in."

In a statement, Associate Environment Minister Andrew Hoggard (ACT Party) said the removal of audits from freshwater farm plans would support a "risk-based and practical approach".

"Only those farms undertaking activities with a higher identified risk to freshwater will be required to have a certified and audited freshwater farm plan," he said.

"Farm plans will be straightforward for most farmers to develop, giving them a practical way to identify, manage, and reduce the impacts of farming on their land and freshwater.

"We've heard from farmers that they want a system that's cost-effective, restores certainty, and provides environmental protections without the delays of the old RMA. I believe we've achieved that."

Conflicting goals and ministerial overrides

Labour and the Greens both pointed to the legislation being split into two bills, saying the overarching goals and purpose of them appeared to be at odds in some places.

Labour said there had been "no cogent explanation" for the separation.

"We suspect the reason is an attempt to end the 'integrated management' approach of the RMA. This is both dangerous and foolish. Our environment exists everywhere; including urban environments."

The party - which also had its reforms split into two - said its approach did not affect integrated management and had been split to ensure the spatial plans in their legislation could work with different infrastructure development approaches.

"These two replacement bills will result in a lot of duplication and cause unnecessary uncertainty and inefficiency."

Labour pointed to the "funnel" approach taken under the new version which would see lower-level planning overruled by higher-level planning, with national directions from the ministers able to override council plans, for example.

"When goals conflict with each other, the Minister will determine how the conflict is resolved - this is in effect the Minister establishing a hierarchy. This is a lot of power and leaves no wiggle room should a poor decision be made at the top of the funnel."

The Greens echoed the concerns of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, saying the powers granted to ministers had the potential for "endless church following every change of government", and with Te Rūnanga o Toa Rangatira which said the new system would be top heavy and centralise decision making.

Te Pāti Māori said it agreed with those who presented to the select committee that the two bills were "conceptually different and it is difficult to understand how they would integrate", and said the focus on enjoyment of land "promotes aggressive development" under ideological values of private property and extraction.

The party called for a goal to be added to the legislation of supporting and enabling enhancement of the natural environment, and that although the legislation appeared to retain responsibility for regional councils over freshwater allocation the government was looking to abolish those councils.

Iwi, Treaty changes

Labour said the bills' removal of a clause guaranteeing Māori culture and traditions within their ancestral lands, water, sites, wāhi tapu and other taonga was to be recognised and provided for would degrade Māori rights.

"There will be Treaty Settlement litigation around these changes that downgrade mana whenua participation because these settlements were reliant on the general settings of the RMA."

The party - whose response came before the government announced its plans to remove Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements - noted feedback that those agreements "assist with the timeliness and efficiency of the resource management system, so it is not in anyone's interests to remove them".

The Greens' report said Treaty obligations and the rights and interests of Māori had been "weakened and narrowed", pointing to the Waikato River Authority's comments to the select committee that the bills would be "eviscerating" Crown-Māori relationships.

The party said a proposed two-year timeframe - during which the bills would be enacted and post-settlement iwi organisations would need to agree on how their Treaty redress could have "the same or equivalent" effect was "a retrograde insult to iwi and hapū.

Bishop said the bills had retained an approach to provide for Māori interests "through a system goal and iwi participation in national instruments and plan-making rather than relying on broad, open-ended Treaty provisions."

He said the committee had made "helpful recommendations to clarify the obligations related to upholding Treaty settlements, which the Government has committed to do. We intend to provide further specificity regarding some settlements through an Amendment Paper".

Te Pāti Māori said the bills - even without the removal of the Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements - would not adequately allow for recognition and protection of Māori relationships with ancestral land, water and other taonga.

"This includes insufficient support and recognition for existing redress arrangements and planning arrangements established through existing Treaty settlements."

"Renegotiating Treaty Settlements, including the role and status of these in legislation is a serious matter that calls into the question the good-faith

keeping and undertakings by the Crown. It is a serious matter that requires care so as to avoid destroying the principle of Crown partnership with Māori," the party said.

Te Pāti Māori said hapū and iwi Māori should be engaged in decision-making from the start, rather than consulted with but being kept distant from decision-making, and said the existing Mana Whakahono agreements were insufficient - let alone that they would be replaced by narrower agreements.

Bishop said the Mana Whakahono agreements had been agreed to under a National-led government in 2015, and there remained "a range of mechanisms" for iwi and mana whenua to participate through the new system.

"It's about actually streamlining and simplifying what that looks like in practice, and we think it's a it's a good step forward."

He said both coalition agreements required that Treaty settlements be honoured "in a streamlined and effective way".

"And to be honest, iwi are some of the biggest users of Fast Track - for the reason that they are as frustrated as anybody else by the strictures of the RMA."

Climate change not recognised

The Greens highlighted the absence of the recognition of climate change in the bills, saying mitigation and adaptation should be a "core driver" of decisions.

"There is a risk the system may stay focused on responding after events, rather than driving the major shift needed to build long-term regional resilience ... This omission signals a misalignment between the Bills and New Zealand's national climate commitments and adaptation frameworks."

The party said land use planning fundamentally impacted greenhouse gas emissions and the effect of climate-driven weather events on communities.

World.title: Tribunal upholds three-match ban for Crows forward Darcy Fogarty
World.content:
The Crows have failed in their challenge to Darcy Fogarty's three-match striking ban at the AFL Tribunal, the panel finding Fogarty had time to decide to swing his arm at Sydney's Harry Cunningham.

Fogarty was charged after his high hit on Sydney's Harry Cunningham in the second quarter of Adelaide's game with the Swans at the SCG.

Cunningham jumped to try to get the ball deep inside Sydney's defensive 50, and Fogarty came in and caught the Swans player high.

Cunningham was ruled out of the game with concussion and will miss this week's match against cross-town rivals GWS.

The hit was assessed as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact.

The Crows argued that Fogarty's actions did not constitute a strike, and that even if they did it should be high, not severe impact.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, said the actions were careless and a breach of the duty of care. He said it was no surprise the incident resulted in a concussion.

The contact "was flush, it was direct, and it was on a player whose eyes were on the ball, so he was vulnerable in that moment".

"Cunningham goes to ground, he is visibly severely impacted," Woods said.

"He remains on the ground and requires the help of support staff to get up and exit the field."

After deliberating for less than 20 minutes, the panel returned and chair Jeff Gleeson said they were "comfortably satisfied" that Fogarty had indeed committed the offence of striking.

"Fogarty had time to consider how he would tackle Cunningham in those circumstances. He chose to do so by swinging his right arm forcibly in the direction of Cunningham's upper body and head," Gleeson said.

Fogarty will now miss Crows matches against Collingwood, Essendon and Richmond.

Look back at proceedings in our live blog.

World.title: Electric Tiwi football final sees back-to-back victory for Imalu Tigers
World.content:
Just minutes into the men's Tiwi Islands football grand final, black-and-yellow-clad supporters jumped the sideline fence and started storming the field prematurely, caught up in the excitement of their first goal.

The Imalu Tigers had not yet won the flag, but their devoted supporters never gave them a reason to doubt their hopes of securing back-to-back premiership glory.

Some Tigers fans were so passionate, they ran onto the field each time their team scored. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For the thousands of people living on the Tiwi Islands, Aussie Rules is much more than a friendly sport. It's a religion, and it all culminates on grand final day.

And for the many visitors attending the grand final game at Wurrumiyanga Oval on Bathurst Island, about 80 kilometres north of Darwin, it is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

Tapalinga Super Stars players and supporters hug after their win in the women's grand final match. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Each year, hundreds of tourists charter planes and catch ferries across to the Tiwi Islands to watch some of Australia's most promising upcoming AFL players battle it out in front of their home crowds.

This year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was one of them, becoming the first Australian leader to attend the game while in office.

The Tigers' opponents, the Ranku Eagles, also had plenty of supporters. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Victory for Imalu Tigers, Tapalinga Super Stars

Despite the opposing team, the Ranku Eagles, having the home-ground advantage, Melville Island's Imalu Tigers had the real upper hand, with droves of loyal supporters dominating the fence lines.

With reigning premiers Imalu only having lost a single game this season, it was always going to be a David-and-Goliath battle.

The men's grand final game was close early on before the Tigers pulled away. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

At half-time, it appeared the Eagles stood a chance, with the Tigers only narrowly in front by 12 points.

But in the third quarter, Imalu doubled their lead and soon became unstoppable.

For the second time in as many years, the Tigers took home the premiership cup, claiming victory in a thrilling 11.9 (75) to 7.8 (50) win against Ranku.

The winning Tigers team lifts the cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

One young Tigers fan told the ABC he hopes to be playing alongside his male relatives next season.

"It's the sport we grew up with and we just love playing it," he said.

"We love to beat people in it. It can get a bit rough, but yeah, we love it."

The Imalu Tigers had a dominant season in the lead-up to the final. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In the women's division, it was a tight contest until the end between the Tapalinga Super Stars and the Jikilarruwu.

It was tit-for-tat for much of the first half of the game between the two sides, before Tapalinga created some distance in the third quarter, leaving Jikilarruwu trailing by 10 points.

As the final siren sounded, cheers were met with tears as the Super Stars won the game, defeating Jikilarruwu Thunder & Lightning 8.9 (57) to 4.8 (32).

Player with the Tapalinga Super Stars pose with the premiership cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Huge day of art trade

Grand final day is the largest social event on the Tiwi Islands' social calendar, attracting hundreds of tourists to the community from around the country.

With art centres open amid the influx of visitors, for the islands' artists, the event also doubles as their biggest day of trade and an opportunity to pour money back into the local economy.

Artist Romolo Kantilla said it was also an important time to share their culture.

Romolo Kantilla says the grand final is an opportunity for Tiwi Islands people to share their culture through art. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's a very special day for Tiwi people, it's a big day and we get everyone from the mainland and it's a good time to come see the art," he said.

"The art is based on creation stories, totem and country.

"Art is always part of us Tiwi people."

World.title: Breakthrough win for Bernard Tomic after lean tennis times
World.content:
Bernard Tomic is back in the winner's circle with the Australian veteran cracking his first Challenger Tour title in eight years.

Reaching the final of the Lincoln Challenger tournament in Nebraska, the 33-year-old showed some grit to save a championship point before downing Estonian Mark Lajal 4-6, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3).

With a world ranking of 206, down from a career-high of number 17 back in 2016, Tomic started as the underdog against 23-year-old Lajal, who is ranked world number 159.

The crafty Queenslander nailed his service games, on target with 72 per cent of first serves as well as nine aces to cause headaches for his rival.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tomic also had a three-set battle to book his place in the final, downing American wildcard Spencer Johnson 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2.

It was his fourth Challenger Tour title, with the last coming in Mallorca in Spain in 2018.

A quarter-finalist at Wimbledon back in 2011 and former junior champion, Tomic recently lost in the second round of qualifying, falling to fellow Australian Chris O'Connell 6-4, 6-4.

On the main ATP Tour, his most recent singles title was at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu in 2018.

AAP

World.title: Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars
World.content:
You could see it in the Spanish players as they floated euphorically, each kissing the top of the trophy.

You could feel it from the fans in the stands as they straddled that blurry line between overwhelmed and overjoyed.

And you could hear it rumble through Spain, as a nation united through something which in reality should not mean this much but means more than almost anything else.

Nick Hornby summed it up best in his classic football-themed memoir Fever Pitch.

"I fell in love with football as I was later to fall in love with women: suddenly, inexplicably, uncritically, giving no thought to the pain or disruption it would bring with it."

Argentina felt its force too, the scenes of Lionel Messi in tears, fans distraught, Leandro Paredes losing control and lashing out.

Lionel Messi was crushed after the defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

In that moment they thought may a love like this never find me.

World Cup football can twist and torment, ripping out your heart and stamping on it till you feel like it can never be repaired.

It can also make you fall head over heels and erase all the hurt you ever felt before.

La Roja ruthless in victory

Spain captain Rodri takes in the magnitude of the achievement. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling )

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente spoke about it in his own terms before the semi-final against France, drawing on inspiration from Julius Caesar, and the idea of having to suffer to achieve great things.

And this was a game that was a struggle for all, it lacked the overall quality and excitement you might expect from a final.

Argentina was stubborn and produced heroic defending in the box, but again questionable roughhousing tactics, eventually resulting in Enzo Fernández's send off.

The reigning champions showed little initiative to create much of anything until the final minutes of extra time as their dream dissipated in the warm New Jersey air.

Spain, having only conceded one goal all tournament, and with 20 shots to two in the decider, might not have produced its flashiest performance, but it was its most important.

This is what La Roja has done throughout the past six weeks, control the ball effortlessly, win it back almost immediately, build pressure through well-organised and committed structures, and wait till late to put it all to bed.

Ferran Torres celebrates the goal that proved to be the decider in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. (Getty Images)

The Spaniards were particularly effective in shutting out Messi, who saw little of the ball and was quickly dispossessed or forced into errors when he did have it.

Turns out he can be stopped; it just takes the most exceptional defensive team of this tournament to do it.

The European Champions are now World Champions for the second time, unbeaten for 38 straight matches, a magnificent footballing dynasty growing with every game, becoming the first country to simultaneously hold the men's and women's World Cups.

"I'm so proud of this generation of footballers who have grown up with this philosophy, remained true to it, made it even better and set an example as a team and a family," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said.

"They're excellent, world-class footballers with exceptional talent. I'm very moved. Looking back and thinking about them, we've won everything, absolutely everything, with this generation of players."

Spain's collective triumph

Celebrations in Madrid will continue long after tonight. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Argentina is a team built around one player, the likes of whom we have never seen before.

Spain is built around a collective approach, filled with exceptional players, but all who work in harmony, allowing each other to shine in different moments.

Like Mikel Merino with his repeated winners off the bench, or Rodri holding the side together as the linchpin in midfield, or Ferran Torres with his vital assists, and today's match-winning strike.

"I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people, not just those of us that are here," Torres said.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

"A huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but as I said before, destiny was written."

It says so much that Lamine Yamal, 19, seen by most as Messi's heir, did not play much of an influential role in this final, or at any stage during the tournament.

Lamine Yamal did not quite have the breakout tournament some predicted. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

He was not a passenger, but was certainly not a conductor, and that can only breed even further confidence, and strike further fear into other nations, as he goes from boy to man.

This World Cup started slowly for Spain, a scoreless draw with the tournament's best underdog story, Cabo Verde.

But as the superstars like Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane, and Jude Bellingham took all the headlines and dominated social media algorithms, Spain was the quiet, conscientious achiever.

That all changed with the terrifyingly efficient dismantling of France in the semifinals, and now a completely deserved win in the final.

"This generation of players is an example for Spanish sport, for the Spanish youth," de la Fuente said.

"Together we are much stronger, and that is why we don't forget anyone."

A team forged through fire, built on discipline and togetherness, now enjoying its love story.

World.title: Tears streaming down his face, Messi leaves the World Cup stage a legend
World.content:
Lionel Messi had so desperately hoped his World Cup would end differently.

Tears running down his cheeks, a silver medal around his neck, his teammates in various states of depression, strewn around him like the detritus of some cataclysmic event as Spain roared amid garish golden confetti and an explosion of colour and joy.

Arguably the greatest player to ever grace a pitch was distraught.

It's impossible to know exactly what was going through his mind.

A decade earlier, on the same Metlife Stadium pitch where he was currently sobbing, Messi had tearfully decided to retire from international football after losing the Copa América final against enormous underdogs Chile.

The pain of that defeat was simply too much to bear for Messi, saddled with the expectation of a nation desperate to anoint him as Maradona's heir.

The world was the beneficiary as Messi reversed that decision.

Fans around the world have rejoiced at Messi's success. (Getty Images: Wang HE)

So too were Argentina, who claimed the 2021 Copa América title, the 2022 Finalissima and, most tellingly, the 2022 World Cup under Messi's leadership, cementing his legacy among his fellow countrymen for all time.

But once again in the New Jersey sunshine, Messi's tears were the defining feature for a generation of football fans.

Was this another tearful goodbye to the international stage?

Messi is 39 years old.

With 19-year-olds Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsí on the other side of the divide and winning for Spain, the next generation is not just arriving to force him out but has already arrived.

To play another World Cup in four years may be beyond even his mystic powers, even despite his impressive ability to adapt to the constraints his age has imposed on him.

The next generation, personified by Lamine Yamal, is snapping at Messi's aging heels. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

At this World Cup, Messi has walked for roughly half the time he was on the pitch, strolling and stalking for about 5 kilometres per game.

And yet, inarguably, no one player has had a greater role in his team's success than Messi has for Argentina.

His goals, eight of them, and his four assists dragged the defending champions through the group stage and the knockout rounds.

His ability to bend a game to his will, no matter the situation, made him seem nothing short of inevitable.

Despite all the walking, whenever Argentina threatened, the little magician was there in the heart of the action, conjuring and scheming and dragging his team home just when they needed him to.

His very presence seemed to inspire his teammates to feats beyond their capabilities, a totemic figure to rally around, his energy imbuing those around him with positivity and confidence and class.

Lionel Messi came close to lifting the World Cup for the second time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Tullio Puglia)

Against England in the semifinal, his two assists powered the Albiceleste to a famous victory in stoppage time.

Against Egypt, as his team faced elimination at 2-0 down, he provided the cross for the first and delivered the shot for its equaliser.

Against Spain in the final? It just didn't happen.

The fact that his tears only came after he had been given his silver medal was almost illustrative: No matter how late it got, Messi perhaps still had hope that he might somehow manage to influence the game in his favour.

He'd done it before, after all.

Only when Donald Trump laid the heavy silver slice of defeat around his neck did he realise there would be no more magic, that no amount of sorcery from his phenomenal feet could change history now.

Against Spain, the little master managed just 55 touches, none of which came in the Spain penalty area.

Lionel Messi was unable to stamp his authority on the contest. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

He was stifled as effectively as if Spain wrapped him in a blanket.

And his Argentina teammates simply couldn't back up their superstar when it mattered most.

Messi could not deliver the magical moment that his nation demanded.

It was telling that Argentina offered so little other than niggly fouls and angry words as opposed to the free-flowing football Spain occasionally managed when the mood took them.

Let's not beat around the bush: Argentina were woeful in this final.

Argentina didn't have a single shot on goal in the first 90 minutes of the game, the first time any team has failed to do so in a World Cup final.

Their first attempt on goal did not come until the 26th minute of extra time.

Lionel Messi had Argentina's first shot of the game, in the second half of extra time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

Their 25 total fouls resulted in seven yellow cards, one of which was a second that saw Enzo Fernández up-end Pau Cubarsí, making him the sixth player ever to be dismissed in a World Cup final.

Argentina's nefarious skulduggery was finally, belatedly, penalised by a referee brave enough not to stand for it.

Coach Lionel Scaloni said afterwards that his team "showed that we know how to lose" in his post-match press conference, but nothing could be further from the truth.

The Argentines thoroughly disgraced themselves after the game's conclusion, Leandro Paredes lashing out and sparking a minor brawl that ended with him shown a red card after the final whistle.

Fractious barely covers it.

If this is to be his international swan song, the landscape post-Messi may as well be post-apocalyptic, so absent of joy and light does it appear to hold.

Claudio Tapia, the president of the Argentina Football Association, knows how important Messi is to the team. (Getty Images: Andrew Harnik)

It was not Messi's fault that he could not have the impact on the game he might have hoped for.

Spain were able to successfully nullify a far better team than Argentina in the semifinal with their Rodri-led midfield dominance suffocating their opponents' creativity.

Messi simply didn't have the space.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

He was closed down as ominously and relentlessly as the ticking of the clock that will one day herald the end of his stellar career.

Messi couldn't muster the magic to help Argentina become the third men's team to win back-to-back World Cups.

It is not the finale that Messi might have envisaged.

But if this is to be his tearful sign off, fans will still look back at having been blessed by one of football's greatest of all time.

World.title: The 13 photos that summed up the chaos of the 2026 World Cup final
World.content:
It was a tournament where the football was magical, the off-field antics were questionable, and ultimately, Spain left the United States as the champions of the world.

A day after the utter chaos of the third-placed playoff between France and England, where 10 goals were scored, Argentina and Spain played things a little more conservatively — right up until the game exploded into action.

Here are the 13 photos that tell the story of the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.

1. The Fresh Prince of Barcelona

Teenage superstar Lamine Yamal arrives at the stadium looking like the coolest dude on earth. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

While much of the tournament had been focused on the more established superstar names like Lionel Messi, Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappé, teenager Lamine Yamal had floated under the radar for the World Cup passers-by.

Coming to the final having never lost a match where he had started for Spain, expectations were high on the 19-year-old as he came into the stadium. Would he be the hero Spain needed to overcome the perceived might of Argentina?

Whatever the pressure, he arrived looking like the coolest dude on the planet; calm, collected and rocking a style straight out of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

2. Smoke and mirrors

Mark Carney greets Donald Trump ahead of the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

All eyes turned to the skies before kick-off as US President Donald Trump made his usual subtle entrance into the arena, coming in low and fast in the Marine One helicopter.

Once settled in prime position in a corporate box on the wings, Trump was afforded the questionable chance to give the trophy a little pat as FIFA boss Gianni Infantino brought the iconic gold statue to Trump's seat.

Before that, though, there was the potentially awkward meeting between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, just a couple of days after Trump accused Canada of being "filthy" and "polluted" over its wildfire smoke that had blanketed New York in the lead-up to the tournament.

All-in-all, things seemed reasonably diplomatic, given Mother Nature had done her job to send the smoke packing just in time for the game.

3. America makes a double Buff

American announcer Bruce Buffer turns the World Cup into a blood sport briefly with his iconic introduction. (Getty Images: Sebastian Widmann)

In the most American moment of this entire game, event organisers decided that what this little old soccer match needed was a double Buffer.

Bruce and Michael Buffer, to be exact, the legendary ring announcers from every blood sport imaginable.

Flipping from one brother to the next, the pair excitedly announced that the game was "ready to rumble", in scenes not far off that time that soccer came to Springfield in The Simpsons.

4. The GOAT meets the rising star

Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal share a laugh together early in the match. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Looking a little less cool than when he arrived, but still the picture of confidence, Yamal made a beeline for Lionel Messi before the match to wish arguably the greatest player in history some luck.

It was a full-circle moment for the pair, who originally met on a photo shoot in 2007 when Yamal's parents won a UNICEF raffle to have Yamal photographed for a calendar with the then rising star Messi.

This time around, Messi's hair was a little shorter and his face a little more wearied, while Yamal was a little less nude.

5. The World Cup's Mariah Carey

Shakira performs during the half-time show, a spectacle one England footballing legend would go on to call "crap". (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Shakira was rolled out for the half-time show, with the Colombian star fast becoming to the World Cup what Mariah Carey is to Christmas.

She's just always there.

While her performance was fantastic, the rest of it — from Justin Bieber to Madonna to BTS — left a little bit to be desired.

So much so that English footballing champion Wayne Rooney didn't hold back with what he thought.

"I thought it was crap," he said on the BBC coverage.

6. The spectacular red card

Enzo Fernandez fouls Spain's Pau Cubarsi, leading to the Argentinian's second yellow card and a send-off. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

As soon as we all saw it happen on the TV, we knew that the photos were going to be spectacular.

And veteran Getty photographer Al Bello didn't let us down.

Rising Spanish star Pau Cubarsí was sent flying by Argentina's Enzo Fernández, but it was made all the more spectacular by Cubarsí really leaning into the flip.

Had Fernández not already had a yellow, it's unlikely he would have been sent off at all, but the red card made it all the more dramatic as the scores stood at 0-0 heading into the death.

7. Hydration break goes to a new level

Spain's Dani Olmo takes the hydration break to the extreme as he utilises the sprinklers to cool down. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

Two things have been major talking points during this tournament: it's been bloody hot and the hydration breaks have been bloody irritating.

So it was fun to see the two come together in the final regular-time break of the tournament, as the Spanish players took advantage of the sprinklers to cool off.

Was it the trick that won them the World Cup? Who's to say. But almost certainly yes.

8. Free kick wipes a goal

Nico Williams reacts after his goal was marked off for a foul that was immediately obvious on the replays afterwards. (Getty Images: Carl Recine)

In a moment of brilliance, Nico Williams looked to have won it for Spain when he slotted a goal past the keeper to make it 1-0 late.

But the referee called it back. There was a free kick somewhere in the mess of bodies in the box.

In live action it wasn't immediately clear where the free kick was. On replay, it still wasn't totally clear.

But on the fifth or sixth watch: yeah, no idea.

Williams was furious, and rightfully so.

9. Deadlock ends in headlock

Nico Williams gives Ferran Torres a little chokehold celebration after Torres scored the winning goal. (Getty Images: Nick Potts)

Go back to the very first photo at the top of this story and you can experience the majesty of the Ferran Torres goal that broke the game open.

Hair blowing in the breeze, his teammates running in behind him, the fans screaming and cheering in ecstasy.

And then Williams decided to choke Torres for some reason.

Angry that he wasn't the hero after his goal was wiped? An in-joke that we don't know about?

Who knows. But it made for an odd scene in an incredible moment.

10. Tears of a legend

Lionel Messi slumps to the ground after the final whistle, in what will likely be the football legend's last World Cup game. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

Small in stature but grand in legacy, Messi cut a forlorn figure after the final whistle.

His tiny body huddled in the middle of the massive stadium was enough to make anyone feel sorry for the attacking superstar.

His place as the greatest player the game has ever seen would have been secured had he managed to drag his teammates to victory, but even Messi couldn't get his countrymen through the incredible defensive wall that Spain had built.

11. Infantino chases after Trump

Rodri prepares to lift trophy as Gianni Infantino attempts to move Donald Trump out of frame. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

Trump had made headlines this time last year when he joined Chelsea on stage for the celebrations in the Club World Cup final, despite the apparent confusion of the players.

This time there was surely no way that Trump would be caught right in the middle of the pack as the Spanish players lifted the most coveted trophy in world sport, right?

Well, kind of. This time Trump wandered right across stage as Infantino pivoted left, leaving the FIFA boss to scramble after the US president, with the pair awkwardly caught in the team celebration photos.

On the broadcast, you could hear someone say "they'll crop him out" in an unexpected, but funny, hot mic moment.

12. Utter heartache for Argentina

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez shows his dejection as the ceremony for the winners gets into full swing. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez had been immense through the World Cup.

But as Spain lifted the trophy, the Aston Villa keeper let the emotions flow, caught by the camera as he sat on the sidelines thinking about what might have been.

It was a reminder of what this thing, this silly, epic, immense mess of a game, means to the people who play it.

13. The love of a mum

Lamine Yamal's mum races out onto the field to celebrate the victory with her son. (Getty Images: John Todd)

In the end, all we really want is the hug of a mum who's proud of you.

And that's what Yamal got as his mum, Sheila, ran onto the ground to give her son a big old cuddle.

Having given birth at just 16 years old as an immigrant from Equatorial Guinea, Sheila's story is the one that really captures the essence of the World Cup.

Not the championship rings or corporate boxes. Not the powerful men in powerful suits making powerful political moves.

A mum with a dream for her son to shine on the world stage.

This was the moment that really mattered.
